articles.title_orig: Huawei in collaboration with China Unicom and Peking University Win 2026 Leading Lights Award, Advancing 5G Free-Mobility Private Network to a New Era in Higher Education
articles.title_zh: Huawei in collaboration with China Unicom and Peking University Win 2026 Leading Lights Award, Advancing 5G Free-Mobility Private Network to a New Era in Higher Education
articles.content_orig:
Light Reading, the globally recognized authority in communications industry media, has announced the winners of its 22nd Leading Lights Awards. The " Peking University CARSI 5G Free-Mobility Private Network " jointly submitted by Huawei, China Unicom, and Peking University, stood out among 151 shortlisted projects worldwide, winning the Outstanding Use Case: Network Security & Resilience Use Case Award. This recognition marks a new chapter in the application of 5G private networks within the higher education sector. As AI-driven research and digital campus life accelerate across universities, faculty and students are placing greater demands on campus networks. Previously, access to internal campus resources relied on the traditional internet + VPN model. This approach carries security risks, including data leakage and account compromises. It also delivers a poor user experience, with high latency, unstable connections, and repeated login prompts. These shortcomings no longer meet the needs of modern universities. At the same time, conventional 5G private networks suffer from lengthy service provisioning cycles and elevated management costs. They are ill-suited to the high personnel turnover typical of academic institutions. Breaking through the security and experience bottlenecks of traditional VPN models  and enabling faculty and students to access campus resources securely and conveniently from anywhere outside campus  has become a shared priority in university IT modernization. In response, Huawei and China Unicom have jointly introduced the " Peking University CARSI 5G Free-Mobility Private Network " solution  directly addressing the security risks and experience gaps faced by faculty and students accessing campus intranet resources from off-campus locations. The solution delivers a seamless upgrade in campus resource access: no VPN cluster, no annual licence planning, no SIM approval workflow. Zero-Touch Onboarding: Built on CARSI (Campus Authentication and Resource Sharing Infrastructure), the federated authentication system of CERNET (China Education and Research Network), faculty and students can activate the 5G Mobile Private Network using their existing university credentials. A single phone  without changing SIM cards or phone numbers  provides seamless access to the campus network, eliminating the need to install or repeatedly start and stop VPN clients.
Light Reading judges commented: This architecture  The university, not the operator, remains the sole identity authority  carries significant replication potential. The solution leverages the existing CERNET infrastructure without requiring large-scale campus network modernization, and can be rapidly deployed across the universities already connected to CARSI. The 5G Free-Mobility Private Network is now officially live at Peking University, covering the core scenario of off-campus access to campus intranet resources. Faculty and students enjoy seamless campus network access with a single phone  no SIM change, no number change. During a three-month pilot involving over 100 faculty and students, more than 70% of respondents rated the new service as superior to traditional VPNs in stability, latency, and ease of use. Service provisioning time was reduced from several days to seconds, and the private network deployment cycle was compressed from approximately three months to three weeks. This solution provides a replicable model for 5G private network deployment across the universities connected to CARSI, with the potential for international extension. Looking ahead, Huawei will continue to deepen joint innovation with China Unicom across more universities  focusing on 5G-Advanced, 6G, network security, and AI-native networks (AIDN)  to advance the network-as-a-service vision in the education sector. By helping quality educational resources transcend campus boundaries, Huawei is committed to contributing a China-based solution and Chinas wisdom to global university digital transformation. FAQs: Q1: What is CARSI? CARSI (Campus Authentication and Resource Sharing Infrastructure) is a unified identity authentication platform built by CERNET (China Education and Research Network). It now covers over 1,000 universities across China, enabling cross-institutional identity mutual recognition and resource sharing. Q2: What problem does the 5G Mobile Private Network solve? Traditionally, faculty and students must install VPN clients to access campus intranet resources  a process that introduces security risks and delivers a frustrating experience. With the 5G Free-Mobility Private Network, users reach the campus network seamlessly through China Unicoms 5G service. No new SIM card, no number change, no additional setup is needed. The system also resolves the management overhead caused by frequent faculty turnover and the continuous cycle of student enrollment and graduation, automatically terminating access when users leave the university. Q3: What application scenarios does the 5G Mobile Private Network currently support? The 5G Mobile Private Network is now officially live at Peking University, enabling faculty and students to access campus intranet resources using 5G data from off-campus locations. In the future, this solution can be rapidly replicated across the more than 1,000 universities connected to CARSI, and can extend to overseas universities through eduGAIN.

articles.title_orig: A Swiss retired pastor witnesses the life reality in Lebanon
articles.title_zh: A Swiss retired pastor witnesses the life reality in Lebanon
articles.content_orig:
Rev. Serge Fornerod brings forty years of international experience in development, public administration and ecumenical relations. Following the fall of the Berlin Wall, he managed aid and development programmes in Eastern Europe and later contributed to international relations within the umbrella organisation for Switzerland’s Protestant Churches. Since retiring in 2023, he has remained active in ecumenical networks, supporting the Foundation for Aid to Reformed Protestantism and the John Knox International Reformed Centre in Geneva.
Rev. Fornerod is a former member of the World Council of Churches central committee. He is also involved in preparations for the 2027 Francophone Christian Forum and researches the spread of early Christianity, particularly in the East . He took time to reflect on a new blog he has created that documents his experience at the Near East School of Theology (NEST) in Beirut, and his thoughts on the key to Christian unity.
What inspired you to start your blog to document your experience at the Near East school of Theology in Beirut?
Rev. Fornerod: Through this blog, I ’ d like to share some reflections and convictions I have formed over the last few years within the ecumenical movement and in my personal life.
The first is that when a parent is unwell, seriously afflicted by illness for years on end, telling them – as I often read on social media from “ good Christians” and – sorry to say – even church leaders – “ we ’ re thinking of you” or “ our prayers are with you” only helps the person saying it. Potentially, such phrases eventually add to the parent ’ s suffering, leaving them feeling even more alone. Someone who is ill, someone in despair, someone rendered invisible and voiceless by misfortune and injustice – that is someone you visit. You must take the time to listen and truly understand what the other person is going through. I believe that the Christian West (in general) takes its responsibility towards situations of suffering in the world and the churches experiencing them far too lightly. If we truly believe that the faith and life of churches elsewhere in the world concern us directly, then we must talk less about “ solidarity” – when this has no impact on our daily lives – and take more action. "Witness is with-ness.”
The second message is that in the world of ecumenical relations or relations between churches, the key to unity is not primarily dialogue, but listening. In light of everything that has been happening in the Middle East for decades, but especially since October 2023, I wanted to come and listen to the voices of Christians on the ground. Back home in Switzerland – though I fear this may also be the case elsewhere – I had the impression that opinions were quickly set in stone regarding who the culprits and who the victims were. My limited experience of the Middle East so far has very quickly made me feel uncomfortable in the face of so many so-called certainties, which in fact conceal unacknowledged political and cultural preconceptions. I wanted to give more space to the concrete reality of people ’ s lives and the experiences of the churches here. To listen, one must step back from one ’ s own context; one must be prepared to remain silent for a long while; one must be prepared to place trust first and foremost in the person who is in that situation; and one must draw closer, physically as well. The NEST faculty, with its international and ecumenical identity—driven by young people and researchers rather than officials (whom I also meet frequently and with pleasure!)—strikes me as an ideal place for observation, networking, and gathering information.
What do you hope others gain from you sharing your learning pilgrimage?
Rev. Fornerod: I hope to raise awareness amongst as many readers as possible of the need to take the time to reflect and find out more before forming an opinion on what is happening in this region. But also to show that it is relatively easy to obtain insightful background information on people ’ s experiences and the living conditions under which people here must face these new challenges. Action is easily possible and effective. When you consult the local sources here, it is striking to see, for instance, how many people in Israel oppose the destruction campaign of the Israeli army and how many people in Lebanon are engaged in bringing help. And lastly to hear that, for the Christians here, there is quite simply no alternative but to hold their heads high and carry on fighting day in, day out for dignity and justice – whether in their personal lives, their country ’ s politics or international justice. And if there is a Westerner present at the gatherings where people pray for this here, then perhaps that might do a little good.
Can you describe the way in which you are engaging with people?
Rev. Fornerod: One of the very nice and positive aspects of “ just being here,” free enough to engage with people is indeed to see the ease, spontaneity, hospitality, and kindness with which the Lebanese respond to your presence, however surprised they might be. It is a life lesson to see that, in an international, national, economic, and social situation as complicated and desperate as the one here, people naturally manage to draw strength from and take pleasure in making you happy.

articles.title_orig: S&P 500 futures rise as big banks set to kick off earnings season: Live updates
articles.title_zh: S&P 500 futures rise as big banks set to kick off earnings season: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
S&P 500 futures rose early Monday after the major averages posted a winning week, as investors looked ahead to a busy week of earnings results and inflation data.
Futures tied to the broader market climbed 0.1%, while Dow Jones Industrial Average futures rose by 26 points, or 0.06%. But Nasdaq 100 futures turned negative, reversing earlier gains, and were last seen 0.12% lower.
Wall Street is coming off a winning week for the major averages, as a rally in tech stocks helped investors shrug off higher oil prices and yields. The Dow and S&P 500 each posted their second positive week in three, while the Nasdaq Composite netted its fourth straight week of gains.
President Donald Trump told reporters over the weekend that he was considering joining Saudi Arabia in its fight against Tehran-backed Houthis in Yemen after another deadly attack on Riyadh's international airport. The remarks raised the prospect of escalating tensions in the region.
Meanwhile, Trump announced an 'energy ceasefire' between Russia and Ukraine over the weekend.
Oil prices initially fell, before rebounding higher after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Moscow had already violated the ceasefire . West Texas Intermediate futures were 0.7% higher at $92.49 a barrel, and Brent crude was up 0.8% at $105.59.
Investors hope the third-quarter earnings season will help stocks power through the Middle East turmoil. By all estimations, the incoming results are expected to be strong. According to FactSet's John Butters, the S&P 500 is set to post 29.6% earnings growth in the quarter. That would be the fourth straight quarter that the broader index posts above-25% earnings growth, thanks to the strength of the AI data center buildout.
But it's what managers say that will matter more to investors, given the uncertainty around how businesses and their customers are contending with higher fuel and borrowing costs.
"Investors have kind of narrowed in on some of the important aspects," said Brian Leonard, portfolio manager of Keeley Gabelli Small Cap Dividend Fund (KSDIX). "Can this company withstand what's happening? Pass along, continue to grow margins, and the future is going to be better than the most recent past."
The reporting season will ramp up in earnest this week with the big banks, with Bank of America, Citigroup, Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan Chase, Morgan Stanley and Wells Fargo all expected to post results this week.
Key inflation data is also due out this week, with the September consumer and producer price indexes due out Wednesday and Thursday, respectively.
Across the Atlantic, the pan-European Stoxx 600 was 0.41% higher. The U.K.'s FTSE 100 added 0.56%, and the Italian FTSE MIB gained 0.65%. Germany's DAX rose 0.49%, and the French CAC 40 moved 0.11% higher.
In Asia, South Korea's Kospi fell 3.65%, while the small-cap Kosdaq dropped 4.83%. Australia's benchmark S&P/ASX 200 gained 0.76%. Mainland China's CSI 300 closed 0.68% lower. Markets in Japan were closed for a holiday.
— CNBC's Terri Cullen contributed to this report.
Oil prices reversed course Monday, moving higher amid skepticism over U.S. President Donald Trump's so-called 'energy ceasefire' between Ukraine and Russia.
Futures for international benchmark Brent crude for December delivery were last seen 0.95% higher at $105.68 a barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures for November ticked 0.86% higher to $92.64 per barrel. Prices on both benchmarks had fallen by around 1.5% earlier in the session.
Oil reversed its losses after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy welcomed such a ceasefire, but warned Monday that Moscow must do the same.
Europe's carmakers moved higher Monday morning after the EU and China reached an agreement to cut the number of hybrid cars China exports to the bloc.
The Stoxx Europe 600 Automobiles and Parts Index was 0.96% higher by 3:47 a.m. E.T.
Shares in French carmaker Renault were up almost 3.1%, while multinational Stellantis , which owns Jeep, Chrysler, Maserati and Peugeot, added 2.7%.
French automotive parts suppliers Valeo and Forvia also advanced 2% and 1.2%, respectively.
South Korea's Kospi fell 3.65% to 6,384.24 in choppy trade, while the small-cap Kosdaq dropped 4.83% at 849.19
Hong Kong's Hang Seng index was marginally higher in its last hour of trade on Monday, while mainland China's CSI 300 closed 0.68% lower at 4,287.98.
Australia's benchmark S&P/ASX 200 gained 0.76% at 8,783.20.
Markets in Japan were closed for a holiday.
Volkswagen said it delivered 6 million vehicles in the first nine months of the year, down 9% from the same period in 2025. The decline steepened in the third quarter, when deliveries tumbled 14.3% year-on-year.
The fall was driven mainly by plunging demand in China, where third quarter sales dropped 38.5% year-on-year to 405,800.
In North America, third-quarter deliveries fell 5.8% to 232,000 vehicles. Deliveries in western Europe slipped 2.8% to 780,000, but central and eastern Europe bucked the trend, rising 1.4% to 135,000.
"The sharp decline in the overall market in China remains an industry-wide challenge," said Martin Sander, a member of Volkswagen's extended executive committee for sales.
Sander said VW was seeing a "significantly accelerated trend towards all-electric vehicles" in its home market. Higher fuel prices have helped drive the shift, he added, with all-electric models now making up about 40% of Volkswagen's European order book.
Shares in the German car giant were up 1.4% in early dealmaking.
European stock markets opened higher on Monday, with most regional sectors and major bourses moving higher shortly after 8:00 a.m. in London (3:00 a.m. E.T.).
The pan-European Stoxx 600 gained 0.45% shortly after the opening bell.
Europe's banks led gains, adding 1.39%, while car makers notched a 1.11% gain in early dealmaking. Utilities were up 0.94%. Oil and gas companies led losses, shedding 0.30%, with tech stocks off by 0.28%.
Italy's FTSE MIB led the continent's bourses, advancing 1.21%. Germany's DAX gained 0.40%, as the U.K.'s FTSE 100 rose 0.38%, with France's CAC 40 up 0.33%.
European stocks are set to start the new trading week in positive territory.
Stoxx 50 futures were up 0.65%, with the continent's main bourses all expected to open Monday's session higher.
Italy's FTSE MIB is set to lead gains, rising 0.68%. The German DAX is seen opening 0.58% higher, while France's CAC 40 is seen up 0.51%. The U.K.'s FTSE 100 is seen 0.32% higher ahead of the market open.
The South Korean won appreciated to a two-year high against the greenback on Monday, hitting 1,332.88 per dollar.
According to Bloomberg , heavy selling of the greenback by local companies as well as on lower oil prices helped lift the won. The currency has gained 7.4% so far this year against the U.S. dollar.
Currency traders will keep a watch on the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank this week, with the Bank of Korea Governor Shin Hyun Song in attendance.
Thailand will narrow its budget deficit to below 3% of its gross domestic product within a few years, Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas said, as the government leans on private investment to drive growth with public debt edging toward its official ceiling.
"I am trying to lower our fiscal deficit year by year," Nitithanprapas said in an interview with CNBC on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok.
The country's deficit for the current fiscal year is reportedly pegged at 4.3%, while public debt stood at nearly 68% of GDP in August , against a 70% ceiling set under Thailand's fiscal discipline framework. The finance minister has indicated that the government could raise the cap if needed.
Nitithanprapas disagreed that Thailand risked testing the limits of fiscal sustainability and a credit-rating downgrade, saying that the government was watching rising global bond yields and will stick to its medium-term fiscal framework.

articles.title_zh: Oil prices volatile after Trump claims ‘energy ceasefire’ in Ukraine war
articles.content_orig:
Ukrainian president tells Warsaw security conference that Putin ‘does not read Truth Social’
Trump announces partial ceasefire in Ukraine war as Zelenskyy says deal is ‘news to me’
Addressing the conference virtually, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy commented on Trump’s “sudden but very important” energy ceasefire declaration over the weekend.
He said it is clear that Putin “does not read Truth social”, the site that the US president posted his ceasefire declaration on.
As we have been reporting, Russia’s strikes continued despite the announcement. “Immediately after the post Russia launched a targeted strike on a power plant in Kharkiv, causing further damage to our energy system,” Zelenskyy said, noting that Ukraine is facing a wave of escalatory attacks from Russia ahead of the winter.
In other news, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government came under renewed pressure this morning after a key minister from its junior coalition partner, the SPD, unexpectedly quit.
Baerbel Bas, labour minister and co-leader of the centre-left SPD, cited personal reasons for her resignation, saying she needed time to grieve after the death of her stepdaughter.
But she also criticised Merz’s conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which is in crisis after heavy recent electoral defeats, notably the far-right AfD’s victory in Saxony-Anhalt last month .
“I must unfortunately note that the public attacks against me – regrettably including those from within the ranks of our coalition partner – have continued to intensify during this difficult time for me personally,” Bas said. She will reportedly replaced as labour minister by Alexander Schweitzer, one of the SPD’s vice-chairs.
The resignation comes amid turmoil for the government, which is grappling with a sluggish economy and low poll ratings.
The Nobel Prize for economics has been awarded to Robert E Hall and Michael Woodford, for their work on the “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”.
[Reminder: As we flagged earlier , Woodford was among the predicted winners – he’s one of the architects of modern forward guidance, the idea that central banks can control the economy through influencing public expectations about inflation, rather than just through interest rates.]
The S veriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel is worth 12 million Swedish kronor (£900,000), plus the glory of course, and the knowledge that every pronouncement you make now comes with the authority of a Nobel Prize winner.
You can read more in our live blog here:
Zelenskyy said Trump’s energy ceasefire announcement caught him by surprise, first hearing about it through the media.
double quotation mark No, we did not know about that. We’ve learned that from the media as well that the president of the United States has secured an energy ceasefire.
I thought perhaps their team reached out to the Russians. I think they are in constant contact in a certain format.
During a Q&A with journalists, Zelenskyy said he’s ready to find ways to alter the constitution to be able to hold elections “very quickly” if a “full” energy ceasefire is implemented. He said this may require “difficult (legislative) solutions”.
“As of now, it is very difficult because of the security level in our cities and villages and communities. It is also impossible now because of our military. More than a million people who must vote – but how will they vote while being on the frontline?”
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the country has been under martial law, meaning elections are suspended.
But Donald Trump , under pressure ahead of the November elections, said on Saturday it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war and blaming him for high diesel prices in the US, even though they have largely been affected by his war on Iran.
The Baltic states have reacted sceptically to Donald Trump’s diesel deal with Vladimir Putin and the US president’s so-called energy ceasefire.
Lithuania’s foreign minister, Keʂtutis Budrys, said Trump’s diesel deal with Vladimir Putin was not helpful. Budrys said:
double quotation mark This deal doesn’t help, neither the crisis of the oil products, nor the unity within the transatlantic community when it concerns Russia. And it is not the European way. Our way is to increase pressure because we already see how it works.
His Estonian counterpart, Margus Tsakhna, gave a similar assessment: “I don’t think that in real life this diesel deal is actually going to change anything on the oil price or diesel price in the market.” He drew a link between US domestic politics and the upcoming midterms.
Estonia’s foreign minister was also sceptical about Trump’s self-proclaimed energy ceasefire. Tsakhna said:
double quotation mark [The] energy ceasefire is not working as President Zelenskyy has said as well. And Russia is really putting more attacks against Ukraine. So what we need to do in Europe, we need to focus on what we can do.
He cited EU sanctions against 1,600 Russian individuals and entities that are due to be signed off later today by the bloc’s 27 foreign ministers, the largest ever-listing of its kind.
Zelenskyy says Ukraine is waiting for the specific details of the “conversation” between the US and Russia after the latest peace talks.
On Friday, negotiators from the US, Ukraine and European countries also held talks in Miami aimed ⁠at ​reaching agreement on a unified peace proposal ​in the coming weeks that could be presented to Russia.
Zelenskyy said in his address that the energy ceasefire could be a “major step” toward ending the war if Trump makes sure Putin honours it.
The Ukrainian leader says Kyiv needs the US to apply real pressure on the Kremlin, not sanction relief or “concessions”.
Zelenskyy said Russia is trying to tactically use the period of cold weather against Ukraine , targeting the country’s power plants and power grids.
“This winter if Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire, we will respond,” Zelenskyy said, adding that he supports Trump’s energy ceasefire proposal, but vows that if Russia doesn’t agree to it, then Ukraine “will respond”.
“If Russia wants us to stop our long-range strikes against its oil refineries and oil exports, then Russia must stop its strikes against our energy system and critical infrastructure, and stop killing our people. This is only fair,” Zelenskyy said.
“We are ready to respect an energy ceasefire if Russia is ready to do the same. We agree, if they agree. And we have already shown that we mean it. Last night, Russian oil refineries were not burning but at midnight a Russian jet powered Shahed strike against a production facility in Ukraine.”

articles.title_orig: Fontaines D.C.'s decadent, dystopian vision of our time
articles.title_zh: Fontaines D.C.'s decadent, dystopian vision of our time
articles.content_orig:
"We're in a glorious age of distraction," says Grian Chatten, the lead singer of the Irish band Fontaines D.C. "I just want to make people really feel things about the world that they live in. Because it's such a terrifying world at the moment." Elizaveta Porodina hide caption
At almost exactly the midpoint of our conversation about the fifth album made by his band, Fontaines D.C. , Grian Chatten said to me, "It's an interesting time to be a self." We'd been talking about the themes on Dopamine Chamber , which comes out on Friday, Oct. 16, and could serve as a soundtrack to the era we live in now, what Chatten calls our "glorious age of distraction."
It's also an interesting time to be a rock band in the mainstream, and that's where Fontaines D.C., which formed in 2014, definitely lives these days. The Irish quintet's next tour has them in stadiums and arenas, and the one guest on Dopamine Chamber is pop's universal "it" girl, the Spanish singer Rosalía .
The 2024 album Romance took Fontaines to another level, earning them two Grammy nominations and their best sales ever, with hits like the sweet and earnest " Favourite ." Following it up, Fontaines didn't take the easy way. Instead, they explored new sounds to create a captivating sonic travelogue that somehow connects the decadent beauty of old Europe with the narcotic ethereality of cyberspace.
Things really gel for Fontaines on Dopamine Chamber . Using vintage synthesizers and studio effects, the band builds on the hypnotic energy that has always been its calling card to make something huge and seductive and haunting. I was lucky to speak with Chatten about his evolution as a storyteller and his place within a band that's always growing, but which remains utterly true to itself.
This conversation has been edited for length and clarity. You can listen to an extended version of this interview, plus a conversation with Fontaines D.C. bassist Conor Deegan, in the audio at the top of this page, or in the NPR Music podcast .
Ann Powers, NPR: This album comes at a kind of a milestone point in the career of Fontaines. You're playing these huge venues now, and emerging as a truly superstar band at this point. I don't know how you feel about that, but I wondered if the fact that your audience has grown so much influenced the direction this album went in. I mean in a very positive way that you seem to be kind of aiming for a monumental sound to connect with this new level of your career.
Grian Chatten: You know, the fact that there is an audience that has grown and continued to listen and moves with us, I certainly feel like it's a collaboration between ourselves and our audience, if you know what I mean. It's like, through each album, we're kind of getting closer in a spaceship to this black hole or something like that.
Well, I hope you don't fall down the black hole, because then I won't be able to hear your music anymore.
Maybe you'll have already heard it, years ago.
Oh my god, you're blowing my mind. On Dopamine Chamber there's this experience of displacement that you're getting at, and you sing a little bit about [immortality], the hubris of someone who thinks they might live forever. So how does this new album relate to those themes?
I feel like I'm writing about a metaphysical place or an imagined place that represents or reflects where I think we might be headed. And I want to do it with all the trappings and all the details of the things that I find affecting in my life: things that scare me about the future and things that warm me about the past, things that kind of comfort me. I like the idea that it's almost like a spectrum. You know the Italian singer Mina ? She came through in the '60s and she maintained a career for decades after, she's still alive, and I'm really in love with her music. And that informed and kind of armed the sense of humanity that I wanted to imbue this record with.
And then on the [other] end of the spectrum is kind of a darker, more industrial … dare I say the cliche word now: dystopian. That's people like John Mouse, who, I don't know if I [should] plug him, or like Depeche Mode and New Order and like Disintegration by The Cure . I wanted the record to feel like it was a distinct place where you walked through and you felt both of these things interacting with each other so that you could kind of get a sense of what we're losing and where we might be headed towards, you know?
Well, a dystopian story is only effective if there is a strong sense of humanity. I think about a film like Under the Skin . I mean, if Scarlett Johansson isn't there in her beauty, it doesn't have the same effect. You need to have that in any dystopian [setting]. You have to have that depth of emotion, and physical sensuality to counter and be in a dynamic relationship with machines. So maybe that's what you're going for?
Bjork does it. She's got such a beautiful, emotive and human voice. To have that piercing through the industrial music on, like, Homogenic , she had it sewn up there. I really like the feeling in Ridley Scott's films. You know, they might be isolated in a vacuum in space like how many thousands of miles or light years away from planet Earth, but they're still falling in love with each other and they've got a job to do, and a mission.
I [heard] something you said about your process to Jools Holland . You said you like to write on toilet paper because it has to go in the bin, which I thought was a little bit of that Irish humour, perhaps, but also the idea for a writer to say, "I want to cling to a notion of ephemerality about my own process." Does that free you up? The idea that your lyrics, your words, your poetry moves through space and might dissolve?
I think it's going to sound painfully, incredibly Irish of me but it's very it's important for me to recognize the transience of my own ideas and my own work, particularly before I kind of actually kind of cast them in stone in the recording and put it out there, you know, into the into the astral plane. You know, I think it's important to consider the fact that each thing I write is doomed or is to be forgotten unless I decide to actually sit down and do something about it. And I think what that does — I don't know if this makes sense — but what that does to me as a writer is it builds up my confidence in myself as the generator of the ideas, as opposed to kind of becoming beholden to one lucky burst of an idea.
But then, you know, you're writing about digital spaces on this record, and there's a sense of, everything lasts forever in digital space. I wonder if that was something you were thinking about.
That very concept of everything lasting forever immediately just makes me feel sick with how meaningless that renders everything. Like, things acquire their meaning because they're ephemeral. People love each other fiercely because they know that they're going to get old and die, you know?
A thread on this record is cinema, the idea of life as a movie. But also I know you're very inspired by films. Let's just talk about "Marianne" for a minute. I know it was inspired by the Netflix version of The Talented Mr. Ripley with Andrew Scott. When you watch something like that, how do you translate it into a song?
For me, often it takes me a while to process things.
It's not like I watched the first couple of episodes and started writing things down. It kind of ruminated for a while until I realized that the feelings I wanted to express, I was kind of like, "Oh yeah, that's how I felt when I was watching that thing." And then I kind of, at least emotionally, just thought about Andrew Scott's performance and that cinematography, the lingering shots of Italy and someone running away and, I suppose, trying to replace a human soul with material possessions and a life that isn't your own. For some reason [it was] profoundly resonant for me.

articles.title_orig: The world's hottest AI stock market has gone cold
articles.title_zh: The world's hottest AI stock market has gone cold
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
South Korea went from the world's hottest stock market to its coldest in months.
Taiwan is pulling ahead as investors broaden AI bets beyond memory chips.
Asia's AI trade is expanding from memory chips to the broader hardware supply chain.
South Korea's stock market has gone from the world's hottest to its coldest in just a few months.
The Kospi, the world's best-performing major stock benchmark in the first half of 2026, has since fallen about 24%, making it the worst-performing major market in the second half. It's still more than 50% higher this year.
The AI trade isn't losing its appeal. But investors are increasingly looking beyond South Korea's memory-chip giants to companies with broader exposure to the AI hardware boom.
In July, analysts at GlobalData.TS Lombard pointed out that much of the earnings growth at Korean memory-chip makers came from higher memory-chip prices. By contrast, TSMC and Japanese chip-equipment makers relied more on advanced manufacturing and process expertise, giving them more durable growth prospects, they added.
Taiwan's Taiex has climbed about 7% in the second half of the year, taking its year-to-date gains to about 70% as investors broaden their bets across the AI hardware supply chain.
South Korea's rally was driven largely by Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, whose soaring memory-chip profits made them among the biggest winners of the AI boom. Together, the companies account for more than half of the Kospi, leaving the market unusually dependent on a single segment of the semiconductor industry.
Even blockbuster earnings are no longer enough to excite investors. Last Thursday, Samsung forecast a nearly ninefold increase in quarterly operating profit, yet its shares have fallen for two straight trading sessions.
The reversal followed months of extraordinary volatility. The Kospi plunged 22% in July, its worst month since the 2008 financial crisis, before rebounding 18% on the month's final trading day for its biggest one-day gain on record. The swings triggered multiple market-wide circuit breakers as leveraged bets on chip stocks amplified the moves.
Young South Koreans flooded social media with memes and dark humor about their battered portfolios, while regulators tightened rules on leveraged single-stock exchange-traded funds after concerns the products had fueled speculation.
Trading has cooled sharply. Turnover has dropped 70% from its late-May peak, while foreign investors have continued pulling money from Korean equities.
The shift didn't happen overnight.
Even before Korea's selloff, investors were debating whether the next phase of the AI boom would continue rewarding memory-chip makers or broaden to companies with exposure across the semiconductor supply chain.
Taiwan appears to be benefiting from that shift. Its market offers exposure across AI infrastructure, from advanced chip manufacturing and packaging to servers and networking equipment.
That includes TSMC as well as companies involved in advanced packaging, servers, networking equipment, and other AI infrastructure.
The Taiex outperformed the Kospi by more than 23 percentage points in the third quarter, as Taiwan's benchmark gained nearly 4% while South Korea's plunged more than 19%.

articles.title_orig: Preview: No Asian stars makes Santiago more open
articles.title_zh: Preview: No Asian stars makes Santiago more open
articles.content_orig:
It is one of the last major competitions of the outdoor season in para archery but arguably one of the most open.
Santiago 2026 is the penultimate stage of the inaugural Hyundai World Para Series, following on from Bangkok , Nove Mesto and Ahmedabad , with the circuit closing in Dubai in December.
However, the action in Chile's capital city promises to be one of the most open fields of the year, as all of Asia's top archers will not travel to South America due to the first day of the Asian Para Games overlapping with the individual finals on Sunday 18 October.
This includes athletes such as India's Paralympic medallists Singh Harvinder and Sheetal Devi and Singapore's Ken Swagumilang, the runner up of the Beijing 2025 Asia Para Archery Championships .
They may be big hitters in their respective categories, but what their absence does do is pave the path for some of the best para archers from the Americas to win world ranking points - where the vast majority of entries for Santiago come from - and potentially create new stars.
That still may be a tall order in the W1 men and women categories, however, as world number ones Jason Tabansky and Sarka Pultar Musilova are shooting at the Peñalolen National Training Center, as is the second-ranked Samuel Molina in the para recurve men discipline, who won stage three in Ahmedabad earlier this year.
Host nation Chile has the largest squad, with 12 total competitors, whilst countries outside of the Americas have travelled as well, including three from Musilova's Czechia and four from Romania.
What’s happening? The fourth stage of the Hyundai World Archery Para Series from 14 to 18 October at the Peñalolen National Training Center in Santiago, Chile.
What’s at stake? World ranking points.
Who’s competing? 52 archers from 10 nations.
What’s the story? No Asian archers means Santiago is one of the smallest para competitions of the year but offers the chance for the best archers in the para compound, recurve, visually impaired and W1 categories from the Americas and Europe to win world ranking points, as well as birthing new stars from those regions.
Watch live footage of the finals on 17-18 October with a subscription to archery+ .
Live scores will be available on the World Archery website, with coverage across World Archery’s digital platforms throughout the competition.

Competition at the Santiago 2026 World Para Series begins with qualifying on Thursday.

articles.title_orig: A defining moment for Central Asia
articles.title_zh: A defining moment for Central Asia
articles.content_orig:
Uzbekistan’s landmark National Investment Fund IPO is more than a capital-raising exercise. It is a test of international confidence in Central Asia’s economic future, governance standards and ability to attract long-term global investment
The recent IPO of Uzbekistan’s National Investment Fund (UzNIF) marks a turning point for Central Asia. With $2.4bn in assets and a valuation of $1.95bn – implying a discount of roughly 20 percent – the offering is intended to do more than raise capital. Uzbekistan wants to establish its credibility as an investment destination. But the IPO also represents a regional milestone. For the first time, a Central Asian country is offering international investors a diversified basket of strategic assets through a London Stock Exchange listing overseen by a major global asset manager. At its core, the UzNIF IPO will test whether international investors are willing to view Central Asia not just as a risky frontier market, but as a region with real growth potential and reliable governance frameworks.
The IPO’s structure reflects a sophisticated understanding of investor concerns. The valuation discount compensates for perceived country risk, and the choice to place the fund under the management of Franklin Templeton alleviates fears of political interference and lack of transparency. Meanwhile, an initial $300m commitment from anchor investors, including BlackRock and Franklin Resources, provides a stable base for secondary-market activity. Taken together, these measures directly address many of the longstanding barriers to investment in Central Asia. Yet the significance of this IPO extends well beyond the mechanics of the deal itself. The interest it generated highlights Central Asia’s transformation over the past three decades. What was once a peripheral region has become one of the world’s most remarkable emerging-market growth stories.
Architects of growth The numbers speak for themselves: over the past 25 years, Central Asian economies have grown at an average annual rate of 4.8 percent, far outpacing the global average of roughly 3.4 percent. Over the same period, the region’s economy has roughly tripled in real terms. The past five years have underscored the region’s resilience. Despite the Covid-19 pandemic, supply-chain disruptions, and escalating geopolitical tensions, Central Asian economies have continued to deliver solid growth. Uzbekistan, for example, has maintained annual growth rates above five percent, supported by strong domestic demand and structural reforms, including gradual liberalisation. Kazakhstan, though more exposed to commodity-price fluctuations, has relied on its resource wealth and institutional reforms to maintain macroeconomic stability. Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan, for their part, have benefited from remittance inflows, infrastructure investment, and greater regional integration.
Geography is another major advantage. Long viewed as a constraint, Central Asia’s location is increasingly viewed as a strategic asset. As geopolitical instability and conflicts such as the Iran war force governments and businesses to seek alternatives to traditional maritime chokepoints, the region is emerging as a critical overland corridor connecting East and West. The so-called ‘Middle Corridor,’ which links China to Europe through Central Asia and the Caucasus, is rapidly becoming a major commercial artery, accelerating investment in rail, road, and port infrastructure. Against this backdrop, Uzbekistan’s integration into global capital markets is a defining moment for the region. The UzNIF IPO is not an isolated deal, but an early step toward building a regional equity-market ecosystem.
By consolidating minority stakes in 13 state-owned enterprises across sectors such as transport, energy, telecommunications, utilities, and banking, the fund gives investors an opportunity to invest in the Uzbek economy through a single market vehicle. More importantly, it introduces a market-based valuation benchmark – something the region has historically lacked. Over time, this could generate positive spillover effects, reducing the informational asymmetries that have long limited inflows of foreign investment.
Emergence accelerated The financial implications could be significant. If successful, the UzNIF model could pave the way for a wave of IPOs by individual companies, both in Uzbekistan and across Central Asia. It may also accelerate the emergence of hybrid financing structures that combine public assets, private capital, and international management expertise to fund large-scale infrastructure and energy projects. In a region where limited access to financing has prevented strategically important investments, such mechanisms could unlock opportunities that have remained out of reach for decades. For example, capital mobilised through vehicles like UzNIF could be directed toward large-scale, cross-border projects such as Kyrgyzstan’s Kambarata-1 Hydropower Project or the Rogun Dam in Tajikistan. Crucially, the credibility of the UzNIF project rests on governance. By entrusting the fund’s management to Franklin Templeton, Uzbekistan has effectively signalled its willingness to subject state assets to international standards of transparency, accountability, and fiduciary discipline.
This also highlights a major risk. The IPO’s success will not be judged solely by initial demand or short-term price performance. Investors will watch closely for any indication of political interference, policy inconsistency, or erosion of minority shareholder protections. In that sense, UzNIF’s IPO is as much a political test as it is a financial one. What is at stake is not simply the success of a single fund, but the potential repositioning of an entire region.
If the IPO succeeds, it could help establish a new narrative in which Central Asia is defined less by risk and more by economic opportunity and financial returns. The question now is whether Uzbekistan can translate its current economic momentum into a new regional reality.

articles.title_orig: World Bank jobs council urges 'crisis-era' employment support measures as IMF warns of AI ‘tsunami’
articles.title_zh: World Bank jobs council urges 'crisis-era' employment support measures as IMF warns of AI ‘tsunami’
articles.content_orig:
BANGKOK — Policymakers are moving from debating whether artificial intelligence will hit jobs to issuing stark warnings about AI-led disruption and recommending measures on cushioning the fallout.
International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned on Monday that artificial intelligence was hitting the global labor market like a "slow-moving tsunami," with young graduates first in line to be knocked down.
"People to worry about, first and foremost, [are] young people that are coming into the labor market," Georgieva said at a panels on Monday. "Normally, they would get into these routine, repetitive jobs and then grow up the ranks. But if they're gone, I don't think any young person wants to be a barista in a coffee shop as ... professional future."
Speaking on the same panel, Singapore President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, who co-chairs the World Bank's Jobs Council, called for governments to make "crisis-era" support measures a permanent tool for getting young people into work.
What governments did during the Covid-19 pandemic and, in some cases, the global financial crisis "now has to be thought of not as a crisis measure, but as part of the structural, the menu of structural policies," he said.
That means working with the private sector, and incentivizing firms to hire fresh graduates, because "the first rung in employment, your first job upon graduation, is now seeing less demand," Shanmugaratnam said.
The remarks show that policymakers are moving from debating whether AI will disrupt jobs to deciding how to cushion the fallout, at a time when rapidly aging populations, particularly in Asia, already threaten to shrink workforces.
World Bank President Ajay Banga, estimates 1.2 billion young people will turn 18 over the next 15 years, and the private sector, which already generates 75% to 85% of jobs in any country, will have to absorb most of them.
Governments' role is to make that possible, he said, by building infrastructure, setting policy and "de-risking" private capital, or lowering the risks that deter investors from putting in money at scale. "It is private capital that creates jobs," he said.
The IMF estimates that about 40% of jobs worldwide will eventually be "augmented, downgraded or eliminated." Exposure is about 60% in advanced economies and 23% in low-income countries, she said, but poorer nations are not better off: that is "just because AI is further away."
The squeeze is clearest in tech, Shanmugaratnam said, adding that in the U.S. "for the first time in a century, demand for graduates has gone down," with the wage premium for a college degree also shrinking. Without action, a cohort of graduates loses more than a year of skills: "you lose trust in the future," he said.
AI has also been the major driver propping up growth this year. AI-related investments and trade have lifted output in a handful of economies, helping keep global expansion near 3% despite an energy supply shock, Georgieva said.
"Love it, hate it, or fear it. It [AI] is here, and we are already seeing the first wave of impact," Georgieva said, estimating AI adoption could lift growth by 0.5 percentage point to 1 percentage point in advanced Asia, and 0.2 percentage point to 0.8 percentage point in emerging Asia. At the high end, that "would more than offset the loss that comes from aging population," said Georgieva.
Shanmugaratnam cautioned that growth alone may not necessarily deliver job creation. China, India and developing Southeast Asia are "growing quite well, but job creation is weak," he said, and AI "is going to widen that divergence if we are too passive about it."
AI-induced job displacement, however, will come "task by task," he said, "and that gives us time" — provided workers can learn on the job and universities shift toward applied training.

articles.title_orig: Nations of the world have forgotten responsibility toward the less privileged
articles.title_zh: Nations of the world have forgotten responsibility toward the less privileged
articles.content_orig:
Children are served their school meal at a school in India in this 2017 photograph. (OSV News/Courtesy Mary's Meals)
The glory of God is being fully alive; this has given us the impetus to live life to the fullest. The changing face of the universe has impacted the responses of us humans, maybe for the worst. Though to be honest a few good people do struggle to keep alive some values which are so essential for the coexistence of all living organisms.
There was a time when we experienced interdependency and we happily lived by it. Over the years what has been frightening is the role of power in our lives. Instead of being facilitators we have become owners, holders of power — the remote control lies in the powerful.
Nations of the world have forgotten their responsibility toward the less privileged.
The Global North and Global South are socioeconomic and political classifications, not strict geographic ones. The North includes wealthy, developed nations (U.S., Europe, Japan, Australia), while the South encompasses developing regions (Africa, Latin America and most of Asia). The South holds roughly 85% of the world's population but only accounts for about 40% of the global GDP.
The Global North and the Global South are often defined in terms of their differing levels of wealth, economic development, income inequality and strength of democracy, as well as by their political freedom and economic freedom, as defined by a variety of indices. Countries of the Global North tend to be wealthier, and export technologically advanced manufactured products, among other characteristics.
In contrast, countries of the Global South tend to be relatively poorer, and heavily dependent on their largely agrarian-based economic primary sectors. Some scholars suggest that the inequality gap between the Global North and the Global South has narrowed since globalization. Others contend that the Global South has instead become poorer vis-à-vis the Global North.
According to this data there is an urgent question which we need to ask: Who then is responsible for this lopsided development? Due to longstanding wars with the Middle East, the Global North is drastically cutting funds for the welfare of poorer nations. This is going to affect the Global South in a very serious manner. The poorer nations will be denied welfare services that were being carried out by the nongovernmental sector.
Being in the social sector, I hear many painful stories of retrenchment of staff, as funds are not available. What has shocked me most is the cutting of staff at the U.N. office here in Patna-Bihar. So many of the agreements which have been signed by countries will no longer stand valid. In other words, who will we question? The global world is becoming less accountable. We are losing our ethos as nations who once reached out as a moral responsibility to the less privileged.
What is more frightening is what I hear — people who have worked in this sector in big international agencies for three decades saying what's next. One said: "I can't sleep at night. I have a young family. What's their future? I am in midlife now, I can't all of a sudden change my profession. Where will I get a job? How will I become self-employed?"
This is a nightmare for many of the youth of our country. India being a young nation, unemployment being high, industries being insufficient, basic necessities of life are going beyond the reach of the common person. In this present scenario, I am asking myself, do we have a role to play?
Vulnerability is on the increase, life is becoming fragile. The question before us is how will we differentiate; what will we prioritize and at what cost? These are soul-searching questions each human person has to face every day. When peace of mind is not possible, when one is weighed down with heavy burdens — how does one live? The big question today is, are we moving backward? Has development in the real sense of the word affected us?
The fragility of security seems to have become a privilege of a very few, those in administrative services or political parties. These are the ones who make decisions which will affect the whole of humanity into the future.
I am reminded of the talisman of Mahatma Gandhi:
Whenever you are in doubt or when the self becomes too much with you, apply the following test. Recall the face of the poorest and the weakest man whom you may have seen and ask yourself, if the step you contemplate is going to be of any use to him. Will he gain anything by it? Will it restore him to a control over his own life and destiny? In other words, will it lead to swaraj [freedom] for the hungry and spiritually starving millions? Then you will find your doubts and your self melting away.

articles.content_orig:
Grey Bull Rescue CEO Bryan Stern talks about global terrorism threats and warns an attack that dwarfs 9/11 could hit America if the U.S. does not learn more about its adversaries.
The FlyDubai attempted hijacking shows the U.S. and its allies are still using outdated counterterrorism assumptions against increasingly sophisticated enemies, a U.S. rescue expert and 9/11 first responder warns.
"They’re good at chess," Bryan Stern, chairman and CEO of Grey Bull Rescue, told Fox News Digital on Monday, saying the radical ideology behind the FlyDubai attack is a ringing "bell" for global aviation security and Western counterterrorism strategy.
"And we’re, if we’re lucky, playing checkers – if we’re lucky – and I would argue we’re not even playing checkers that well."
TERROR CELLS INSIDE FOREIGN AIRLINES 'CERTAINLY A POSSIBILITY,' RETIRED PILOT WARNS
Grey Bull Rescue's Bryan Stern speaks to Fox News Digital about the world guarded against the next 9/11 terrorist attack. (Fox News Digital)
Stern, whose global nonprofit conducts evacuations from war zones and hostage situations, said the thwarted FlyDubai attack by "an angry, radicalized, Sunni bad guy" is showing just how far behind our enemies we are in this post-9/11 world.
"They understand us significantly more than we understand them," Stern, who has been "hunting the bad guys" for 30 years, said. Stern said the U.S. has to understand the "asymmetric warfare" as well as the increasingly sophisticated enemy does.
"The reason why a football coach watches game tapes is not to watch his own team play, it's to watch the bad guys play," he said. "We gotta start watching some game tapes."
AMERICA BUILT A FORTRESS AFTER 9/11. THEN THE THREAT STARTED HIDING IN PLAIN SIGHT
Captain Smit Machchhar, the Indian pilot who was attacked on a FlyDubai plane heading to Israel last week, has been hailed globally as a hero. (Israel Foreign Ministry)
Stern is intimately in tune with the playbook on the ground in war zones, including the Middle East and Iran.
"We conduct these operations in these places still to this very day," he said. "We're actually on the ground, meaning I know people in Hezbollah, I know people in the Taliban. I know people in ISIS. I know people in ISIS-K. I've met with radical jihadi weirdos and whack jobs personally."
United Arab Emirates investigators have described the incident aboard FlyDubai flight FZ1073 as an attempted terror attack after the co-pilot allegedly stabbed the captain and tried to hijack the plane , which was carrying more than 170 passengers and crew, most of them Israelis. Australian authorities have also said a counterterrorism unit is investigating the co-pilot’s links to Australia.
INTEL CHIEF WARNS OF 'EVOLVING' THREATS AS TERROR GROUPS NOW 'RECRUIT THEIR AGENTS ONLINE'
"The bad guys are completely not afraid. They're completely emboldened. They have got the whole world to hate Israel, the whole world to hate us," he said. "It's a tough problem."
Since the incident, there has been renewed vigilance in aviation and foreign airline security. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu instructed his national security council to review security procedures for foreign civil aviation to Israel, while Vice President JD Vance said Monday that flight security procedures are also under review in the U.S.
IRAN COULD MOVE SHADOW WAR IN A DANGEROUS DIRECTION, EXPERTS WARN ON BACK OF TWO POSSIBLE TERROR ATTACKS
"I was asked years ago when I was still with the government," Stern said. "A team was put together and the question before the court was, if you were al-Qaeda , what would you do?"
"What I came up with was ... I would get 19 hijackers, and I would hijack four airplanes, and I would fly them into buildings in America, and then issue a communique that said: 20 years of war, you are no safer today than you were before – that for TSA, and Homeland Security, and Iraq, and Afghanistan and all the different things, you are actually no safer, America, today than you were before," he said.
"We're seeing, sadly," he lamented, "that academic hypothetical situation has now become a reality, or certainly a possibility."
Despite President Donald Trump and the War Department's best efforts to rid the world of terrorist groups – and Iran of nuclear weapons aspirations – "you can't bomb your way into peace," Stern claimed.
'CRAZY' FLYDUBAI LANDING EXPLAINED BY ISRAELI PILOT, WHO OFFERS STEPS TO PREVENT FUTURE CRISES
"They have been in holy war against us," he added. "We have now engaged in a holy war against them."
"On Ramadan, the holiest month of the year in Islam, on the first day, which is the holiest day, we detonated the leader of the Shia faith, the Ayatollah," he said, likening it to "if somebody assassinated the pope on Easter Sunday while he's giving mass at the Vatican."
Stern explained that rooting out ideological terror in the U.S. is more complex than ever, because even if the border is not open any longer under Trump, the terrorist networks might be infiltrating America with U.S. passport holders – making them tough to investigate, if not impossible to spot before an attack.
NETANYAHU PRAISES HEROIC BYSTANDER IN BLOODY COCKPIT ATTACK FOR PREVENTING ‘ANOTHER 9/11’
Stern likened it to the release of the suspects in the RAF Fairford investigation – potential terrorist passport holders walking free.
"Until I actually squeeze the triggers, I haven't committed a crime yet," he said. "Now give me an airplane."
Stern noted that the nature of America's adversaries in the current conflict is unlike what the U.S. faced in places like Afghanistan.
"We need to remember we are very used to shooting people like the Taliban who don't know what plumbing is – who literally for years lived in caves until we showed up and gave them stuff," he continued. "The bad guys that we're talking about today are extremely sophisticated. They are extremely resourced, extremely resourceful. They're very intelligent, they're very smart, and they're very good at what they do."
IRAN UNDER SCRUTINY AFTER PLOT FOILED NEAR UK BASE USED BY US MILITARY
"The Persian Empire is the only empire of empires who have been all the way on top and all the way defeated at the bottom – six times," he said. "They're looking at us going, you're 250 years old. How adorable. You're cute, America."
Stern predicted that some day even 9/11 — which he survived as a first responder — is ultimately going to be dwarfed.
"What will happen, probably is we'll get attacked – just like 9/11, we'll get attacked," he said. "We'll say, 'Oh my God, how did this happen?' People will wake up."

"I promise you there will come a time, it will be, you know, June 26 or whatever, where we're gonna read about 9/11, and we're gonna say, 'Wow, that wasn't so bad, only 3,000 died,'" he warned.
"Why? Because we have created a holy war. We have now gotten into the crazy. And you cannot unring that bell."

articles.title_orig: Kazakhstan Receives IJF Flag Ahead of 2027 World Judo Championships
articles.title_zh: Kazakhstan Receives IJF Flag Ahead of 2027 World Judo Championships
articles.content_orig:
By Dana Omirgazy in Sports on 12 October 2026
ASTANA — Kazakhstan has officially received the International Judo Federation (IJF) flag to host the 2027 World Judo Championships in Kazakh capital on June 7-14. The event will be the country’s second time hosting the sport’s premier global competition and an important step toward the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
Photo credit: Press Service of the Kazakhstan Judo Federation
The handover ceremony took place in Baku, Azerbaijan, during the World Championships. IJF Secretary General Lisa Allan presented the flag to Kuanyshbek Yessekeyev, president of the Judo Federation of Kazakhstan, following its transfer by Elnur Mammadli, vice president of the Azerbaijan Judo Federation, reported the federation’s press service on Oct. 10.
The 2027 championships will serve as an important stage in Olympic qualification, with athletes competing for ranking points toward securing places at the Los Angeles Games.
Yessekeyev said hosting the event reflects the international community’s confidence in Kazakhstan’s ability to organize major sporting competitions. He added that the federation would focus on meeting IJF organizational standards and preparing the national team for competition.
Kazakhstan first hosted the World Judo Championships in 2015. The country has also hosted the Qazaqstan Barysy Grand Slam from 2023 through 2026, an international tournament on the IJF calendar that contributes to Olympic qualification.

articles.title_orig: From commando to world champion: Toman Kumar’s second act
articles.title_zh: From commando to world champion: Toman Kumar’s second act
articles.content_orig:
Four years after losing his leg in a blast during a counter-insurgency operation, Toman Kumar stood on top of the podium in Gwangju as a World Archery Para champion.
Now, as he prepares for his first continental Games at the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Para Games , the Indian compound archer is facing another major challenge – and doing so with a remarkable transformation behind him.
Forced to adapt to a completely different life after his injury, he found a new direction through archery and, less than five years after taking up the sport, has established himself among the world’s leading para archers.
“I had never thought I would do sport after the injury,” said the 31-year-old Kumar, who comes from Nawagaon, a rural village in Balod district in the central Indian state of Chhattisgarh. “I had never played sport before either. Nobody in my village played sport.”
Kumar joined India’s Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) in 2017 before undergoing training with its elite Commando Battalion for Resolute Action (CoBRA) unit in 2021.
That same year, he was caught in an improvised explosive device blast during a Naxal operation and had his left leg amputated.
The physical injury was only part of the challenge.
“Initially, I went through a lot of depression,” Kumar recalled. “But when I came to Hyderabad, I saw people with disabilities that were more severe than mine. That motivated me.”
Kumar had travelled to Hyderabad, in the southern Indian state of Telangana, for rehabilitation and to receive an artificial limb. It was there that he met coach Pankaj Singh , a meeting that would change the direction of his life.
“Toman had lived a completely normal life before the accident. As a commando, he was extremely fit, had taken part in operations and undergone extensive training,” Singh said.
“Suddenly he had to deal with such a major change. That creates a lot of difficulties.”
Singh saw in Kumar the physical and mental qualities that could translate to archery and spent nearly two hours persuading him to give the sport a chance.
His introduction was gradual, beginning with just an hour at the training ground before the sessions became more regular and his scores started improving.
The early days were not easy.
At one of his first local tournaments, Kumar watched young children drawing their bows while he struggled to draw his own.
“He did not know that everyone had different draw weights,” Singh said, explaining that the children were using bows of around 20-30 pounds while Kumar’s was considerably heavier.
For someone accustomed to the physical demands of commando training, the experience came as a surprise.
“He saw the smaller children shooting and thought, ‘They can shoot and I cannot.’ That gave him a bit of a shock,” Singh recalled. “Then he said, ‘I will do it.’”
Singh’s message to his new athlete was equally straightforward: “Your job is to shoot. The rest is my responsibility.”
What followed was an intense training period.
Kumar had entered archery much later than many of the athletes he would eventually face internationally. Singh knew they could not recreate years of experience, but they could try to close the gap by putting in more hours.
“I used to tell him that if we trained an extra two hours every day, we would be putting in many more hours over a month than someone who was taking a break,” Singh said. “Slowly, we could cover the gap created by five or 10 years of experience.”
After being selected at the SAI centre in Aurangabad, a city in the Indian state of Maharashtra, Kumar began competing against archers without disabilities.
At the CRPF departmental trials, he finished second in the open category with a score above 700 before claiming silver at the All India Police Championship.
“For a para athlete to compete at the All India Police level and win a medal was a historic achievement,” Singh said. “It was, as far as we know, the first time this had happened in our organisation.”
Kumar later shot 703 at the National Games, further underlining his ability to compete alongside other elite archers.
Singh believes Kumar’s fitness and discipline from his commando days helped him progress quickly. He was already calm under pressure, physically strong and accustomed to demanding training.
The progress soon carried onto the international stage.
Kumar made his World Archery Para Championships debut in Gwangju in 2025 and reached an all-Indian compound men’s final against seasoned Paralympic medallist Rakesh Kumar .
A technical failure forced Rakesh to retire from the match, handing Kumar the world title barely a year after taking up the sport.
“I have put in a lot of effort to practise,” Kumar said after the victory. “We had camps. I practised day and night to get here. So, I’m very happy with the result.”
He also partnered world number one Sheetal Devi to compound mixed team bronze in Gwangju.
The success continued into 2026.
At the opening stage of the Hyundai World Archery Para Series in Bangkok , Kumar beat Australia’s Rio 2016 Paralympic Games bronze medallist Jonathon Milne 146-142 to claim the compound men’s individual title.
He also won mixed team gold with Devi, the Indian pair beating Indonesia 153-146.
Kumar and Shyam Sunder Swami later won compound men’s doubles gold at India’s first international para archery event in Ahmedabad , beating Iraq 152-139, while Kumar added individual and mixed team bronze medals.
Kumar is now preparing for his next major challenge – his first continental Games, the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Para Games .
With experienced compound star Rakesh missing selection after finishing fourth at the national trials, the reigning world champion will lead India’s compound men’s challenge alongside Swami at the fifth Asian Para Games.
Kumar is also expected to partner Devi in the compound mixed team event.
Devi won the compound women’s individual and mixed team titles at Hangzhou 2022 , the latter alongside Rakesh. This time, she and Kumar will look to keep the mixed team crown with India, having already tasted success together on the international circuit.
For Kumar, however, preparations are not only about scores and technique.
The former commando admits nerves still arrive when he steps onto a major competition field.
“You feel a little nervous in the first round. You are scared and wonder how it will go, whether it will go well or not,” he said. “But once you keep going, you get more comfortable and it becomes easier.”
Breathing exercises and meditation have become part of his mental preparation.
“During that time I just do some breathing – take a deep breath,” he said. “I meditate quite a lot.”
Asked what archery has taught him most, Kumar’s answer was simple.
“Hard work,” he said. “Earlier, I used to work much less hard, but in this sport, you have to work much harder. Another thing is that you have to concentrate. A lot.”
And despite his rapid rise from novice to world champion, Kumar knows exactly what he wants to sharpen before his Asian Para Games debut.
“I need to improve my focus.”
For someone whose life changed in an instant four years ago, it is another step forward – from rehabilitation to a bow, from a first local tournament to a world title, and now towards his first Asian Para Games.
The next chapter starts in Aichi-Nagoya. With thanks to Neha Buswal .

articles.title_orig: North Korea fires multiple ballistic missiles towards the sea
articles.title_zh: North Korea fires multiple ballistic missiles towards the sea
articles.content_orig:
North Korea has fired multiple ballistic missiles towards the sea off its east coast, South Korea’s military says.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) said one of the missiles launched from the Pyongyang area flew more than 900km (559 miles) on Monday. The joint chiefs did not specify how many missiles were detected.
Japan’s Deputy Defence Minister Takashi Koyari said at least two missiles were launched 17 minutes apart and landed in waters outside of its exclusive economic zone.
Koyari said the first missile flew about 220 kilometres (137 miles) and the second more than 910 kilometres (565 miles), following an “irregular” flight path and suggested it may have been a hypersonic weapon.
South Korea’s presidential office said that Pyongyang’s repeated missile launches violate United Nations Security Council resolutions, urging an immediate stop.
Monday’s launches add to heightened tensions on the Korean Peninsula, as both countries have been conducting weapons tests.
JCS spokesperson Jang Do-young said the latest missile launch appears to be a show of force, days after South Korea tested its own hypersonic weapon.
On Thursday, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung oversaw the country’s first test-firing of a hypersonic missile, a rare public showcasing of a missile test by a South Korean president.
Lee’s office said the hypersonic weapon, once fully developed, would enhance South Korea’s ability to strike key targets by surprise in the “Korean Peninsula theatre of operations”.
On October 3, North Korea also tested a hypersonic intermediate-range missile designed to evade missile defences in South Korea and Japan.
Last week, Seoul demanded an apology after a landmine blast wounded three soldiers in the Demilitarized Zone between South and North Korea. A joint South Korean-UN investigation concluded that two landmines were planted by North Korean forces about a year ago. Pyongyang dismissed the claim and accused South Korea of provocation.
Prior to the border mine blast, Seoul said it was conducting “preliminary coordination efforts” to facilitate dialogue between Pyongyang and Washington.
Lee pledged to reopen dialogue with North Korea in his first speech after taking office in 2025.
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un continues to flaunt his nuclear weapons programme, while rejecting US and South Korean offers to resume stalled diplomacy.
Talks between Kim and United States President Donald Trump abruptly ended in 2019. Kim Jong Un’s government continues to demand that Washington abandon its “hostile” policy towards Pyongyang and drop demands for North Korea’s denuclearisation as a condition for talks.

articles.title_orig: Rejection of streamed execution unites Australia — but sets collision course with Trump
articles.title_zh: Rejection of streamed execution unites Australia — but sets collision course with Trump
articles.content_orig:
Washington — Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Sunday defended the Pentagon's plan to livestream the execution of an ex-Army major who was convicted of the 2009 killing of 13 people at Fort Hood, while saying that he doesn't see an "elevated risk" to U.S. security amid criticism.
"I think people need to understand, if you attack America, we will come after you and we will make sure that the punishment fits the crime," Mullin said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan ."
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said last week that the Pentagon planned to publicly livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, who is set to die by firing squad on Dec. 3 in what will be the first military execution since 1961. The announcement sparked intense criticism , including from some Republicans, like Sen. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, who urged the Pentagon to reverse the "gruesome decision," saying there is "no need to livestream any execution, including this one."
"I would expect this from terrorists and dictators, but not here in America," Murkowski wrote in a post on X. "It would give this individual, who deserves no further notoriety, the martyrdom he seeks."
While Mullin defended the Pentagon's move, he said, "No one has to watch it if they don't choose to."
"I follow President Trump. He's the commander in chief of the country, and he does a phenomenal job," Mullin said. "He leads this country with a very, very, very direct, forward, straight hand, and he's restoring America values."
Mullin added that he has "no sympathy" for Hasan, adding, "I give absolutely zero thought to the way that this man dies."
"My job as secretary of homeland security is to protect the homeland, and that's what we do," Mullin said.
The comments come as Vice President JD Vance on Friday cast some doubt on whether the Pentagon will go ahead with the plan, saying he would not tune in if the livestream happens. The vice president said Hasan committed "the worst terrorist attack on American soil outside of 9/11" when he killed 13 people and wounded more than 30 others in the attack on the Fort Hood Army base in Texas in 2009.
"So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don't forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people," Vance said. "Now that said, I mean, look, if it's ultimately livestreamed, I'm not going to be watching it."
Mr. Trump told reporters on Saturday that there are two schools of thought on whether to livestream the execution, saying, "I'll make a decision, ultimately."
