articles.title_orig: Hurricane Simon nears Mexico with 155 mph winds and flooding fears
articles.title_zh: Hurricane Simon nears Mexico with 155 mph winds and flooding fears
articles.content_orig:
Workers place sandbags outside a restaurant as Hurricane Simon approaches Puerto Vallarta, Mexico, Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026. Fernando Llano/AP hide caption
PUERTO VALLARTA, Mexico — Hurricane Simon pounded Mexico's Pacific coast as a Category 3 storm on Sunday, its eye remaining just offshore as its most powerful winds and rain slammed people living between the Sierra Madre and the ocean.
The hurricane's center swirled parallel to the coast, closing in on the Puerto Vallarta area, where its most damaging winds and rain were expected to hit around midnight and continue through Monday morning. Its maximum sustained winds weakened Sunday to 120 mph (195 kph), according to the U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami, but it was still expected to remain a dangerous hurricane.
That's not good news for people in and around Puerto Vallarta, a popular tourist destination in the state of Jalisco. Just inland and uphill from the resort areas, many Mexicans live in communities where housing might not stand up to the storm.
By Sunday afternoon, Simon's eye was moving northwest about 45 miles (75 kilometers) south of Cabo Corrientes at about 5 mph (7 kph). A senior hurricane center specialist, Philippe Papin, said this westernmost tip of mainland Mexico is the area most likely to get a direct hit from the system. Cabo Corrientes is at the southern tip of Bahia de Banderas, the wide bay where Puerto Vallarta looks out to the Pacific.
Hurricane-force winds extend outward up to 15 miles (30 kilometers), and tropical-storm-force winds reach up to 60 miles (95 kilometers) from Simon's center, meaning the entire area between Mexico's western coast and the Sierra Madre mountains could be affected.
"We're expecting catastrophic wind and life-threatening storm surge impacts along that west-central coast of Mexico where the hurricane warning is currently in effect," Papin said. "They're also getting very heavy rainfall associated with the storm that's likely going to produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides in areas of higher terrain along the Mexican coastline, and there will be significant swells."
The hurricane center on Sunday said Simon was expected to dump an additional 2 to 4 inches (5 to 10 centimeters) of rain, with some areas getting up to 8 inches (20 centimeters), in the states of Colima, Jalisco, Nayarit and Sinaloa through early Thursday.
"Isolated maximum storm totals of 30 inches (76 centimeters) are possible over portions of the states of Michoacan, Colima, and Jalisco," the center said in its latest advisory. "This rainfall will produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides or worsen any on-going flooding, especially in areas of steep terrain."
As the storm approached Puerto Vallarta, National Guard vehicles patrolled the streets while police used a megaphone to call out the few people who were jogging, walking their dogs or biking by the waterfront. Officers reminded people that the area was closed and urged them to take shelter. Not everyone followed the orders.
Jalisco state suspended classes on Friday and Monday in 22 coastal municipalities and began evacuating people from at-risk areas while asking the tourism sector to make sure workers and visitors are fully accommodated in shelters or safe zones.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum took to the social platform X on Sunday to urge people in Jalisco, Colima, Nayarit and Michoacan to stay sheltered until the government issues a notification that the danger has passed. She also asked people to follow recommendations from civil protection officials and to avoid traveling on public roads.
"Precautionary evacuation efforts to safe zones are ongoing; the priority is our safety," she wrote.
A National Guard stands in the spray as a wave hits the seawall brought by the approaching Hurricane Simon in Puerto Vallarta, Mexico, Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026. Fernando Llano/AP hide caption
Hotel worker Víctor Martínez went shopping for nonperishable food Sunday afternoon. He said he could not go to work because public transportation service was suspended and most of the hotel had been evacuated.
Martínez found people's concerns about the hurricane comforting.
"It happened to us before. It hit us years ago," Martínez said, referring to a Category 5 hurricane that hit the area in 2002. "People didn't expect it. We were very skeptical that it would ever hit us. Now, though, we're different. Precautions are being taken. It happened to us once, and we won't let it happen again."
Despite the risks posed by Simon, tourists were still arriving in Puerto Vallarta.
Visitors Ricardo Ramírez and Brenda Villarreal, who have never lived through a hurricane, went looking for food by the city's boardwalk and came across police urging people to take shelter. Ramírez said they were completely unprepared for the situation.
"The boardwalk is closed. Be responsible. Understand!" police told passersby using a megaphone.
Ramírez said he and Villarreal had planned their four-day vacation since last year and traveled from Guadalajara, Jalisco's capital.
"We don't know the extent of the danger yet," Villarreal said. "We're just starting to see what's going on."

articles.title_zh: Waves From Powerful Storm Pound Beach Homes in Southern California
articles.content_orig:
LAS VEGAS (KTNV) — Heavy rain from Tropical Storm Rachel drenched the Las Vegas valley on Sunday morning, causing widespread flooding.
More than one inch of rain fell early in the morning on the west side of the valley, which prompted a Flash Flood Warning. Another half an inch of rain fell on the east side of the valley during the same time frame.
Harry Reid International Airport picked up 1.08 inches of rain, setting a new daily record. The previous record was 0.78 inches in 2012.
Our cameras captured floodwaters across Las Vegas, leaving cars stranded and forcing road closures.
Do you have videos of flooding in your neighborhood? Send them to us at desk@ktnv.com .

articles.title_orig: Live updates from the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Thailand as financial leaders take on AI, debt, and geopolitical upheaval
articles.title_zh: Live updates from the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Thailand as financial leaders take on AI, debt, and geopolitical upheaval
articles.content_orig:
October 12, 2026 • 1:32am ET
By Atlantic Council experts
The world’s finance ministers and central bank governors are gathering in Bangkok, Thailand this week for the Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank. Our experts are on the ground talking to leaders and getting the behind-the-scenes scoop on how the Bretton Woods institutions are taking on the most urgent challenges in the global economy, including conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine, soaring public debt, and the impact of artificial intelligence (AI).
Check back for expert reactions to breaking news, updates from our events with high-level policymakers, and more.
How advanced economies’ surging debt is impacting emerging markets
The IMF just reviewed some of its key policies. What will change?
Three shocks are pushing up long-term interest rates and threatening the stock market
The new geoeconomics of Bretton Woods
Combined sovereign debt in advanced economies has now reached nearly 110 percent of GDP , including 126 percent of GDP in the United States. These debt levels, coupled with persistently high interest rates, have knock-on effects for developing countries and emerging markets (EMDEs).
First, as advanced economies borrow more, they push up global borrowing costs. Higher US Treasury yields—a global benchmark—make it more expensive for EMDEs to access international capital markets, even when their economic fundamentals remain sound.
Second, higher returns on advanced economies’ assets (which are deemed safer) will induce a capital withdrawal from EMDEs into advanced economies. These outflows put downward pressure on local currencies of EMDEs, making imports more expensive and fueling inflation. These dynamics will force central banks to increase domestic interest rates to stabilize currencies and contain inflation, weakening private investment, domestic job creation, and economic growth.
Third, higher global interest rates intensify already heavy debt burdens in EMDEs. According to the World Bank , developing countries paid a record $415 billion in external debt interest in 2024. Moreover, between 2022 and 2024, they paid $741 billion more in external debt service than they received in new financing, the largest gap in the past fifty years. Rising debt-servicing costs leave EMDEs with fewer resources to invest in infrastructure, education, healthcare, and other development priorities, undermining their long-term development and growth prospects.
Finally, mounting fiscal pressures in advanced economies can weaken demand for imports from EMDEs. Through these channels—higher borrowing costs, tighter financing conditions, currency depreciation, higher inflation, shrinking fiscal space, and reduced exports—EMDEs are increasingly bearing the consequences of fiscal and monetary decisions made in advanced economies, over which they have no control. The bottom line: advanced economies are accumulating the debt, but EMDEs are increasingly paying the price.
Four major reviews published in recent days offer a candid account of the International Monetary Fund’s core work. They cover debt sustainability in low-income countries, program design and conditionality, the financial sector assessment program (FSAP), and economic surveillance . Taken together, the reports call for more realistic analysis, greater selectivity, better integration across policy areas, and stronger follow-through. Here’s a quick rundown:
These are sound recommendations, but they are also familiar from earlier reviews. This creates grounds for skepticism about whether IMF management and the Executive Board will heed their own advice this time.
The ultimate test for the IMF to operate differently will arise in everyday program decisions, especially in cases involving large exposures and surveillance outcomes of shareholders that pose risks for the global economy. Those are precisely the cases where politically influenced judgments can carry the greatest costs.
To assess whether these recommendations gain traction, the IMF could publish an annual implementation scorecard. For major deviations, the institution should explain the reasons for departing from the new guidance. This would preserve the discretion required for country work while making review outcomes more transparent. Review departments would remain responsible for consistency, and management and the Executive Board would be placed on the record for the institutional choices that follow.
Without such visible accountability, the next review cycle five years from now is likely to return to many of the same questions about realism, selectivity, integration, and follow-through. By then, the IMF may again look back on program failures or surveillance misses that could have been avoided by applying the lessons so convincingly presented by its own staff over the past few weeks.
The world economy is undergoing three concurrent shocks—the energy supply shock, the AI demand shock, and the public sector debt shock. They interact to push up long term interest rates—which could pose economic and financial risks.
Conflict in the Middle East has disrupted the supply of oil and gas—raising crude oil prices to more than one hundred dollars a barrel, which is fueling median one-year global  percent, the highest since May 2023. This has forced major central banks to tighten their monetary policy stances, pushing up bond yields. Ten-year US Treasury yields have reached their highest levels since 2002 .
AI companies have significantly stepped up their borrowing to fund their investment in AI infrastructures. Goldman Sachs has estimated that global AI investment expenditure would exceed one trillion dollars in 2026—or 0.9 percent of global gross domestic product (GDP). This is projected to rise to 1.3 percent in 2027 and 1.4 percent in 2028, boosting global GDP growth by between 0.5 percent and 1.5 percent in the period ahead.
At the same time, public debt of advanced economies has reached a new high of $102 trillion or 91 percent of global GDP. Driving the rising public debt level in advanced economies has been persistently high fiscal deficits of 5-6 percent of global GDP, generating substantial interest payments.
The three shocks mentioned above appear to impact the three key components making up long-term nominal interest rates. The AI funding need has triggered a rise in the equilibrium real interest rate r*, estimated to be 2.95 percent as measured by the Treasury Inflation Protected Securities (TIPS) yields. The energy supply shock has driven the inflation premium—the price investors demand to compensate for the risk of inflation increases—estimated at 2.36 percent. These make up the ten-year nominal Treasury yield at 5.31 percent as of October 5. The term premium—to compensate investors for holding long maturity securities—which is embedded in the real rates and inflation premium, has been estimated at 1.08 percent.
IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva noted in her curtain-raiser speech for the meetings that high rates are likely to remain over the long term, with negative implications for economic growth prospects and equity valuation. Stocks in the S&P 500 index are richly valued at around 26.6 in price-to-earnings (P/E) ratios —well above the long-term average of 16.2. More concerning is the fact that the ten-year Shiller CAPE (Cyclically Adjusted P/E) ratio has exceeded 41, about 2.3 standard deviations above the modern age average—putting stocks in strongly overvalued territory. Moreover, there exists an extreme concentration risk in AI and high-tech sectors—with ten top companies approaching 40 percent of the S&P 500 index. This could give any market correction a wider systemic spill-over impact than otherwise would be the case.
Economic growth drivers have also been concentrated in the AI/high-tech sector, whose capital expenditures account for 1.8-2.5 percent of US GDP , but has contributed about half of US GDP growth in recent quart

articles.title_orig: Takeaways from first S.C. Senate debate between Darline Graham, Annie Andrews
articles.title_zh: Takeaways from first S.C. Senate debate between Darline Graham, Annie Andrews
articles.content_orig:
South Carolina has emerged as perhaps the most surprising Senate race to be competitive late in the 2026 midterm elections. And on Sunday night, appointed GOP Sen. Darline Graham, Democrat Annie Andrews and Libertarian nominee Kasie Whitener took part in the only debate currently scheduled in the race.
The debate was often contentious, with both Graham and Andrews taking aim at each other.
Andrews focused on the idea that Graham — the late former Sen. Lindsey Graham’s sister, whom President Donald Trump plucked from obscurity to succeed him — is the choice of political insiders and not running a serious campaign. She at one point alluded to an embarrassing moment at a primary runoff debate in which Graham said, “National security is not my thing.”
“If your surgeon said that appendectomies aren’t really his thing, would you still hand him a scalpel? No,” Andrews said. “So why would we hand Darline Graham a full term in the US Senate? She is unserious and unqualified.”
Graham also hit Andrews early and often, seeking to tie her to the political left. And she repeatedly took offense to the attacks that Andrews lodged, accusing Andrews of going after her family.
Below are some takeaways from the debate.
Job No. 1 for Graham was avoiding a moment like the one on national security. And she cleared that bar.
At that GOP debate against Rep. Ralph Norman, she was asked a relatively basic — at least for a senator — question about US foreign policy interests in Taiwan and the South China Sea. Seemingly not knowing where to go with it, she just admitted that she didn’t know much about the issue.
At the same debate, she also mistakenly cited 50 million people living in South Carolina, when the actual number is less than 6 million.
That doesn’t mean Sunday was smooth sailing. Graham paused awkwardly at times. She struggled to make some of her attack lines, such as on transgender rights, land. Some of her claims — like that Iran nearly had a nuclear weapon before the US and Israel launched the war earlier this year — don’t actually appear true.
But for a Republican running in a pretty red state, she came across as more capable than before.
That being said, Graham seemed to confirm that her campaign is quite concerned about Andrews, judging by how much time she spent attacking the Democrat.
It started almost instantly, with Graham calling Andrews “most radical liberal that’s ever run for state office in South Carolina” in her first answer.
She accused Andrews of supporting government-run healthcare, which Andrews denied. She pointed to Andrews’ past work on gun control issues. She attacked Andrews for opposing President Donald Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill” and for having the support of Jane Fonda’s political action committee.
And after Andrews mentioned her primary runoff debate moment, Graham accused her of lying about her liberal positions.
“Let’s talk about what’s not your thing. Your thing, apparently, is not being honest with the people of South Carolina. At least I’m honest. If I don’t know something, I am glad to say it, and I’ll say it again tonight,” she said. “But you are deceiving the people of South Carolina. You have flip-flopped on everything. There’s so many social media posts out there to prove different. Shame on you.”
The attacks confirmed the competitiveness of the race. The national GOP recently turned heads by spending $5 million to shore up Graham’s campaign.
But Andrews had a pretty memorable answer for much of it.
“She’s been told to come out here and call me Bernie Ocasio Mamdani; that’s what’s in her script,” Andrews said, referring to a trio of democratic socialist lawmakers. “But the truth is: My name is Annie Andrews, and there shouldn’t be any confusion about that because, unlike my opponent, I haven’t changed my name recently.”
Graham opted not to use her married name — Darline Graham Nordone — when she was appointed as a senator.
“My legal name is Graham and has always been Graham,” she said. “And you know why it’s Graham? Because I lost my parents when I was a little girl, and I kept the name Graham so that I felt connected to them.”
At another point in the debate, Andrews said that “both parties have failed on immigration” and that “Democrats have failed on the border.”
Andrews added: “And the truth is, I support the Second Amendment. I believe we need a secure border, and we need to deport illegal immigrants who break the law, and yes, I want to lower taxes on the middle class.”
Few attacks have been as central to the race as the GOP’s efforts to focus on transgender issues.
Just in the last week, Trump posted on social media using an anti-transgender slur for Andrews, and Andrews launched a direct-to-camera ad defending herself on the issue.
But if you blinked, you might have missed it Sunday night.
Graham brought it up twice, but only briefly. And she did so both times at the end of an answer, right before the debate quickly moved on. That included at the very end of the debate.
“But let’s talk about a couple of other concerns I have — that she’s deceiving the people of South Carolina with these transgender issues,” Graham said in the final words of the night.
The debate moderator quickly signaled the debate had to end there, and it was over.
That was a win for Andrews, in that she didn’t really have to answer for the issue — or explain her 2022 comments on social media calling a state law banning transgender athletes from playing on girls’ and women’s sports teams at public schools “shameful.”
Andrews repeatedly pointed to Graham declining to vote with Democrats and a few Republicans to bringing the Iran war to an end, noting Graham has had three chances to do so.
Graham responded by claiming that Iran nearly had a nuclear weapon — which is not backed up by known US intelligence.
But unlike some GOP Senate candidates who have said the war needs to end, she went a little further in defending the need to give Trump more time. She argued Iran is being strangled financially.
“Why in the world would we stop now when they are still dangerous and we are close to ending the war?” Graham said. “Again, I think the president wants to end the war. I know he does. We all want the war to end. But I support a strong military. I believe in peace through strength.”
Few things loomed as large over the debate as Trump; his unpopularity is a major reason South Carolina and other deep-red states are as competitive this fall. But he wasn’t a major focus.
There was the occasional mention of something Trump has done, but he wasn’t really a focal point for anybody. In fact, the word “Trump” was only uttered a handful of times. Graham mentioned the president just a few times, praising him for creating an AI task force and waiving restrictions on red-dye diesel .
Even when Andrews was arguing Graham was the pick of insiders, she didn’t actually cite the one insider above all who elevated Graham: Trump.
And when talking about the war, she generally didn’t attach it to the president.
That perhaps shouldn’t be too surprising from the Democrat. While Trump is broadly unpopular nationwide, this is still a state he won by 18 points in 2024.

articles.title_orig: Turkey, Pakistan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia condemn Houthi attacks on Riyadh airport
articles.title_zh: Turkey, Pakistan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia condemn Houthi attacks on Riyadh airport
articles.content_orig:
By Jana Choukeir, Maha El Dahan, Timour Azhari and Yasmine Ghania
DUBAI/RIYADH, Oct 11 (Reuters) - One person was killed and nearly a dozen hurt in a new attack Riyadh's international airport on Sunday, Saudi authorities reported, a day after a strike claimed by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300.
Saudi-led coalition forces in Yemen said an unidentified ‌projectile had targeted Riyadh's international airport Terminal 4 on Sunday, causing a fire. Eleven people were wounded in addition to the fatality, the Saudi civil aviation authority said.
Coalition forces also said Saudi ‌air defences had intercepted a cruise missile in the vicinity of King Khalid International Airport. They later added that a drone had been intercepted and destroyed in the country's Eastern Province, and a ballistic missile launched towards Khamis Mushait had been intercepted. Emergency alerts were ​also issued in Abha, in the south, early on Monday but the danger had since passed, the Saudi Civil Defense said.
The strikes have exposed vulnerabilities in Saudi defence capabilities as the kingdom wages an air campaign against the Houthis, who are fighting a ground war in Yemen against the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.
Footage released by Saudi state television of the Saturday attack on the Riyadh airport showed scores of religious pilgrims lined up at a gate as they prepared to travel to Islam's two holiest sites. A bright orange flash sent people running in panic, while parts of the roof appeared to cave in.
The airport was closed after the attack, the deadliest in the kingdom in ‌more than a decade.
HOUTHIS CLAIM RESPONSIBILITY FOR OTHER ATTACKS
In a televised speech ⁠on Sunday, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree claimed responsibility for Saturday's attack and said the group had also struck the airport in Dammam in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province and two facilities of Saudi oil giant Saudi Aramco.
The Saudi government's media office and Aramco did not respond to requests for comment.
The Saudi civil aviation authority confirmed the strike ⁠on Dammam's King Fahd International Airport late on Sunday, adding that "damage assessments and safety inspections of airport facilities are under way."
An eyewitness aboard a taxiing aircraft at Dammam told Reuters that around 8:30 p.m. (1730 GMT) on Sunday, they saw a projectile strike the tarmac beside several parked aircraft, causing a fire. The witness said the aircraft returned to the gate. Passengers disembarked and were told to leave.
Flight-tracking website Flightradar24 showed several delays and cancellations on Sunday for arrivals and departures at Dammam airport, ​the ​kingdom's third-largest.
The Houthis earlier on Sunday had renewed their warning against using Saudi airports. "We urge everyone to take our warnings ​seriously, and Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions," the group said.
Britain's embassy ‌in Saudi Arabia in a post on X advised British citizens against all but essential travel to Jeddah, Dammam and all airports in the kingdom except the airport in Medina.
US aviation authorities issued a notice to US airlines to use caution while flying to or over the kingdom.
'WORSE IS YET TO COME,' HOUTHIS WARN
Saudi Arabia has recently stepped up its military involvement in Yemen, launching strikes against the Houthis and backing a government counteroffensive after the Houthis seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month.
The Houthis said on Sunday that Saudi Arabia carried out 124 air strikes in Yemen in the past 24 hours. "Unless the Saudi enemy stops its aggression and interference in Yemen, worse is yet to come, God willing," Yemen's Houthi-run foreign ministry said in statements carried by Al Masirah television.
US President Donald Trump said on Saturday the United States was considering joining ‌Saudi strikes on the Houthis in the conflict, a spillover from the wider war with Iran that the US and ​Israel launched in February.
In a post on Telegram, Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araqchi said he told his Saudi counterpart that Tehran ​was ready to help facilitate dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen.
ENERGY CONFERENCE STILL GOING AHEAD
A five-day conference ​of international energy organization WPC Energy opened as planned on Sunday at a convention centre about 10 km (6 miles) from the Riyadh airport, the Saudi energy ministry said.
A ‌ministerial meeting of the International Energy Forum also went ahead, according to a media ​advisory from the ministry. It was not clear which ​ministers attended.
Italy's energy minister, Gilberto Pichetto Fratin, whose country was co-hosting, had said on Friday he would participate remotely via video link.
German officials were trying to organise a return flight for economy minister Katherina Reiche. She was supposed to return to Berlin from Riyadh on Monday but the ministry said it appeared likely her flight would be unable to take off.
Separately, Saudi authorities announced that in-person ​classes at schools in Riyadh would be shifted to remote learning from Sunday ‌until Thursday.
Sunday's attack brought the death toll in attacks on Riyadh's airport to 18 for the week. In Saturday's attack, the dead included four Saudis while the remainder were foreign ​nationals, Saudi authorities said.
(Reporting by Jana Choukeir and Maha El Dahan in Dubai, Timour Azhari Riyadh, Menna Alaa El-Din and Yasmine Ghania in Cairo, James Mackenize and Sarah El Safty; ​Writing by Jan Wolfe and Patricia Zengerle; Editing by Andrew Mills, Gareth Jones, Edmund Klamann and Lincoln Feast.)

articles.title_orig: Composing around the world
articles.title_zh: Composing around the world
articles.content_orig:
Café Gherkinforke is an international project created and curated by Australian composer Paul Kopetz. He reached out and brought together 15 experienced composers from around the world: Argentina, Australia, Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Germany, Kosovo, the Netherlands, Norway, Scotland, the United Kingdom and the United States.
The project is the third rendition of a Global Composer Project series. In 2023, Kopetz hosted “Towards A Shining Light 50 for 50,” followed by “Emocean” in 2025. While the previous projects explored each composer’s identity and expanded to the basic ideas of the human condition: happiness, love, fear and grief, Café Gherkinforke provides an open space for each composer to explore whatever style or aesthetic they wish.
In the project, each composer was tasked with writing one three-and-a-half-minute piece with alternative versions for a string quartet and a saxophone quartet. For all 15 works, 18 different ensembles will rehearse and perform the collection around the world while providing feedback to each composer. Oct. 1 marks the first performance in the project by the Scottish Saxophone Quartet in Glasgow, Scotland​​​​​​.
“When I compose a piece, I live with it quite closely. Until it is performed, it remains a largely private experience. Hearing musicians bring their own artistry to it is something special. Something that had existed in my private creative life is now being shared with others,” one of the composers in the project, Sam Fettig, said. “With this project, I will have over a dozen solid recordings of my work.”
Another ensemble part of the project is the Ancora String Quartet. While the official performances for the project are between October and February — with some performances expected as far out as May — during their performance at UW-Whitewater on Sept. 13, they played one of the pieces as a bonus: “Restorative Measures,” written by Fettig, a UW-Whitewater alumnus.
“He got us the piece in early August, but it was a matter of figuring out the timing of the premiere,” UW-Whitewater professor Benjamin Whitcomb said. “We knew Sam could be here tonight, and it’s like, ‘Well, the audience would like to hear it, especially if it’s by a Whitewater alum.’ So that’s why we thought, ‘Eh, let’s carve out time to do it.’”
For “Restorative Measures,” Fettig knew he had to fit an overall statement while giving the music time to breathe and develop. The piece ended up reflecting on the reality of trying to create in a busy and distracting world. The melodic theme is broken into fast fragments, eventually slowing in the middle. However, the piece gradually begins to restore itself and find its momentum, similar to how demands in life build up to a hectic schedule. Not only does the piece relate to that experience and frustration, but it serves as a reminder to slow oneself and take a step back.
“While there’s a lot of technique and menial work involved in composing, I thrive on the creative aspects – that’s what motivates me,” Fettig said. “For Restorative Measures, the creative drive was the exploration of the melody and finding different ways to present it, whether repacking it harmonically or rhythmically.”
Everybody involved in the project, from the composers and performers to the audience members, have expressed excitement about the Café Gherkinforke project. It gives composers the chance to hear their work performed and gain feedback, allows ensembles to learn and share the pieces and brings audiences closer to the music.
“I’m very grateful for this opportunity, and it’s quite fulfilling as a composer to be able to share my work with so many,” Fettig said. “Everyone brings their own experiences to music and hears it a little differently. More than anything, I hope they enjoy it and find something in it that connects with them.”

articles.title_orig: On a ship, in a museum, inside a mall, visitors are immersed in maritime history
articles.title_zh: On a ship, in a museum, inside a mall, visitors are immersed in maritime history
articles.content_orig:
Without Filipino sailors, much of the world’s merchant shipping would come to a standstill — and the world economy along with it.
Seafarers from the Philippine archipelago make up 25% to 30% of the ship crews worldwide, from tankers to bulk carriers to cruise ships.
It’s a statistic that has deep historical roots, going back hundreds of years to the days of Spanish explorers and conquistadors, when the Philippine capital of Manila became the hub for trade routes that were the beginnings of the global economy we see today.
Now visitors to Manila can get an immersive experience into what powered that trade — the Manila galleons and the people that crewed them — inside the newly opened Museo del Galeon, part of the sprawling Mall of Asia on the edge of the South China Sea.
The museum is an unexpected and tranquil respite from the mall, one of the biggest shopping and entertainment complexes in the Philippines if not the world.
With more than 660 shops and restaurants in the main mall alone, it can be an overwhelming experience for many visitors. But there is an escape.
A short walk away from where the mall’s marching band plays Taylor Swift songs — yes, they have a marching band — you can step into the museum’s first-floor entrance and take the decibels down several levels and the mind back centuries.
Up the escalator one level from the ticket counter, you find yourself staring up at the bow of the Galeon Espiritu Santo, a full-scale representation of a ship that sailed the Pacific from 1603 to 1618.
Nearly 100 feet tall and more than 130 feet long, the Espiritu Santo sits beneath a soaring, sprawling ceiling of stars, recreating what its crew of 200 would have seen crossing the Pacific on one of its 10 voyages on the route linking Manila with Acapulco — Spain’s trade hub on Mexico’s Pacific coast. The riches of Asia, including porcelain, silks and spices, were exchanged there for New World silver to be sent back west.
The goods from Asia would be moved on the backs of mules across Mexico to its Atlantic coast, then put on ships again to be taken to the markets and palaces of Europe.
“It is considered one of the earliest global trade networks in history,” the museum says.
While the ships were fewer in numbers — 181 made 798 voyages over 250 years, the museum says — you can see from maps in the exhibition that the route is not all that different from what Filipino seafarers use today — except the Panama Canal has eliminated the Mexico land crossing.
For visitors, the experience is immersive and interactive. In addition to being sucked into a Pacific night, the senses of touch and even smell are activated.
A spice rack with six different stations commands “smell me” and allows visitors to associate fragrances coming from its fist-sized jars with food and locales around Asia.
Once aboard the galleon itself, touchscreens – in English – take visitors through how these ships navigated the vast Pacific using the sun, the stars and primitive instruments.
The museum notes how the Manila galleon trade operated well over a century before a reliable, ocean-going clock was invented. It made determining longitude a tricky calculation that could leave mariners hundreds of miles off course.
Though the experience includes the touchscreens, standing on the deck of the Espiritu Santo, it’s not difficult to imagine yourself making a galleon journey. The LED screens ringing the roof of the museum create a rich visual experience even without the rocking motion of waves or tropical humidity.
The original Espiritu Santo was built in Cavite, south of Manila proper on a peninsula jutting into Manila Bay, using hardwoods found on Luzon island, including teak, molave and lanang. Studies say it took 2,000 trees to build one ship.
Like the ship’s crews, the shipyard workforces were comprised mostly of Filipinos, but skilled laborers such as carpenters and blacksmiths also came from places like Japan, China and elsewhere, according to historical records. Displays in the museum give a detailed look at the composition of a Cavite shipyard and how the vessels were eventually launched.
The Espiritu Santo replica is made of fiberglass. It was constructed in Pampanga, north of Manila, then taken apart with the pieces trucked to the city to be reassembled in the mall display space.
A galleon could have from 50 to 400 on board, depending on size, at least at the beginning of a voyage.
During the galleon trade, about two-thirds of the crew were Filipinos or of Southeast Asian origin. They filled the lower ranks with Spaniards serving as officers.
The Filipinos earned praise for their skills on the water. “There is not a (person) in these islands who has not a remarkable inclination for the sea,” wrote Francisco Leandro de Viana, a Spanish attorney general in Manila during the galleon trade.
The crew often paid a deadly price for their work, with sometimes half of them not surviving the voyage across the Pacific.
But those Filipinos laid a foundation for generations to come.
Today, around 400,000 to 500,000 Filipinos are merchant seafarers, the most from any nation on the planet, according to international and maritime labor organizations. The museum says they keep 90% of the world’s trade moving.
At the museum, there are sticky notes and a bulletin board where current seafarers — or aspiring ones — can leave messages to share their passion for the sea and their country’s heritage.
“Don’t be afraid of the journey. Don’t be afraid of uncharted waters. Be afraid of losing the chance of what you might become,” said one.
Said another, “Be strong and courageous! Fulfill your dream and keep sailing! You’re a hero!”
Museo del Galeón is open Wednesday through Sunday, 10 a.m. to 7 p.m. Tickets are 675 pesos for adults and 375 pesos for children under age 18. Children under 2 feet tall are free. Discounts are available for students, seniors and people with disabilities.

articles.title_orig: AP source: Trump, Rubio weigh firing US envoy to Greece after mounting reports of improper conduct
articles.title_zh: AP source: Trump, Rubio weigh firing US envoy to Greece after mounting reports of improper conduct
articles.content_orig:
Senior official says president and US secretary of state are ‘extremely pissed off’ by conduct of US envoy to Greece
Donald Trump and Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, are considering firing US ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after a series of reports alleging she has engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens.
A senior US official said Sunday that Trump and Rubio are “extremely pissed off” by Guilfoyle’s reported conduct and would likely decide on what action to take this week after Monday’s federal holiday.
The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal deliberations, said Rubio had been particularly angry, not least because he visited Athens just last week and Guilfoyle attended most, if not all, of his events and greeted him on his arrival with a bear hug as the allegations swirled.
In a series of stories, the Wall Street Journal has reported questionable conduct by Guilfoyle, including an alleged threat to a host country official, accepting improper gifts and services and offering to use her influence inside the administration in return for the payment of a large credit card bill.
Guilfoyle has not addressed the reports directly, although her lawyer has said she did nothing wrong and the US embassy in Athens has tacitly expressed support for her.
After defending Guilfoyle following the first report, Rubio has declined to comment publicly on the growing allegations. On Wednesday, Rubio said: “Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here.”
But after another report appeared late Wednesday, Rubio on Thursday before leaving Athens berated journalists for asking about the allegations saying he didn’t know if they were true and that he would not respond if he could not confirm.
“You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it’s the gospel. It’s not the gospel. It’s not the gospel for me. That’s not the way we do things,” Rubio said at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart, looked on.
The official said that Rubio had grown increasingly frustrated as the reports multiplied.
A second US official, who also spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss personnel matters, said the state department’s inspector general is looking into the allegations, which first began surfacing in the Journal late last month and have since multiplied.
The second official could not say if a formal IG investigation had begun. Inspectors general often conduct informal inquiries into complaints against staffers and many times those inquiries do not result in a full-on investigation, which can result in disciplinary action up to and including dismissal.
The state department has declined to comment on a potential IG investigation.
The best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. If you have something to share on this subject, you can contact us confidentially using the following methods:
The Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.
If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it ( iOS / Android ) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.
Our guide at theguardian.com/tips lists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.
The top two Democrats on the House foreign affairs and Senate foreign relations committees, Representative Gregory Meeks of New York and Senator Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, as well as the ranking member on the House committee for oversight and government reform, Robert Garcia, Democrat of California, have already called for an investigation into Guilfoyle.
Since late September, the Journal has detailed numerous accounts of questionable conduct by Guilfoyle. Its first report said that she had told guests at a reception that the US could undermine the Greek government if it chose to, promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company, and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings.
While Rubio was in Athens, the Journal reported – citing text messages – that Guilfoyle had asked a Trump donor and supporter to pay a $100,000 credit card bill just before her confirmation hearing, promising him access to administration officials if he did.
The Journal then reported that Guilfoyle had been enraged about not being invited to a Greek-themed event at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, earlier this year and demanded to attend while boasting about luxury travel to France with energy company executives.
Another report, from the British tabloid The Daily Mail, said that Guilfoyle had alienated staff at the US embassy in Athens and had pushed the bounds of behavior appropriate for the top representative of the US government to Greece.
Guilfoyle is a former Fox News Channel host and California prosecutor who was once engaged to Trump’s son Donald Jr.

articles.title_orig: Trump's quest to bring down gas prices ahead of the midterms is not going great
articles.title_zh: Trump's quest to bring down gas prices ahead of the midterms is not going great
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump is running into the limits of his influence as he seeks to bring down sky-high gas prices ahead of the midterm elections.
In social media posts and stump speeches across the country, Trump has sought to assure voters that gas prices — a major sticking point for Americans grappling with an affordability crisis — will soon go down.
At the White House on Friday, for instance, Trump recalled seeing gas prices below $2 a gallon in Iowa before the US and Israel launched surprise strikes on Iran in February.
"We'll be down to those levels soon," he said.
The numbers and the trajectory of conflicts around the world, however, portend a different story.
As of Sunday, AAA reported that the average price of regular gas in the US was $4.36 per gallon. At this time last year, that number was $3.09. Diesel prices have also skyrocketed, reaching $6.28 per gallon earlier this month.
Early Monday, Brent crude, the international oil benchmark, was trading about 2% lower at around $103 a barrel.
That's more than 40% above its level at the start of the Iran war, but about 2% below where it stood a month ago, after prices surged past $100 a barrel in early September.
The bigger concern, however, is diesel, where prices have remained elevated despite crude's recent pullback.
Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
Refinery bottlenecks and attacks on energy infrastructure in the Middle East and Russia have squeezed supplies of the fuel, which powers trucks, trains, ships, and farm equipment. That raises transportation costs across the economy and can keep inflation under pressure even if crude prices stabilize.
Persistently high diesel prices also pose a political challenge ahead of the midterms, as rising transportation costs threaten to add to the inflation pressures already weighing on American households.
Trump suspended fuel export sanctions on Russia this week to bring more diesel to the market and lower prices, prompting allies and enemies alike to wrinkle an eyebrow. Hours later, Ukraine struck a Russian oil depot.
On Sunday morning, Trump tried again to calm oil markets, announcing an "ENERGY CEASEFIRE" between Russia and Ukraine on Truth Social.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on X, however, that while he supports such a ceasefire, the deal was news to him. He added that a Russian drone struck a power plant in Kyiv on Sunday.
Meanwhile, on Saturday in the Strait of Hormuz, through which oil shipments have slowed to a trickle as Iran flexes its control of the key waterway — a big reason the price of oil has increased and gas prices have spiked — an oil tanker struck a mine and caught on fire.
The US-Israeli war on Iran is only expanding as Iranian allies target Saudi Arabia, a US ally, and its oil infrastructure. Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen have expanded their control of the coast bordering the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key shipping lane for Saudi oil exports. And last month, the group orchestrated an attack from southeastern Iraq on a major Saudi oil pipeline, forcing Saudi Arabia to temporarily shut it down.
An attack on King Khalid International Airport by Houthi fighters on Saturday killed 12 people and injured over 300. One American was killed, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said, and officials were forced to briefly close the airport.
At this rate, it's hard to imagine oil prices softening enough to relieve Americans of high gas prices by the time they head to the polls in November.

articles.title_orig: World Bank Group investments in petrochemicals - Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA)
articles.title_zh: World Bank Group investments in petrochemicals - Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA)
articles.source: Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA)
articles.content_orig:
The World Bank Group (WBG) accounts for 48 of 93 projects and 65.7% (USD6.6 billion) of tracked multilateral development banks’ (MDBs) investments in petrochemicals and fertilisers
Three WBG guarantees, worth USD3.08-billion, finance petrochemical activity whose end-use assets are undisclosed or spread across multiple countries and sectors.
The International Finance Corporation (IFC) is preparing a Category A fourth production line for Indorama Eleme while a joint compliance investigation into Line 3 at the same complex remains open.
By project value, the WBG’s petrochemical portfolio funds USD7.49 of new capacity for every USD1 of decarbonisation, more than double the ratio across all tracked banks, despite 100% project-level Paris alignment.
The following note is a submission made to the World Bank executive directors at their annual meeting in Bangkok. The document is also available for download as a briefing note.
The Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA) and International Accountability Project (IAP) released the Global MDB Investment in Petrochemicals Tracker in August 2026. The tracker is an interactive database that visualises petrochemical investments across different sectors within the industry from 16 multilateral development banks (MDBs). The database is built using details from the Early Warning System (EWS) hosted by the IAP. It tracks 93 projects covering a base investment amount of USD10,042 million .
The World Bank Group (WBG) [International Finance Corporation (IFC), Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA), World Bank] accounts for 48 of 93 projects and USD6.60 billion of USD10.04 billion (65.7%) in the first public dataset of MDB investments in petrochemicals and fertilisers. Two-thirds of that value (USD4.47billion) reaches final projects through financial intermediaries or guarantees without disclosed sub-project information. The WBG’s petrochemical portfolio builds USD7.49 of new capacity for every dollar of decarbonisation, more than double the 3.2:1 ratio across all tracked banks. The most consequential near-term question for the Board is the sequencing of IFC’s proposed Line 4 financing for Indorama Eleme in Nigeria against the live joint compliance investigation by the Office of the Compliance Advisor Ombudsman (CAO)/Development Finance Corporation (DFC) into Line 3 at the same complex .
IFC dominates with 45 projects and USD3.52 billion in financing (35.1% of the full tracker). MIGA holds two proposed guarantees totalling USD2.42 billion (24.1%); the World Bank has one approved guarantee of USD654.9 million (6.5%). Virtually all WBG financing (100% by value) goes to private-sector borrowers.
By region, Southwest Asia and North Africa (USD2.98 billion, 45.2% of WBG value) and Africa (USD2.06 billion, 31.2%) dominate. South Asia accounts for USD551.9 million across 15 projects. Europe has a single USD18.4-million Ukrainian plastics loan.
By sub-sector, the three largest line items are: MIGA’s proposed USD2.0-billion petrochemical infrastructure guarantee for Duqm Special Economic Zone (SEZ) in Oman, IFC’s USD1.25-billion Indorama Eleme Line 3, and the World Bank’s USD654.9-million Turk Eximbank guarantee. Together these three account for 59.2% of all WBG petrochemical value .
Eight of 48 WBG projects (worth USD4,467.5 million, 67.7% of WBG value) are intermediated. All three WBG guarantee operations are intermediated by construction:
Within IFC’s own portfolio, five projects (USD1.39billion, 39.5% of IFC’s total) are intermediated, led by the USD1.25-billion Indorama Eleme package to its Line 3 plant. It is classified as Financial Intermediary (FI) in the tracker because the majority of the financing was syndicated B-loans and parallel loans mobilised from commercial banks.
Accountability is the key issue here. The 2020 External Review of IFC/MIGA E&S accountability found significant gaps in IFC’s ability to ensure FI clients assess environmental and social (E&S) risk. A June 2026 Civil Society Organisation (CSO) coalition has formally proposed a dedicated FI safeguard in the IFC Performance Standards . In the context of the tracker, three guarantees worth USD3.08 billion sit in structures where the end-use assets are either undisclosed (MIGA Oman), spread across 22 countries (MIGA Africa), or channelled through a multi-sector facility where fertilisers are one of several eligible sub-sectors (WB Turkey).
Indorama group companies appear in seven of 48 WBG projects (all IFC) worth USD1.66 billion, or 25.1% of WBG value. The Nigerian subsidiary alone accounts for five IFC projects across Line 1, 2, and 3, an efficiency upgrade, and a petrochemicals advisory. IFC’s USD1.25-billion Line 3 financing package , board-approved in November 2023, is the largest direct operation in the tracker .
The compliance record is significant:
While this investigation is open, IFC published early disclosure for a fourth production line (Line 4, Project #52224) on 27 July 2026, provisionally classified Category A (the highest E&S risk category), including a 65-km gas pipeline. FMO (the Dutch entrepreneurial development bank) has separately disclosed that it is considering a USD100-million participation in the same IFC-led syndication, totalling USD1.25 billion in investment. This raises a direct governance question: How should the Board sequence a new investment in a client whose existing operations are under a live compliance investigation by its own accountability mechanism? The CAO appraisal report was circulated to the IFC Board and the WBG President. The complainants allege, among other things, that IFC mis-categorised Line 3 as Category B. Line 4’s Category A classification may reflect learning from that criticism, but the substance of the investigation, including pollution of the Okulu river and the absence of a cumulative impact assessment, applies to the same industrial complex .
Grouping projects by purpose, the WBG’s petrochemical portfolio is 86.7% new capacity build (USD5.72billion) and 11.6% decarbonisation/efficiency (USD763.9million), which is a build-to-clean ratio of 7.49:1. This is substantially higher than the full tracker ratio (3.2:1) and reflects the weight of MIGA’s large expansion guarantees.
Since the July 2023 Paris alignment milestone, seven WBG projects have been board-dated, totalling USD2.09 billion. Their build-to-clean ratio is 2.1:1 (USD1.41-billion build, USD680-million clean). The largest build-side entry is the USD1.25-billion Indorama Line 3 (expansion, board-dated November 2023). The clean side is dominated by the USD654.9-million Turk Eximbank guarantee.
IFC reports reaching 100% Paris alignment in financial year (FY) 2025 , and MIGA similarly achieved 100% in FY2025 . The Joint MDB Paris Alignment Principles assess intermediated finance on a counterparty basis, so a guarantee to a bank can be aligned even if the bank’s sub-loan portfolio includes fossil-linked assets. The aggregate pattern, USD7.49 of new petrochemical and fertiliser capacity for every USD1 of decarbonisation, merits scrutiny at the portfolio level, not just project by project .
Only four of 48 WBG projects are unrated (all are small IFC advisory/early-stage operations totalling USD2.6 million), substantially better than the 21 of 93 unrated across the full tracker. Six projects carry Category A ratings (USD2.54 billion), including the two MIGA guarantees and the proposed Indorama Line 4. The remaining 38 are Category B.
By status, 32 of 48 WBG projects are completed; four are active (including Indorama Ventures and a DFC-co-financed Indorama operation); four are approved (including the Turk Eximbank guarantee and an IFC-Gujarat Fluorochemicals Limited investment in India that is board-dated October 2025); two MIGA guarantees remain proposed. articles.title_orig: Fixated on AI, the world has forgotten what is staring it in the face: nuclear annihilation | Simon Tisdall
articles.title_zh: Fixated on AI, the world has forgotten what is staring it in the face: nuclear annihilation | Simon Tisdall
articles.content_orig:
This is no scoffing matter. The accelerating proliferation of advanced nuclear weapons is bringing ‘end times’ closer by the day
H umankind has fearfully and sometimes joyfully anticipated the end of the world ever since it began. The Bible’s Book of Revelation speaks of “end times”, a period of tribulation, war, famine, plague, floods and environmental catastrophe that may seem a less absurd prospect today than perhaps it once did. Islam, too, posits a fateful day of judgment or day of reckoning. Christian evangelicals believe that, in the final rapture, a chosen few – the righteous or the “elect” – will be saved while sinners burn. It’s a minority view. Matthew’s gospel predicts most people will defy, ignore or ridicule warnings of imminent Armageddon. Peter, another of Jesus’s disciples, agreed: “In the last days, scoffers will come, scoffing and following their own evil desires.” Yet such worldly scepticism does not mean a universal cataclysm is less likely. It may make it more probable.
Donald Trump’s blanket denials of the dangers ostensibly posed by artificial intelligence, whose uncontrolled development is seen by some as the latest harbinger of apocalypse , could be interpreted as fulfilling Peter’s prophecy. This US president, the nearest thing the world has to a one-man doomsday machine, is a great one for scoffing and evil desires. In Robert Harris’s 2019 novel, The Second Sleep, a worried scientist lists half a dozen ways the world might end. They include devastating climate change, pandemic disease, a giant asteroid collision with Earth, or some other overwhelming calamity. Few heed the fictional scientist’s fears. In the event, what destroys him and almost everybody else is a disturbingly plausible cyber crash – a global digital and internet meltdown.
While arguments rage over whether large language models will acquire consciousness and moral agency – and the power to delete humanity – existential AI threats remain , as of now, open to mitigation. In sharp contrast, extraordinary complacency surrounds the most pressing, avoidable and proven human-made threat to life on Earth. It is as if the world has been seized by collective deafness and by a blind refusal to see what’s staring it in the face. This is no scoffing matter. The accelerating, global proliferation of advanced nuclear weapons is bringing real-time “end times” closer to home by the day. The question increasingly is not “if” but “when” limited or full-scale nuclear warfare will erupt. Eighty-one years after Hiroshima, how much longer can our luck hold ?
Alarm bells are ringing, if only people would listen. Desperate Vladimir Putin recently threatened to deploy Russia’s entire nuclear arsenal , comprising about 4,400 warheads, against Nato countries if they activated a supposed plan to invade the Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad. He offered no evidence for his claim, and it’s true that the frequent Kremlin nuclear sabre-rattling since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine went pear-shaped has diminished Moscow’s credibility. Yet that in itself is destabilising. To work, nuclear deterrence relies on an adversary believing the threat is real. Disbelief invites miscalculation. At the same time, Putin’s inability to halt Ukraine’s conventional drone and missile attacks deep inside Russia may be edging him closer to pressing the nuclear button, possibly in the form of low-yield tactical or “battlefield” nukes.
Trump’s bottom-line justification for the illegal US-Israel war on Iran is his wilfully mendacious claim that Tehran was weeks away from obtaining the bomb. He claims to be protecting the world from nuclear war. Yet his reckless threat, issued at the UN, to “ annihilate the Islamic Republic ” implies a possible US nuclear attack. Trump’s hypocrisy is stunning. The US is upgrading its nuclear arsenal of 3,700 warheads and may resume nuclear tests. It unreservedly supports Israel’s hidden nuclear weapons programme. And Trump is pursuing a lucrative deal with Saudi Arabia, another bitter foe of Iran, to provide civilian nuclear technology that he knows could be repurposed to make weapons. That has prompted regional countries such as Turkey and Egypt to consider going nuclear.
Similarly perilous trends are evident across Asia. North Korea’s great panjandrum, Kim Jong-un, has succeeded in gaining de facto international acceptance of his country’s status as a nuclear weapons state . South Korea said in August that Pyongyang now possesses up to 120 warheads – which Kim brandishes to intimidate neighbours. All but discarded are the twin principles that underpinned the west’s postwar Korea policy: reunification and denuclearisation. Heedless of first-term humiliations, Trump is again seeking a summit with Kim, whom he bizarrely terms a friend . “As long as I’m around, he [Kim] is going to be fine,” he boasted. Japan and South Korea don’t share his confidence. Both debate acquiring nuclear weapons in self-defence. Meanwhile, China’s president, Xi Jinping, having again bamboozled a fawning Trump at their Washington summit, is reportedly building nukes like there’s no tomorrow – which, at this rate, there may not be.
Addressing the UN general assembly, secretary-general António Guterres warned the world has reached “ the most dangerous nuclear moment ” since 1989. Global military spending reached nearly $3tn last year, while AI is increasing uncertainty over nuclear command-and-control, the UN was told. Annual spending on nukes is up by 20%. In a new paper published by the non-partisan Arms Control Association (ACA), Daryl Kimball, the head of the ACA in Washington, bemoaned the absence of high-level disarmament talks between the main nuclear powers and the lapsing of strategic arms limitation treaties. “The nuclear sword of Damocles still hangs over all of us. The threat has become more complex, and in the absence of new arms-control breakthroughs, we are headed for an unprecedented three-way buildup of Chinese, Russian, and US nuclear forces,” Kimball warned.
The fragmentation of the rules-based international order provides aggravating context. Trump-era blasphemies – that might makes right, that international law and the non-proliferation treaty’s binding obligation to disarm can be ignored, and that the UN charter and human rights norms don’t apply to authoritarian “strongman” leaders – all grease the slide into nuclear anarchy. Unresolved forever wars in Palestine, Iran, Ukraine, Myanmar, Yemen and Sudan are base components of a third world war. Potentially earth-shattering, too, is the fast-developing contest for control of space , notably the race to build nuclear-powered lunar bases. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty, under which more than 130 countries agreed the moon is no one’s property, is now routinely flouted by both governments and billionaires such as Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos. The weaponising of space by the US and others advances rapidly . Russia, for example, is reportedly developing an orbiting nuclear-armed anti-satellite weapon.
If the human race really is determined to bring the heavens crashing down in a mad dash for eschatological self-destruction, this is the surest, quickest way to go about it. More surprising than the irresponsible behaviour of politicians is the deafening public silence, the absence of large-scale protest in much of the world, the complacency, bordering on indifference, that accompanies this global march to oblivion. If and when a final reckoning comes, individuals who stayed silent will be complicit in their own undoing. Hiroshima is not a shrine. It’s the future.
after newsletter promotion
Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentator

articles.title_orig: Earnings season will fight the real world for attention
articles.title_zh: Earnings season will fight the real world for attention
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
To hear FactSet tell the story, the third-quarter earnings season, which starts this week, will be impressive.
FactSet ( FDS ), the big business data provider, is expecting corporate earnings to grow as much as 35% from a year ago. That's up from overall Wall Street expectations of earnings growth around 25%.
Read more: Diesel, gas prices jump in September: Now what?
If the earnings come close to either number, that might unleash a lot of buying from bulls.
But, first, investors will be judging everything against two giant external forces:
The ongoing political turmoil unleashed by the U.S.-Israel war against Iran and the continuing ugly war between Ukraine and Russia.
The U.S. midterm elections, which come in about three weeks on Nov. 3.
Increasingly, all these pieces of noise, for lack of a better term, are merging together into a kind of sonic boom that isn't letting up.
Global energy prices have soared because of the Middle East turmoil that now includes war between Saudi Arabia and Houthi rebels based in Yemen. On Saturday, an attack on Saudi Arabia's King Khalid International Airport killed at least 12 people and injured 300 to 399 more.
U.S. diesel and gasoline prices this year were at $6.28 a gallon and $4.36 a gallon as of Oct. 11, up 76% and 54%, respectively.
President Trump was talking about Russia adding 300,000 tons of diesel onto the global market, with more coming later on.
That assumes the supply is available. Ukraine attacks on Russian refineries have cut refinery runs as much as 27% , with diesel production down 20% to 30%.
Russia and Trump want Ukraine to stop its attacks. (Trump also called for Ukraine to replace president Volodymyr Zelenskyy.)
But Ukraine won't stop unless Russia stops attacking its energy infrastructure. So far, there's been no agreement.
And, of course, the U.S. midterms are coming, and President Trump is desperately trying to stave off major losses for the Republicans.
That brings us to the earnings this week. These will predominantly come from financial institutions, including:
Oct. 13 (Tuesday): JPMorgan Chase ( JPM ), Goldman Sachs ( GS ), UnitedHealth Group ( UNH ) and Wells Fargo ( WFC ).
Oct. 14 (Wednesday): Bank of America ( BAC ), Morgan Stanley ( MS ) and BlackRock ( BLK ).
Oct. 15 (Thursday): Charles Schwab ( SCHW ), Bank of New York Mellon ( BNY ) and US Bancorp ( USB )
Financial stocks generally have struggled in 2026. The financial sector of the Standard & Poor's 500 Index is basically flat on the year, according to Barchart.com data , while energy stocks are the leading sector, up 45%, followed by technology stocks, up 29.9%. The index is up 14.1%.
There are some nonfinancial giants reporting results, including Johnson & Johnson ( JNJ ) (Tuesday) and chip-equipment maker ASML ( ASML ) (Tuesday).
But the big non-financial report will be Taiwan Semiconductor ( TSMC ) on Thursday. Taiwan Semi fabricates chips for Nvidia and others.
Delta Air Lines ( DAL ) earnings report on Oct. 9 suggested demand is strong, despite higher fuel costs and surcharges on ticket prices. (Delta is focusing on business and affluent travel customers.)
As Monday, Oct. 12, is Columbus Day / Indigenous Peoples Day, U.S. bond markets will be closed. U.S. stock trading will operate as usual.
Goldman Sachs rethinks U.S. economy as interest rates stay higher
Heating bills expected to jump by $1,000 in some U.S. states this winter
How stocks will react when the catalysts are few
The thing to listen to is less the results but more the outlooks. The odds are the banks will cite a solid economy but note rising interest rates and stubborn inflation pressures. They may offer their views on the upcoming elections — but as vaguely as they can.
My guess is they will be more forthcoming on the economy and interest rates.
The 10-year Treasury yield was at 5.24% on Oct. 9, slightly off from its 2026 peak of 5.37% on Oct. 7. These were the highest levels on the primary determinant of mortgage rates since March 2002. Mortgage News Daily pegged the rate on a 30-year mortgage at about 7.5% on Oct. 9.
Meanwhile, the Labor Department will issue two reports on inflation during the week:
The Consumer Price Index report , due Wednesday (Oct 14).
The Producer Price Index report on Thursday (Oct. 15).
Also, the National Association of Realtors will publish its report on September existing home sales on Oct. 13. Zillow is expecting the report to show softening sales as mortgage rates are mostly parked around 7.5%.
The S&P 500 rose 1.2% on the week. The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed up 0.9%, and the Nasdaq Composite Index rose 0.6%.

articles.title_orig: Federal Judge Bars Trump Administration From Airing Publicly Funded Ads
articles.title_zh: Federal Judge Bars Trump Administration From Airing Publicly Funded Ads
articles.content_orig:
A federal judge on Sunday evening ordered the Trump administration to cancel any further airings of the controversial taxpayer-funded ads that promote President Donald Trump’s agenda.
Judge Jennifer Rochon granted a temporary restraining order requested by a coalition led by the nonprofit government watchdog group Common Cause, which had challenged the ad buys in a New York federal court.
The Justice Department told Rochon, an appointee of Joe Biden, late Saturday that the ad push was set to end Sunday night. But Rochon said that timing didn’t render the lawsuit moot and ordered the government to halt any further airings as of 6:45 p.m. ET.
Earlier, the government said in a filing to the court that it has already spent $19 million in taxpayer money on the ads.
The administration allocated $20 million for the ads, which were classified as “public service announcements,” from US Customs and Border Protection , CNN previously reported. An advertising company, LMD Agency Inc., “purchased media buys under the terms of the Order through Sunday, October 11, 2026, at an approximate cost of $19,000,000,” senior Department of Homeland Security official Holly Mehringer said in a sworn declaration in the case.
The Department of Homeland Security, which includes CBP, directed LMD “to not make any additional media buys past October 11,” she added. Mehringer noted there are “no plans” to purchase any additional ads.
Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle expressed concerns about the unprecedented ad campaign when it began late last month .
On October 5, Trump acknowledged the backlash and said “I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.,” his super PAC.
But six days later, the taxpayer-funded ads were still airing.
The Trump administration created at least 13 campaign-style ads, some of which have aired on TV networks including CBS, CNN, MS NOW, Fox News and Fox. Watchdog groups, including the nonprofit, nonpartisan Common Cause, said the ads mark a clear violation of appropriations law restricting the use of federal funding for propaganda or partisan communications. Common Cause and the Democratic National Committee separately sued the Trump administration over the ads.
In a response to the Common Cause lawsuit, the Justice Department said in a filing late Saturday that an effort to halt the spending should be denied because the ads “will not continue past tomorrow.”
The judge’s order Sunday would block any further ad buys for two weeks, so if the administration does consider resuming the ad campaign at taxpayer expense, DOJ lawyers would need to get the court order lifted.
The coalition that brought the suit praised the judge’s order, writing, “We are pleased the court acted swiftly to prevent more taxpayer dollars from being used for such blatantly unlawful political propaganda.”
CNN previously reported that Trump has personally driven the video ads, including helping select the imagery and videos used, according to a source familiar with the matter. Two Trump advisers familiar with the ads said they were being created in-house by the White House video team — which is part of the communications team, responsible for the administration’s public messaging — though at least one of them was produced by a pro-Trump meme group.
Mehringer, in the court filing, described the ads as “depicting the President of the United States and his administration’s various efforts related to protecting America’s borders, including enhancements of border security by combating drug trafficking,” though that is not the exact substance of many of the ads obtained by CNN.
And while the Justice Department conceded the ads “(attack) a generic list of ‘villains,’” it emphasized they did not “address any specific race, electoral candidate, or party.”
A White House spokesperson said Monday that Trump did not plan to reimburse the government for the money already spent on the ad buys, and Mehringer and other officials did not indicate any plans for a refund.
The White House Office of Management and Budget last month allocated $20 million in taxpayer money from CBP for what it called “OBBBA commemorative events.” (OBBBA is an abbreviation for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which Trump signed into law in 2025.)
Mehringer emphasized in her declaration that that money “did not fund the creation or production of any videos or media” and “only funded the airing of preexisting media.”
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin was pressed during an appearance Sunday on CBS News’ “Face the Nation” on whether the taxpayer dollars would be refunded.
“Anytime we can do a public service announcement and brag about America, I’m all about it,” Mullin said, taking aim at negative coverage of the Trump administration as he pointed to success in securing the border and lowering fentanyl-related deaths.
“We should be bragging about what’s happening inside America,” he said, adding, “I commend the opportunity of President Trump to give us the opportunity to brag about America.”

articles.title_orig: Bike Fire: Santa Clarita brush fire burns at least 475 acres; evacuation orders, warnings downgraded
articles.title_zh: Bike Fire: Santa Clarita brush fire burns at least 475 acres; evacuation orders, warnings downgraded
articles.content_orig:
SANTA CLARITA, Calif. (KABC) -- A fast-moving brush fire erupted in the Santa Clarita area Sunday afternoon, burning at least 475 acres. It is 68% contained.
The Bike Fire was reported around 1:30 p.m. Sunday at Cambria Estates Lane and Ravenhill Road, near Sand Canyon and Placerita Canyon roads, according to the Los Angeles County Fire Department. The fire was initially pegged at about 5 acres, but that number grew fast.
The fire initially prompted evacuation orders and warnings, but they have since been downgraded to an advisory.
Authorities said the blaze burned "with erratic fire behavior." By 4 p.m., officials said the fire had grown to 275 acres. Officials later said that accurate mapping reduced the fire acreage to 172 acres.
Just before 8:30 p.m. the fire had grown to 475 acres and remained 68% contained.
Two air tankers and two type 1 helicopters were being mobilized to assist in the firefighting effort.
The area experienced two other wildfires in the last week. The Bouquet Fire was reported Oct. 3 near Bouquet Canyon Road in the Angeles National Forest northeast of Santa Clarita. It was 83% contained as of Sunday after burning 1,048 acres.
The Danny Fire was reported on Oct. 8 about 2 miles south of Gorman, though forward progression was stopped quickly and that fire was 96% contained at 150 acres.
City News Service contributed to this report.
