articles.title_orig: Rachel slams Southern California, bringing high tides, flooding, coastal damage
articles.title_zh: Rachel slams Southern California, bringing high tides, flooding, coastal damage
articles.content_orig:
Here’s what you need to know:
After damaging weekend high tides, weather service says more to come
Forecasters say Sunday saw the greatest risk from high tides, but Monday and Tuesday mornings will also bring surges that could damage vulnerable, lowing-lying areas in coastal Southern California.
Currently, the most extreme high tides are occurring around 10 a.m., with milder secondary high tides around 11 p.m.
Preliminary readings near Long Beach and Santa Monica measured Sunday morning’s high tide at 7.6 feet, qualifying as minor flooding. The National Weather Service estimated high tides for Monday and Tuesday mornings around 7.5 feet.
The weather service warned that significant beach erosion was likely and noted an increased risk for ocean drownings due to large waves and strong rip currents. The Coastal Flood Advisory for the county is set to lift Tuesday at 2 p.m.
The secondary evening high tides have not been reaching flood levels. Saturday evening’s high tide registered at 6.6 feet near Long Beach and 6.4 feet near Santa Monica.
Heavy surf, red-tagged homes, a battered boardwalk: Long Beach confronts costly climate reality
A trio of storms since early September has put considerable strain on the historic Long Beach boardwalk, which collapsed further between 64th and 65th Place on Seaside Walk during a weekend of heavy surf.
The city’s public works team and its Parks, Recreation and Marine bureau were working to secure it, putting up sandbags and rebuilding the berm to stop water intrusion. Officials are also continuing to monitor coastal homes that were red- and yellow-tagged during the weekend onslaught.
Two people lifted to safety in swift-water rescue in San Bernardino
The San Bernardino County Fire Department rescued two individuals trapped in a flood control channel that feeds into the Santa Ana River on Sunday morning, the Fire Department said in a Facebook post .
The department received a call at 8:40 a.m. from an adult man who said he was trapped in rising flood waters. Firefighters found him and an adult woman inside a tunnel that feeds the main flood channel. A first responder lowered into the channel via a cable attached to a fire truck’s ladder overhanging the channel and rescued the individuals one at a time.
Neither of the two individuals — whom the Fire Department said lived in a camp outside the channel — said they were injured, and both declined evaluations by paramedics.
The San Bernardino County Sheriff’s Department had flown along flood channels over the last few days, alerting individuals that a storm was approaching and advising them to seek higher ground. The rescued man acknowledged that he had heard the warnings but said he had sheltered in the tunnel in previous storms and didn’t think the flooding would get too bad, according to the Facebook post.
Video of the rescue showed brown water rushing through the channel, not far below the tunnel entrance. A stream was also flowing through the tunnel and into the channel.
Rachel deluges Southwest with rain, but battered coast catches a break
Wide swaths of the Southwest were deluged Sunday as the remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel weakened and moved inland, but coastal communities already battered by high surf emerged with less damage than some officials feared.
The National Weather Service said Sunday morning that Rachel was no longer a tropical storm. But danger remained as waves crashed into beachfront homes in Long Beach, large rocks and mud hurtled down a mountain onto a highway south of Palm Desert, and flood water submerged the parking lot of a casino on the Las Vegas Strip.
Video: Heavily damaged Long Beach home close to collapsing into ocean
A home along the Long Beach Peninsula appeared severely damaged on Sunday.
The boardwalk was destroyed near the home, which according to Long Beach Fire Department lifeguards had begun to collapse Sunday morning.
Warning: Saltwater poses unique risks to EVs with lithium-ion batteries
Ahead of what is expected to be a wet El Niño season, Long Beach — which took a considerable pounding Saturday by high surf and Tropical Storm Rachel — has issued a warning reminding residents that saltwater poses unique safety risks for electric vehicles.
EVs, like cars, trucks, e-bikes and golf carts, are often powered by lithium-ion batteries. When those batteries are exposed to saltwater, it can create what is known as a “salt bridge” within the battery pack, which can cause the batteries to overheat, catch fire or explode, according to a warning the city issued Sunday.
The city said EV owners in flood-prone coastal areas should move their vehicles away before the storm to avoid saltwater inundation. And much like their gas-powered counterparts, EVs should not be driven through flooded saltwater areas.
Here’s what to do and, importantly, what not to do, in case your EV was flooded with saltwater:
How Newport Beach adjusted strategy to avoid more flooding—for now
Newport Beach spent the weekend working around the clock to protect homes after waves breached the city’s defenses along Balboa Peninsula.
Since Hurricane Marie pounded Southern California in early September, the city has been building and reinforcing berms along its peninsula. But on Friday, a combination of high surf and unusually high tides, often called king tides, hit the Orange County suburb and broke through the berms along the Balboa Peninsula.
Residents along Balboa Boulevard suddenly found themselves and their vehicles in knee-deep saltwater, prompting Seimone Jurjis, city manager and director of emergency services, to declare a local emergency.
George Rios, spokesperson for Newport Beach, said the declaration allowed the city to use more resources such as contractors and heavy machinery to shore up the berms.
That day, city crews and contractors fanned out to rebuild the berms. They opened tide valves and ran pumps to drain the water from the street. Residents recalled seeing the water recede within two hours after the city’s response.
The city then spent Saturday building 23-foot berms along the Balboa Peninsula. The city added additional berms in west Newport Beach.
About 20 workers reinforced the berms  Saturday night and early Sunday to prevent a repeat of Friday’s flooding. They also had 40 pumps on standby in case the tide  breached the berms.
The around-the-clock work paid off; there were no reports of major damage or flooding. Residents were grateful for the city’s response and its continued efforts to defend the homes throughout the weekend.
Georgia Rios, spokesperson for Newport Beach, said this wouldn’t be the last time the city needed to defend beachfront homes, as more king tide events are expected in late October, as well as in November and December.
Rios said the city planned to maintain the berms to protect homes along the peninsula.
“In the long term, with the elevated surf as well as El Niño, we’re seeing the need to really keep them in place,” she said.
City officials have not determined what the response will cost the city, but they will lean on and work with Orange County leaders to determine how best to respond to the weather conditions.
Man dies at Dockweiler Beach; authorities investigate possible drowning due to storm conditions
A possibly unhoused adult man died on Sunday morning on Dockweiler Beach in Playa del Rey, according to the L.A. County Fire Dept. Lifeguard Division.
The incident occurred in the 6900 block of Pacific Avenue, on the beach near Tower 42, not far from Marina Del Rey. The 911 call came in around 8:30 a.m.
Two bystanders had seen a man “acting erratically near the water line,” said Jake Miller, an ocean lifeguard specialist with the department. “He was in and out of the water, swimming and on land. They were on a morning walk and saw him rolling around near the shore on the surfline.”
The lifeguard on patrol responded immediately and initiated CPR, Miller said. Soon after, two additional lifeguard units arrived.

articles.content_orig:
The energy careers of senior Communist Party cadres have given them technical expertise, foresight and management skills
With the rising strategic significance of energy, especially due to the need to support China’s artificial intelligence (AI) development, members of the Communist Party’s 20th Central Committee with energy backgrounds – the country’s “movers and shakers” in this strategic sector – merit closer attention.
Among them are former or current power-company executives, petroleum managers, nuclear-safety officials and specialists in water administration. Many built their expertise over decades, establishing themselves as energy technocrats before taking on responsibilities beyond their original industries. Their biographies reveal a recurring route into political leadership – deep specialisation first and diversification of political experience later, highlighting the growing presence and power of this leadership cohort.
Our data set identifies 34 energy sector members, including 21 full members and 13 alternates. They account for 10.2 per cent of the 205 full members, 7.6 per cent of the 171 alternates and 9 per cent of the combined membership. Three of them were elected to the Politburo in October 2022, representing 12.5 per cent of its 24 members. As of this year, their median ages are 64 among full members and 60 among alternates.
By October 2022, 29 of the 34 had at least 10 years of energy experience. This included 16 of the 21 full members. Nineteen had careers spanning 20 years or more.

articles.title_orig: South Carolina Senate rivals spar over Iran war, AI and Trump in fiery debate
articles.title_zh: South Carolina Senate rivals spar over Iran war, AI and Trump in fiery debate
articles.content_orig:
Republican Sen. Darline Graham of South Carolina and Democratic challenger Annie Andrews clashed Sunday night in their first and perhaps only debate of the general election, tangling over President Donald Trump’s “one big, beautiful bill,” the high costs of gas and goods, the Iran war and AI data centers.
South Carolina is a ruby-red state where Trump remains popular among Republican voters. But the race has tightened in the closing stretch of the campaign, and Democrats believe they have a shot at knocking off Graham, who was appointed to fill her brother Lindsey Graham’s Senate seat after his sudden death in July. The top Senate Republican super PAC has pledged to spend $5 million to shore up Graham’s campaign.
At the start of the debate, hosted in Columbia by South Carolina ETV , Darline Graham noted that Sunday night marked exactly three months since her brother unexpectedly died at age 71.
Andrews, a pediatrician, sought to portray Graham, who previously led a state agency, as an inexperienced empty suit who refuses to stand up to Trump or his unpopular policies. She mocked Graham as “the White House’s ambassador to South Carolina.”
Graham attacked Andrews as the “most radical liberal” to run in South Carolina and as sympathetic to the Democratic Socialist Party. “Annie Andrews will not stand up to the Socialist Democratic Party; she’s only going to join them,” Graham said — a characterization Andrews rejected.
Graham has “been told to come out here and call me Bernie, Ocasio, Mamdani — that’s what’s in her script. But the truth is my name is Annie Andrews, and there shouldn’t be any confusion about that,” Andrews said. “The truth is I support the Second Amendment, I believe we need a secure border, and we need to deport illegal immigrants who break the law. ... The real difference between me and Sen. Graham is that I will stand up to my own party, and I will always put South Carolina first.”
Graham and Andrews are running for a full six-year Senate term; the winner will make history as the first female senator elected from South Carolina. The debate also featured Libertarian Kasie Whitener.
Graham and Andrews tussled over issue after issue. As the country faces Social Security insolvency, Andrews said she would raise caps to make wealthier people pay more but would not hike the retirement age. She added that Republicans like Graham want to privatize Social Security so “Washington insiders” can profit. “Unfortunately, my opponent is in the race to do what Washington insiders tell her,” she said.
Graham shot back that she understands what people in her state are facing. When her parents died at a young age, Social Security benefits helped her and her brother survive. Graham said Andrews’ criticism of Trump’s “one big, beautiful bill” is misplaced because it lowered taxes on tips and Social Security. “You called it the one big, ugly bill, so here you are deceiving the people of South Carolina,” Graham said.
On affordability, Graham said she has “lived paycheck to paycheck” before and acknowledged that “gas prices are high right now. ... I feel the pain, too.” She said that she supports suspending the gas tax and that easing regulations on drilling would permanently bring prices down.
Andrews pinned blame for high gas prices on Graham, who she said voted several times against a war powers resolution to restrict Trump’s war with Iran.
“The war is the exact reason we now have record-high gas and diesel prices. Farmers are getting crushed, and everything costs more,” Andrews said. “My opponent is the only one who had the opportunity to vote to end the war, but three times in a row she voted to continue it.”
Andrews also dinged Graham for admitting during a previous debate that “ national security is not my thing .” “South Carolina, if your surgeon said that appendectomies aren’t really his thing, would you still hand him a scalpel? No,” Andrews said. “So why would we hand Darline Graham a full term in the U.S. Senate? She is unserious and unqualified.”
Graham retorted that she wants the war to end, like everyone does, but said she believes in “peace through strength.” Then, she went after Andrews over the national security quip.
“But talking about not my thing, let’s talk about what’s not your thing. Your thing apparently is not being honest with the people of South Carolina. At least I’m honest. If I don’t know something, I am glad to say it, and I’ll say it again tonight,” Graham said without getting specific. “But you have, you are deceiving the people of South Carolina. You have flip-flopped on everything. There’s so many social media posts out there to prove it. Shame on you!”
The proliferation of data centers, which power artificial intelligence companies, has become a major flash point in the midterm elections.
Andrews went right after Graham on the issue, nicknaming her “Data Center Darline.” Andrews said her data-center plan calls for a “two-year moratorium, protections to ensure your rates don’t go up and a return to real local control.”
Graham fired back that stopping construction of all data centers would allow China to win the race for AI dominance. She said she voted for the Ratepayer Protection Act , which aims to shift higher energy costs from building data centers from consumers onto AI companies.
“Under her Bernie Sanders plan, a two-year moratorium, that is dangerous to the national security of our country, because in two years China is going to be so far ahead [that] we are going to be in so much trouble,” Graham said, adding that local communities should decide whether data centers get built in their backyards.
“I want communities to decide. She wants the federal government to decide.”
Scott Wong is a senior congressional reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s Zelensky attack, Russia diesel deal draw criticism in U.S. and abroad
articles.title_zh: Trump’s Zelensky attack, Russia diesel deal draw criticism in U.S. and abroad
articles.content_orig:
By agreeing to open Russia’s taps and release hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel into a starving global market, the Kremlin has achieved something that raw military might on the battlefields of eastern Ukraine could never deliver.
The deal, which involves suspending fuel export sanctions on Russia for six months to allow for diesel sales at market prices, will be a welcome boon for a Russian economy that is creaking under the strain of a war in Ukraine that has dragged on far longer than anticipated.
But for Vladimir Putin, Russia’s strongman president, the real benefit isn’t the billions of dollars in fresh revenue. It is the wedge this deal, and the rhetoric around it, drives right through the heart of the Western alliance, which has aimed to isolate Moscow over it’s war in Ukraine.
US President Donald Trump spelled out the new and extraordinary reality in stark terms as he mocked the angry reaction of Ukraine’s wartime leader, Volodymyr Zelensky, who derided the deal as a “weak decision by a strong partner” that provides “extra money for this war.”
“We said you can do whatever you want to Russia. Don’t hit the refineries because that’s a world problem that’s caused and he wants to make problems for the world. He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers,” Trump said before calling for a new Ukrainian leader, essentially blaming high global fuel prices, especially acute in the United States, on Ukraine.
Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney sided with Zelensky as the two leaders spoke on Sunday, saying that the agreement stands “in direct opposition to the efforts of Ukraine, Canada, and our allies to create peace and stability in Europe.”
In recent months, relentless Ukrainian drone strikes, flying deep into Russian territory with terrifying precision, have systematically crippled oil refineries that serve as both the economic engine and the fuel tank for Russia’s military.
Amid domestic fuel shortages and severe production cuts, the Kremlin suspended all diesel exports this month so that it had enough for its own needs — a stunning setback for a country that used to be the second-biggest diesel exporter in the world before the Ukraine war.
Whether Russia can actually provide the promised diesel or not, by framing the Ukrainian drone strikes on refineries as an assault on American interests, Washington is effectively aligning its economic priorities with Moscow’s survival — even as analysts have suggested the deal is unlikely to dramatically move the needle on diesel prices.
The US has powerful levers it can pull to get Ukraine to play ball.
Washington no longer provides money and weapons to Kyiv. But vital American intelligence sharing — the digital backbone of Ukrainian defense — risks being cut off if Ukraine now continues to strike at the Russian infrastructure Trump wants left untouched. The threat is real — the US did just that in the wake of the notorious Oval Office blowup last year.
Mindful of the risk , Zelensky has indicated he is willing to cooperate, but only if Russia does the same. “Ukraine will be ready to stop striking Russian oil refineries if Russia stops striking our energy infrastructure,” Zelensky said in a recent statement.
For Ukraine, this entire episode may seem like yet another bitter, existential betrayal by an American leader who has at times acknowledged a begrudging respect for Kyiv’s bold military tactics. Now, its most effective asymmetric weapon — relentless drone strikes on oil refineries — is being undermined and may be neutralized, not by Russian anti-air batteries, but by American diplomatic pressure along with Trump’s irrepressible urge to do a deal with the Kremlin.
In Moscow, on the other hand, the mood is upbeat.
“The Russian side confirmed its willingness to supply oil and petroleum products to the US market and global markets at large,” Putin said in an official statement after a prearranged telephone call with Trump on Friday night.
“I am convinced this will have a positive impact on the entire global economy,” he added.
Privately, the Kremlin leader must be rubbing his hands with glee.
Both he and Trump want Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries to immediately stop.
Both want Ukraine’s president to be replaced with someone who will agree a quick deal.
And just a few weeks after Trump signed a bill into law, sponsored by the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, allowing for punishing sanctions to be imposed on any country that bought Russian oil, Washington has now become a customer itself.
All at once, it seems, a battered but relatively unified Western front that has stood against resource-rich Moscow for more than four years looks like it is being dealt another powerful blow.

articles.title_orig: UK PM Andy Burnham says it is ‘clear’ Russia interfered in 2016 Brexit vote
articles.title_zh: UK PM Andy Burnham says it is ‘clear’ Russia interfered in 2016 Brexit vote
articles.content_orig:
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said it is “clear” that Russia interfered in the country’s 2016 Brexit vote, warning French and German voters of the same threat.
“I asked the question coming to Downing Street: Was there interference in the 2016 referendum from Russia? And I’ve had the clear answer that yes, there was,” Burnham said in an interview with The Rest Is Politics podcast released on Sunday.
Burnham’s comments mark the first time a UK prime minister has publicly acknowledged that Russia interfered in the UK’s vote to leave the European Union. Burnham did not provide evidence for or details on the claim.
He said that “these things are important now to put clearly on the record, and, I believe, help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia.”
Burnham said he spoke with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz about possible links between Russia and the far-right Alternative for Germany party when the two leaders met last week in Berlin.
In his address to the United Nations General Assembly in September, Burnham also condemned Russia’s attempt to interfere in the UK’s 2019 general election.
According to a 2020 report by Parliament’s Intelligence and Security Committee, the UK government had failed to ask for a deep assessment of Russia’s interference in the 2016 referendum. The report did confirm that Russia had meddled in the 2014 Scottish independence referendum , however.
Russia has repeatedly denied meddling in Western democracies or interfering in another country’s elections or referendums, casting the UK as being gripped by “anti-Russian hysteria”.
Last month, Burnham argued that the UK should reconsider options for a future relationship with the EU, including rejoining the bloc, reigniting the decisive debate more than a decade after the historic vote.
He said that the UK’s departure from the bloc had failed to fulfil Brexit supporters’ pledge of “taking back control”, and instead has made the UK weaker economically and on immigration.

The city’s public works team and its Parks, Recreation and Marine bureau were working to secure it, putting up sandbags and rebuilding the berm to stop water intrusion. Officials are also continuing to monitor coastal homes that were red- and yellow-tagged during the weekend onslaught.
Mud and sand inundated the Long Beach Peninsula as waves breached the boardwalk’s protective timber bulkhead.
Inspectors red-tagged nine buildings along Seaside Walk, the Long Beach Post reported, with one building yellow-tagged. Red indicates an address is unsafe to enter, while yellow restricts use.
That fact that the damage to the boardwalk is cumulative presents a particular challenge, Long Beach Fire Department spokesperson Melanie Miller said Sunday.
“The collapse began when [Hurricane] Marie came,” in early September, she said, “and it’s been building off of that. Then Hurricane Polo, now [Tropical Storm] Rachel. It’s been continuous damage since then.
“There have been preparations — we even deployed 3,000-pound sandbags,” Miller added, “but you can only do so much during low tide; there are limited windows of opportunity. And the dynamics are working against you.”
Long Beach Mayor Rex Richardson said that the city was taking the situation “very seriously” and that it underscored “an importance to be incredibly serious in our region and in our state around climate resilience and coastal resiliency.”
He said the crumbling boardwalk is a historic thread in the city’s fabric.
“This is one of the oldest boardwalks in California and lots of memories were made on that boardwalk,” he said in an interview Sunday. “If we want to retain these iconic spaces on our coastline, it’s going to take real investment to make sure that we have an iconic, quality waterfront, a coastline that is resilient and acknowledges the changing climate.”
That investment will be expensive, Richardson said.
“You have to build more climate-resilient infrastructure. Because 100 years ago it wasn’t necessarily anticipated that we’d have this cadence of pressure — three major storm systems in six weeks is unprecedented in this region.”
The city of Long Beach has designed a “seven-point plan,” formalized shortly after Hurricane Marie, that addresses repairing what’s been damaged, putting more sand back on the beach, creating additional layers of protection and pursuing longer-term solutions and funding, Laath Martin, a spokesperson for the city manager’s office, said.
“As we responded to [Marie], we also looked at future plans and ways to address [the storms] in the immediate, moderate and long term,” Martin said. “We’ve had two additional storms since then. Some of the work is underway, and some is coming within days, weeks and months, depending.”
As of now, the city of Long Beach is in emergency response mode. It’s reinforcing the boardwalk with lumber and using the aforementioned 3,000-pound sandbags to “deflect wave energy on the beach side of the bulkhead, the seawall,” Martin said. “It takes a lot of the brunt of the damage.”
Martin said the city had accelerated certain projects to start as soon as the week of Oct. 19, particularly the Alamitos Bay Entrance Channel Dredging Project, which will relocate sand from the Peninsula and widen the beach by about 200 feet.
“We have to do a few things before then to ready it,” Martin said, “so our crews can safely work in those conditions.”
Longer term, the city has secured a contractor to carry out permanent repairs. The cost is estimated at $1.5 million to $3.6 million, Martin said. The money will come from the city’s Tidelands Emergency Reserves for coastal projects.
“Because we’re using a lot of materials right now to make emergency repairs to keep people safe, we then have to purchase more materials to do the permanent repairs,” Martin said. “That’s why there’s such a wide range.”
Martin said the city expected to complete permanent repairs to the bulkhead and boardwalk by the end of this year.
“With El Niño, we expect more storms. They built the timeline around anticipated storms to the best in our ability,” he said. “But this far in advance, you never know.”

articles.title_orig: Saudi Arabia vows retaliation against Houthis after airport strike kills at least 12
articles.title_zh: Saudi Arabia vows retaliation against Houthis after airport strike kills at least 12
articles.content_orig:
A projectile has struck Saudi Arabia’s King Khalid International airport, killing one person and injuring 11, according to the country’s civil aviation authority.
The General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) identified the deceased in Sunday’s attack as a Pakistani resident and said the injured were transferred to several hospitals for medical care.
The strike on terminals 3 and 4, which serve domestic flights, occurred a day after a Houthi missile hit the airport, killing 12 people and wounding more than 300, according to the Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen.
India’s embassy in Saudi Arabia said one of its citizens died on Sunday due to injuries sustained in Saturday’s attack, bringing the death toll to 13.
Following Sunday’s attack, GACA said damage assessments and safety inspections of the airport were under way.
A witness on board a taxiing aircraft at the airport told the Reuters news agency that a projectile struck the tarmac next to several parked planes at about 8:30pm (17:30 GMT) on Sunday, causing a fire.
The witness said the aircraft returned to the gate, where the passengers disembarked and were told to leave.
The Riyadh airport has been struck four times in the past five days. Houthi attacks on King Khalid airport on Thursday killed at least three Saudi citizens, including a pilot, according to GACA.
The airport has been closed since Saturday’s attack, which was the deadliest in the country since the US-Israel war on Iran began in late February.
The Houthis claimed responsibility for the strikes before Sunday’s.
The airport attacks have escalated the war in Yemen and threaten to draw in the US military. US President Donald Trump says he is weighing whether to join the fight against the Houthis.
The escalation puts further pressure on global oil supplies and prices, as well as on commercial shipping through the Bab al-Mandeb strait off the Yemeni coast, a crucial alternative waterway to the Strait of Hormuz.
Trump had said he intends to speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who is seeking help against the Houthis, but there were no signs on Sunday that the US president had followed up on his claim.
There are fears that US intervention could prompt the Houthis to halt shipping through Bab al-Mandeb, further restricting the flow of oil out of the Gulf.
The rebels seized key areas along the strait last month. The Saudi-led coalition, backing forces loyal to Yemen’s internationally recognised government, has been trying to seize them back.

articles.title_orig: Tropical Storm Rachel swamps San Diego County with heavier-than-expected rain
articles.title_zh: Tropical Storm Rachel swamps San Diego County with heavier-than-expected rain
articles.content_orig:
Remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel hit San Diego County harder than expected before dawn Sunday, sending surf crashing into beachside cottages in Oceanside, flooding parts of Highway 101 near Carlsbad, and triggering several water rescues.
The quick-moving system also knocked out power to more than 330 customers in the Otay Mesa-San Ysidro area, and significantly tore into the berm that protects the Del Mar Lifeguard headquarters. The Tijuana River estuary flooded a street in Imperial Beach.
The National Weather Service had forecast that roughly 1 inch of rain would fall in coastal cities and 2 to 3 inches would fall and drench inland mountains and valleys between late Saturday night and early Sunday.
The outer ridge of Rachel surged ashore about 8 p.m.— earlier than anticipated — and let loose. By 12:30 p.m. Sunday, the system had dropped 5.16 inches on Palomar Mountain, 2.69 inches in eastern Oceanside, 2.11 inches in the Bay Ho neighborhood of San Diego, 1.75 inches in Carlsbad, and 1.36 inches at Camp Pendleton.
San Diego International Airport got 0.92 inches.
The weather service reported varying amounts of precipitation around the region: Julian, 3.04 inches; Otay Mountain, 2.99 inches; Poway, 2.69 inches; Ramona, 2.52 inches; Alpine, 2.30 inches; Fallbrook, 2.22 inches; Valley Center, 2.10 inches; Rancho Bernardo, 2.06 inches; San Diego Country Estates, 2.06 inches; Escondido, 1.81 inches; Campo, 1.81 inches; Santee, 1.56 inches; National City, 1.52 inches; Borrego Springs, 1.14 inches.
Despite the weather service’s Saturday plea that the public stay away from local beaches because of the possibility of coastal flooding, crowds still flocked to the coast. In Oceanside, motorists lined up to drive on The Strand early Sunday to get a close look at the water. Cars and trucks were soon being hit by waves.
A crowd also gathered south of the pier to watch Bruce Parker, a well-known local who goes by the nickname Trenchcoat Guy, stand on The Strand and repeatedly get hit by big waves.
“Why am I doing this?” said Parker, 79. “Because it’s fun.”
Before long, other people were doing the same, including children.
“We just like watching Mother Nature,” said Collin Smith of Encinitas, who was standing with his son, Cedric. “It doesn’t happen every day.”
Down in South County, the swollen Tijuana River estuary flowed onto Seacrest Drive in Imperial Beach.
By Sunday morning, San Diego Fire-Rescue personnel had responded to more than 50 traffic collisions, five transformer fires and 17 incidents reporting wires being down in the storm, Deputy Fire Chief Dan Eddy said in an Instagram post.
City firefighters and lifeguards also participated in water rescues, including one in the La Mesa area and one in Coronado.
Heartland Fire & Rescue crews worked with San Diego firefighters after a man was swept into a culvert near 70th Street and Alvarado Road, near the border of La Mesa and San Diego, shortly after 10 p.m. Saturday. The man was trapped in rapidly rising stormwater, officials said.
“An extensive rescue operation was undertaken, and the victim was successfully extracted,” Heartland Fire said in an Instagram post. The man was transported to the hospital in stable condition.
A second water rescue occurred near Imperial Avenue and 33rd Street in the Logan Heights area involving a person trapped in a storm drain tunnel, a San Diego spokesperson said.
In that incident, reported shortly after 11:45 p.m. Saturday, a lifeguard rescue team built a rope system to extricate the person. More than 30 personnel, including two lifeguard swift water rescue teams and four fire engines, worked for more than an hour to free the man. He was able to walk away, the spokesperson said.
San Diego lifeguards assisted with a third rescue early Sunday morning after Coast Guard officials received a 911 call around 4 a.m. from a man on a sailboat that ran aground near Coronado and was taking on water.
The Coast Guard sent a small boat crew who located the sailboat near Coronado Beach, but they couldn’t get near it because of the shallow water and hazardous surf conditions, a Coast Guard spokesperson said.
A helicopter crew sent from Ventura lowered a rescue swimmer down to assist. The man was trapped inside the sailboat cabin and was sticking his head out of a small hatch. The rescue swimmer gave the man a snorkel to help him breathe and worked to rip the top off the boat to free him from the cabin. He was rescued around 7:15 a.m. and transported to receive medical care, the spokesperson said.

articles.title_orig: Big Boss Interview | Microsoft President: Britain Should Write World's AI Rules
articles.title_zh: Big Boss Interview | Microsoft President: Britain Should Write World's AI Rules
articles.content_orig:
Artificial intelligence is advancing faster than the safeguards around it, and industry self-regulation is "not sufficient any longer". That is according to Brad Smith, president of Microsoft. Speaking to Will Bain on BBC's Big Boss Interview, Mr Smith said the world should worry more about AI safety than about any previous generation of digital technology in his 33 years in the industry.
Microsoft is one of the world's largest AI developers and an investor in OpenAI. Mr Smith's comments set out a position that goes beyond the "tremendous self-regulation" praised in a recent White House AI accord.
"Right now I'd argue that AI is moving forward faster than the speed of safety," Mr Smith said. "That's not good for the protection of the public. It's not even good for the industry itself."
Mr Smith set out three measures. The first is a "safety brake or emergency brake" on any AI system controlling autonomous devices or critical infrastructure, an idea often described as a kill switch. He said it should sit in the companies running the models and in the cloud infrastructure they run on. The second is a legal obligation to report incidents: if AI agents "break loose" and break into systems, the victims should be told, as they are after a data breach.
The third measure, which he called the biggest and most important, is whether government evaluators should have to sign off frontier models before release. "Just remember, right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI," he said. He added that cartons of milk and passenger aircraft are subject to inspection and certification.
He said the UK was the country best placed to lead. The AI Security Institute, he said, has the strongest technical capability in the world to test AI models: "It's the United Kingdom. They are the best." In his account, the US began building similar capability and then slowed down. Asked about Anthropic declining UK testing of one of its models, he said the question now was when developers should be required to satisfy a government regulator that a product is safe before it is released. He described Britain as "a bridge across the Atlantic and across the English Channel". He also noted that in Washington, people "don't look at London the same way they look at Brussels".
Mr Smith also responded to Vice President JD Vance, who had accused Microsoft of abusing the H-1B visa system more than any other US company. Mr Smith said the vice president's staff "got the maths wrong". He said about 80% of the company's 6,000 visa applications were for existing employees, every green card applicant was already employed by Microsoft, and the company hired 9,000 Americans last year.
On data centres, he said the cost of new grid capacity "should not be the neighbours… it should be the industry itself".
Producer: Olie D'Albertanson

articles.title_orig: Trump faces growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia
articles.title_zh: Trump faces growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia
articles.content_orig:
US President Donald Trump is facing a growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia as the Iran war continues to impact global energy prices.
Trump on Friday announced that Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately "to the American and global marketplace" followed by several other shipments.
That is despite signing legislation to authorise fresh US sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas just weeks ago.
The move has been criticised by some Republican and Democratic lawmakers, who believe the deal violates US laws.
As well as the initial release of 300,000 tonnes of diesel, Trump said Russia would then supply 500,000 tonnes in November and one million more after that.
This would be followed by a further three million tonnes, which would be delivered "within a short period" dependent on the condition of its refineries, which have been attacked by Ukraine during the ongoing war between the two countries.
"Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.
Russia's Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak confirmed these numbers to Tass, the country's state-owned news agency, saying the export volume could reach three million tonnes per month in future.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has called the deal a gift to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended".
It is understood the US Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, but other assets like those in American banks are still frozen.
A group of seven senators - four Republicans and three Democrats – on Sunday said the deal violated US laws, urging Trump to "reverse course".
"The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians," the lawmakers said.
They added that Congress had "explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin's brutal war against Ukraine".
The statement was signed by Republicans Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Thom Tillis and John Curtis, as well as Democrats Jeanne Shaheen, Richard Blumenthal and Ron Wyden.
Not everyone is opposed to the deal. Republican Thomas Massie, who has sparred with Trump a number of issues, said the US should lift sanctions on all petroleum products.
Trump's Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News the agreement would work through existing legal channels the US has to help bring prices down and that anyone in Congress who said it would not was wrong.
Global fuel prices have soared since the US-Israel war with Iran began at the end of February, with the fighting severely disrupting supplies of crude oil - a key ingredient in petrol and diesel.
The rising prices have become a key issue for Americans ahead of next month's midterms elections, which will determine if Trump's Republican Party maintains control of Congress.
Polls show a majority of Americans disapprove of his handling of the economy and the war in Iran and he has been searching for ways to ease his party's political pain.
The toll the war is taking has been acutely felt by US agricultural states, which rely heavily on diesel to operate farming machinery and to transport their products to market.
The average diesel price in the US is currently $6.28 (£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA, down from the record high of $6.53 recorded at the end of September.
Analysts have questioned whether Russia is capable of providing that quantity of diesel and the extent to which doing so will ease prices for American consumers.
The US uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tonnes this month, it amounts to approximately half of the US daily consumption.
It is not only at home that Trump is facing opposition to his diesel deal with Russia. A number of international leaders have criticised it, including Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who said the US and other allies of Ukraine should focus on ramping up pressure on Russia to end the war.
Meanwhile, Trump announced in Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had reached an "energy ceasefire" but did not give more details. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky welcomed this but there was no response from Moscow.

Tim Mulkerin is a freelance writer, editor, and social media manager who has been working in digital media and the tech world since 2016.
He has a bachelor's degree in art history and is currently pursuing a master's degree in communicative sciences and disorders from New York University. He lives in Brooklyn, New York.
If you’re looking for hints and answers for Strands for Sunday, October 11, 2026, read on—I’ll share some clues and tips, and finally the solution to the puzzle with the theme “They don’t make ‘em like they used to.”
For an easy way to come back to our Strands hints every day, bookmark this page . You can also find our past hints there as well, in case you want to know what you missed in a previous puzzle. (If you play Wordle or Connections , check out our hints for those games, too.)
Below, I’ll give you some oblique hints at today’s Strands answers. And farther down the page, I’ll reveal the spangram and the answers. Scroll slowly and take just the hints you need!
How you might describe outdated tech.
Devices you don’t see around much anymore.
We’re about to give away the answers to today’s Strands puzzle.
Today’s spangram is OLDFASHIONED.
The theme words today are TELEGRAM, PAGER, INKWELL, ICEBOX, TYPEWRITER.
Here’s what the board looks like when the puzzle is solved:
I’ll look for words related to quality or craftsmanship and see if that gets me anywhere.
GREET, GRAM, WELL, HEAL, HEALER, FADS, and KARMA aren’t theme words. PAGE isn’t either, but PAGER is, along the left. 🔵It must be retro or outdated tech.
Hmm, what else could fit here? Fax machines, rolodexes, car phones, cassettes? I can make FAX and FAXES in the upper right, but neither work. I can also make BOX and BOXES. Oh, it’s ICEBOX. 🔵

INKWELL is in the bottom left. 🔵
You can find the Strands game on the New York Times website and in the NYT Games app.
When you start playing, you’ll see a game board with an assortment of letters, flanked by a clue that gives a hint at the board’s theme—this will be a phrase, like “Better with age.” Your job is to find the hidden words within the board that reflect the puzzle’s theme.
The most important word to find is the “spangram,” a word that more explicitly states the puzzle’s theme. (For example, the spangram for the puzzle with the theme "Better with age" is FERMENTED, which describes products that are, you guessed it, better with age.) The spangram will span the entire game board, either from left to right or top to bottom (hence the name). When you find the spangram, it will be highlighted in yellow. Solving the spangram usually makes the rest of the puzzle much easier to complete.
In Strands, words can travel any direction (up, down, left, right, and diagonal), and you will only use each letter once. There is only one correct solution. When you correctly identify one of the puzzle’s words (for example, KOMBUCHA, MISO, or KIMCHI), it will be highlighted in blue.
If you are struggling to solve the puzzle, you can submit any non-theme words you see (as long as they are four letters or more) to receive credit toward a single hint. If you submit three non-theme words, the “Hint” button will be clickable; if you click it, all of the letters in one of the theme words will be highlighted for you. You will still have to link these highlighted letters in the right order to form one of the theme words. If there is already a hint on the board and you use another hint before solving for that word, that word’s letter order will be revealed.
Unlike Connections and Wordle, you cannot fail Strands. When you submit guesses, you will either correctly identify an answer, receive credit toward a hint, or the text will shake back and forth, indicating that the word you submitted is too short or not valid. You can't run out of guesses, and there is no time limit.
You win when you’ve correctly used all the letters on the board, meaning that you have identified the spangram and all of the theme words. Like other NYT games, upon solving the puzzle, you will see a shareable card that indicates how you performed that day: blue dots 🔵 indicate theme words you found, the yellow dot 🟡 indicates when you found the spangram, and a lightbulb 💡 indicates words that you received a hint for.

articles.title_zh: The Chinese trend of buying babies abroad
articles.content_orig:

Want to add more newsletters?
As surrogacy remains illegal in China, demand is growing for overseas-born babies.
An “industry of agencies, consultancies and fertility clinics” has sprung up to help Chinese people connect with potential surrogate mothers overseas, said the Financial Times . Many are attracted by the US’s “advanced medical facilities, strong legal protections for the parents and the prospect of an American passport for their child”.
Between 2014 and 2020, nearly a third of surrogate babies in the US were intended for international parents, a survey published in 2024 suggests. More than 40% of those were from China.

There’s a “growing interest” from women who aren’t struggling with infertility, but who fear the impact of pregnancy on their bodies and careers, said the Financial Times. That fear is “well founded”, said Lu Pin, a Chinese women’s rights activist. The so-called “motherhood penalty” is “a product of how the environment works against women” in China.
“If I remain unmarried, I will have to bear all the costs of pregnancy and post-partum recovery myself,” a 25-year-old entrepreneur told the paper. That “really isn’t very different from the cost of having a child through surrogacy”.
Last year, China registered its lowest number of births since records began: the fourth consecutive year of population decline. There has been a “very clear increase among patients who are fearful of getting pregnant and giving birth”, said a Chinese medicine doctor and fertility specialist. “Chinese women worry about how it will impact their appearance and whether they can return to their normal weight and womb health.”
But there is a darker side: “a little-known trend in the largely unregulated US surrogacy industry”, said The Wall Street Journal . Chinese elites and billionaires are paying to “quietly have large numbers of US-born babies”.Some, “inspired by Elon Musk’s 14 known children ”, shell out millions to hire women in America to “help them build families of jaw-dropping size”.
A free daily email with the day’s biggest news and analysis – and the best features from TheWeek.com
In the US, there is a “thriving mini-industry” of surrogacy agencies, law firms and clinics, even services to collect newborns from hospitals. Chinese people can “ship their genetic material abroad and get a baby delivered back”, for up to $200,000. The market is now “so sophisticated” that some Chinese elites have had US-born children – who automatically become US citizens under the 14th Amendment – “without stepping foot in the country”.
One billionaire, Xu Bo, an “online megaposter” and “vocal critic of feminism”, calls himself “China’s first father”. The maker of fantasy video games claims to have 100 children. He told a US court in 2023 that he hoped to have 20 US-born children through surrogacy, preferably boys, to one day take over his business. Another wealthy Chinese executive, Wang Huiwu, hired US models as egg donors to have 10 girls, allegedly “with the aim of one day marrying them off to powerful men”.
He ultimately plans to father 100 “high net-worth babies”, according to The Times . And although the practice is “arousing concern” in both the US and China, there is no US law stopping multiple surrogacy births for the same family. This “extreme surrogacy” is “a perfect mix of liberal Californian attitudes and Chinese productivity”.
Harriet Marsden is a senior staff writer and podcast panellist for The Week, covering world news and writing the weekly Global Digest newsletter. Before joining the site in 2023, she was a freelance journalist for seven years, working for The Guardian, The Times and The Independent among others, and regularly appearing on radio shows. In 2021, she was awarded the “journalist-at-large” fellowship by the Local Trust charity, and spent a year travelling independently to some of England’s most deprived areas to write about community activism. She has a master’s in international journalism from City University, and has also worked in Bolivia, Colombia and Spain.

articles.title_orig: Trump and Rubio weigh firing Kimberly Guilfoyle as misconduct and donor bailout allegations mount
articles.title_zh: Trump and Rubio weigh firing Kimberly Guilfoyle as misconduct and donor bailout allegations mount
articles.content_orig:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle may soon be fired amid reports she sought a six-figure credit card bailout from a Trump donor while offering access to administration officials, adding to mounting allegations over her conduct in Athens.
President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are "extremely pissed off" by Guilfoyle’s reported conduct and are weighing her removal, The Associated Press reported Sunday, citing a senior U.S. official.
The official told the AP that a decision on what action to take would likely come this week after Monday’s Columbus Day holiday. No departure has been confirmed.
Guilfoyle, onetime fiancée of Donald Trump Jr., came under scrutiny this week after The Wall Street Journal reported that she asked Trump donor Eric Deters to pay off a $100,000 American Express bill shortly before her Senate confirmation hearing.
MARCO RUBIO ANNOUNCES SWEEPING FINANCIAL SANCTIONS AGAINST THE INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL COURT
US Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle (R) attends the opening of the sixth round of the Greece-US Strategic Dialogue, in Athens, on October 7, 2026. (Photo by Mark Schiefelbein / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)
According to messages reviewed by the Journal, Guilfoyle urged Deters to wire the money directly to American Express, saying the transaction would not leave a paper trail, while offering to help him gain access to senior Trump administration officials. Deters said he never made the payment.
Guilfoyle's attorney, Jesse Binnall, disputed the authenticity of the messages.
The allegations followed an earlier Journal investigation into Guilfoyle's conduct in Greece, including claims that she promoted the interests of Greek construction and energy company Aktor Group and allowed its registered lobbyist, Christos Marafatsos, to accompany her to private diplomatic meetings with senior officials.
FORMER TRUMP CABINET OFFICIAL HAD 'INAPPROPRIATELY CLOSE' RELATIONSHIP WITH BODYGUARD, IG FINDS
The Journal also reported that Guilfoyle suggested at a dinner with Greek officials that the U.S. would undermine their government, citing political developments in Romania. Greece's foreign minister has since said there was no need to summon Guilfoyle for an explanation because the country's energy minister denied that any threat had been made.
Separately, the State Department 's Office of Inspector General opened an investigation into allegations involving Guilfoyle's treatment of embassy employees, private travel, acceptance of gifts and relationships with business interests, according to a report from the Daily Mail.
3 SECRET SERVICE OFFICIALS UNDER INTERNAL INVESTIGATION FOR POTENTIAL MISCONDUCT
FILE - The State Department's Office of Inspector General reportedly opened an investigation into allegations involving Guilfoyle's treatment of embassy employees. (Photo by Jacek Boczarski/Anadolu via Getty Images)
Sources described a hostile workplace in which Guilfoyle allegedly threatened to fire employees. They also claim that she demoted members of her security detail over minor incidents, including an officer who reportedly failed to answer a 4 a.m. request for ice while she was vacationing in Mykonos.
The inspector general's office declined to confirm or deny the existence of an investigation. Binnall told the Daily Mail that "any implication of wrongdoing by the Ambassador is unsupported."
The allegations have drawn scrutiny from congressional Democrats, including Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, D-N.H., and Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., who have called for a review of Guilfoyle's conduct. Meeks urged her removal if the allegations were substantiated.
Vice President JD Vance addressed the controversy Friday, cautioning against rushing to judgment while acknowledging that misconduct should carry consequences.
OHIO BAKERY WORKERS RECOUNT SURPRISE JD VANCE ENCOUNTER THAT TOOK AN UNEXPECTED TURN
"Let's actually see what the facts are. Let's see what the truth is," Vance told reporters in Ohio. "And obviously, if there was something bad that happened, then people have to suffer consequences for it."
Secretary of State Marco Rubio , who visited Greece this week and delivered remarks with the backdrop of Acropolis, declined to address the allegations directly.
SEC MARCO RUBIO: THE WEST FORGOT WHAT MADE IT GREAT. WE MUST REDISCOVER OUR ROOTS BEFORE WE LOSE THEM
"You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it's the gospel. It's not the gospel," Rubio told reporters Thursday.
Rubio had defended Guilfoyle's performance a day earlier, saying, "Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here."
FOUR AMERICAN TOURISTS AMONG 6 KILLED AFTER EXPLOSION LEVELS BUILDING NEAR ATHENS’ ACROPOLIS
Republican vice presidential candidate, U.S. Sen. J.D. Vance (R-OH) speaks to Donald Trump Jr. (L) as Kimberly Guilfoyle looks on, during preparations for the second day of the Republican National Convention at the Fiserv Forum on July 16, 2024 in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. (Getty Images)
Trump nominated Guilfoyle to the diplomatic post in December 2024. A former California prosecutor and Fox News Channel personality, she previously served as a prominent surrogate and fundraiser for the president.
DONALD TRUMP JR AND BETTINA ANDERSON CELEBRATE PRIVATE WEDDING IN BAHAMAS, SHARE SWEET PERSONAL PHOTO
Guilfoyle was almost Trump’s daughter-in-law. She was engaged to Don Jr. for four years, but the two publicly split in Dec. 2024 — the same month the president nominated her to be the ambassador to Greece.
The president’s eldest son married Palm Beach socialite Bettina Anderson in May of this year.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
She was also previously married to California Gov. Gavin Newsom , a Democrat, from 2001 to 2006, when he was serving as mayor of San Francisco.

articles.title_orig: Las Vegas on the verge of all-time rainfall record as Rachel’s storms surge
articles.title_zh: Las Vegas on the verge of all-time rainfall record as Rachel’s storms surge
articles.content_orig:
The remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel pounded Las Vegas on Sunday.
Las Vegas received 1.08 inches of rain from midnight into the morning, breaking the daily record, 0.78 inches in 2012, and tying the all-time daily record for the month of October, set on Oct. 12, 1947, the National Weather Service’s Las Vegas office posted on X.
Rain chances will diminish after 5 p.m. Sunday, the NWS said, but with more rain expected, the valley is on the verge of an all-time record.
After 0.11 inches of rainfall Saturday night, Las Vegas had just 1.10 inches of rainfall for the calendar year to date, 2.10 inches less than the normal value of 3.20 inches, according to NWS data. Sunday’s offical end-of-day total will close that gap significantly.
The showers are expected to hang around after Sunday, with the forecast calling for a 50 percent chance Monday and 30 percent Tuesday as a cold front from the Pacific Northwest interacts with Rachel’s remnants.
Tuesday’s forecast high is 71 degrees, more than 10 degrees below normal. The cooler-than-normal temperatures, with lows in the 50s, should remain through next week.
A wind advisory is in effect until 5 a.m. Monday for the Las Vegas Valley, with south winds of 20 to 30 mph and gusts between 45 and 55 mph forecast, the weather service said. Tree limbs could be blown down and a power outages may result.
A flood watch is in effect until Sunday night for portions of Southern Nevada, including the Spring Mountains, Red Rock Canyon and Las Vegas Valley, the weather service said. Excessive runoff may result in the flooding of rivers, creeks, streams and other low-lying and flood-prone locations. Flooding may occur in areas with poor drainage and in urban areas. Low-water crossings may be flooded.
Flash flood warnings were issued across several parts of Southern Nevada early Sunday morning. The west Las Vegas Valley was under a warning until 8:30 a.m.
The threat of severe weather prompted organizers of the Age of Chivalry Renaissance Festival to cancel all activities scheduled for Sunday, according to a news release from Clark County Parks and Recreation.
The popular three-day annual event at Sunset Park in Las Vegas will not take place Sunday because of potential safety hazards, the news release said.
“The safety and well-being of our participants, dedicated staff, and partners is always our highest priority,” Patrick Almeido, the director of Clark County Parks and Recreation, said in a statement. “While we are disappointed to cancel Sunday’s festivities, operating under such dangerous wind conditions presents risks we simply cannot take.”
Contact Mark Davis at mdavis@reviewjournal.com.
The popular three-day event at Sunset Park in Las Vegas will not take place Sunday as the remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel are expected to bring severe weather to Southern Nevada.
There’s a 25 percent chance of rain this afternoon, the National Weather Service said, with chances increasing through the night.
The remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel are expected to arrive in Southern Nevada this weekend, the National Weather Service said.
Remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel are expected to bring showers to Southern Nevada beginning late Saturday night and into Sunday.
Remnants from Hurricane Rachel are forecast to bring showers and storms to Southern Nevada on Sunday, Monday and Tuesday, the National Weather Service said.
The Las Vegas Valley chalked up its wettest monsoon season in three years, thanks to some late September rain.
Summerlin and the western valley saw periodic light showers during the morning and early afternoon.
Henderson Fire Department’s technical rescue team removed one person from a stalled vehicle in the area of Moonwalk Terrace and East Paradise Hills Drive
A wave of thunderstorms swept into the valley from the west Monday evening, blanketing most of the valley with at least a few showers.
Hurricane Nolo was moving away from the Hawaiian Islands on Sunday, but the threat of heavy rains, flash flooding and strong winds persisted in areas recovering from previous storms.

articles.title_orig: China tightens rules on new car tech, limits zero-G seats, excessive screens, and headlight messaging
articles.title_zh: China tightens rules on new car tech, limits zero-G seats, excessive screens, and headlight messaging
articles.content_orig:
China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT), usually known for publishing official images of upcoming vehicles, has launched a public consultation on draft laws regarding new vehicle technologies.
The consultation covers vehicle safety, operation, and user interfacing, with an emphasis on “levitating zero-G” seats, infotainment screens, and user-defined headlight & taillight messaging. The MIIT has also reiterated its draft proposal on mechanical door handles, first published in late 2025 after a string of high-profile Xiaomi SU7 crashes .
One section of the draft focuses on interior seating and proposes more stringent crash, anti-pinch, and reliability tests for “innovative” seating functions. It mentions “Zero-G”, rotating, and fold-flat seats as examples.
The MIIT has also recommended that automakers set limits on where and when moving-seat functions can be used to ensure safety. It also proposes banning these functions when the vehicle is in motion.
Another part of the draft raises questions about in-vehicle display units, including centre-mounted infotainment screens, displays with a “large surface area”, and complex head-up displays (HUD).
The ministry is asking automakers to evaluate these displays’ distracting effects on drivers, as well as their reliability and safety in collisions and extreme conditions. It also proposes banning folding and flexible screens, which may be bad news for tech-heavy brands like Xiaomi and Huawei’s HIMA.
The draft also proposes new vehicle lighting regulations, focusing on lighting assemblies, protruding lighting units, and user-defined headlight & taillight messaging. Some NEV models now offer matrix LED lighting, allowing users to project drawings and text from their cars.
That last feature may have spooked some ministry higher-ups, raising fears that drivers could project “unapproved” content on Chinese roads. The MIIT now recommends that automakers moderate content on their lighting units and monitor what drivers write.
This proposed limitation is not unprecedented in the country. Many Android smartphones sold in China have implemented filtering and auditing checks in their operating systems, preventing users from choosing names with sensitive keywords for Wi-Fi hotspots and Bluetooth connections.
The ministry has reiterated its proposed ban on fully-hidden door handles. It previously published diagrams of what it deems “ideal” door handles and specified several preferred designs for both exterior and interior handles.
The latest draft also covers door handles with “innovative designs”, asking automakers to verify the reliability and safety of new handle designs under extreme conditions. It also requires new designs to integrate redundant mechanical linkages and ensure sufficient space for hand operation.
Source: MIIT of the People’s Republic of China

articles.title_orig: 139 migrants, including children, die after boat capsizes off Djibouti
articles.title_zh: 139 migrants, including children, die after boat capsizes off Djibouti
articles.content_orig:
At least 139 migrants including 15 children have died and dozens more are still missing after a boat sank off the coast of Djibouti, the UN's migration office has said.
The boat had been travelling from Djibouti to Yemen with 305 people aboard when it capsized near the port town of Obock on Thursday night. Around 82 people were rescued, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said.
IOM's Djibouti mission chief Alexandre Coissac called the tragedy a "stark reminder" of the dangers migrants face when seeking a new life elsewhere.
Tens of thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa make the perilous journey each year hoping to reach Gulf countries for safety and work, the agency says.
The organisation revised its toll from 109 on Sunday after 30 more bodies were recovered.
"This is a devastating loss of life," Coissac said. "Our thoughts are with the survivors and the families who have lost loved ones or remain without news of their relatives."
Local authorities are also arranging burials for those who have died, while the survivors - all Ethiopian nationals - have medical care readily available to them.
Yemen remains engulfed in a devastating civil war that has lasted more than a decade. Despite this conflict - and growing instability across the wider region - migrants still cross the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Yemen driven by poverty, insecurity and the growing impacts of climate change.
Since 10 September, the IOM said its Displacement Tracking Matrix had observed more than 20,000 "movements" from Ethiopia to Djibouti.
IOM said it was providing assistance to 64 of the survivors at its response centre in Obock, including healthcare and support to "restore contact with their families".
The UN agency was working in "close collaboration" with local authorities to help migrants and "prevent deaths at sea and on land", it added.
More than 900 migrants died or went missing taking the same route in 2025, during an 18% increase in the number of people attempting the journey, according to IOM statistics.
In March 2026, nine people were killed and 45 went missing following a similar incident as Thursday's.
The conflict in Yemen has also displaced more than 130,000 people across the country, the UN refugee agency said last month.
Thousands of Yemenis have fled to Djibouti to escape the civil war between Houthi fighters and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.
Djibouti is a tiny former French colony that sits just across the Gulf of Aden from Yemen.

articles.title_orig: Hurricane Isaias in Video and Pictures
articles.title_zh: Hurricane Isaias in Video and Pictures
articles.content_orig:
Hurricane Isaias made landfall in the late evening of Oct. 9 in the Florida Panhandle at Category 2 strength.
Wind gusts over 110 mph were clocked in several panhandle locations, along with storm surge flooding. Over 700,000 customers are without power in its wake.
Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, Friday evening with sustained winds of 105 mph, a Category 2 hurricane.
That was the first hurricane to landfall in the mainland U.S. in exactly two years, since Milton slammed into western Florida on Oct. 9, 2024.
A rarely-issued extreme wind warning was issued Friday evening for the western Florida Panhandle, including Pensacola and Destin, for the likelihood of wind gusts over 115 mph ahead of the eyewall of Isaias.
The highest gust recorded was 116 mph in Santa Rosa Sound, Florida, where sustained winds of 91 mph were also measured.
Set The Weather Company as a 'Preferred Source' to get quicker access to the news you value.
Pensacola reported a 102-mph wind gust earlier Friday evening. Gulf Breeze, Florida, located across Pensacola Bay from Pensacola, reported a wind gust of 97 mph and sustained winds of 83 mph.
Early observations show water levels surpassed 4.0 feet above normally dry ground in Destin and 5.6 feet in Panama City, Florida, and were likely higher in the western Panhandle.
One caveat with these storm surge totals is they are measured relative to the Mean Higher High Water (MHHW) and this number includes tide influences so they should not be interpreted as storm surge heights alone.
The highest wind gust reported was an impressive 117 mph three miles east-southeast of Oriole Beach. Two miles west southwest of Pensacola, at City Hall, a gust of 102 was reported.
There was a roof blown off the Rest and Relax Inn on Plantation Road in Pensacola. Multiple collapsed gas station canopies were reported in Pensacola (Blue Angel Parkway and Mobile Highway) and also in Crestview. Trees were uprooted, one of which crushed a business on Fort Walton Beach. There were also multiple RVs blown over, including one onto US 98 between Gulf Breeze and Navarre.
Less than 12 hours prior to landfall, an instrumented NOAA Saildrone measured a gust of 104 mph near the eyewall of Isaias, according to the National Hurricane Center.
In Alabama, a gust of 75 mph was reported near Orange Beach while Birmingham saw a gust of 49 mph.
Trees fell directly onto residences in Mountain Brook, Birmingham (Five Points & Ensley), Opelika (manufactured home), and Ladonia (tree through a house).
All roads were impassable in Conecuh County due to debris and fallen trees.
Georgia saw a 68 mph gust in Warner Robins while Hartsfield-Jackson Airport saw a gust to 45 mph.
In terms of heavy rainfall, Bellwood, Alabama, saw over a foot of rain in just 13 hours. Caney Creek/FAWN Station, Florida, saw 12.06 inches in 24 hours, with 9.67 falling in 3 hours and 4.15 inches falling in 1 hour.
Flash flooding reports were observed at Westland Apartments in Bellair, Florida, while flash flooding stranded a vehicle in floodwaters near Sale City, Georgia.
In Florida, Bayside Subdivision and Destin saw 7.18 inches and 7.52 inches of rainfall, respectively. The Greater Atlanta area saw 1-3 inches of rainfall in a 6 hour period early Saturday.
A flash flood warning was even in effect for part of Atlanta that morning.
And on Saturday, multiple tornadoes were sighted by storm spotters in the Savannah River Valley including near Newington and Oliver, Georgia.
There were also multiple tornado reports across South Carolina on Saturday. Near Appleton, South Carolina, four homes were severely damaged, as well as numerous trees and powerlines down. Barnwell County Aiken County, and Newberry County also had reports of tornadoes.
On Oct. 11, remnants of Isaias moved into North Carolina, producing heavy rainfall, flash flooding and landslides.
A few tornadoes were also reported in North Carolina, near Candor, Clarendon and Atkinson, North Carolina.
Numerous flood watches and warnings were also issued across Virginia, West Virginia, Maryland and Pennsylvania on Oct. 11.
Isaias replaced "Ike" on one of the Atlantic name lists after that name was retired following the destructive, deadly 2008 hurricane .
It wasn't used during its first year of eligibility in 2014, since we only reached the eighth name, Hanna, that year.
However, the name was used in 2020 for a storm that eventually tracked up the East Coast with destructive winds.

articles.title_orig: Mojtaba Khamenei defies ‘malicious’ attacks as US Army zeroes in on Iran’s 350,000 troops
articles.title_zh: Mojtaba Khamenei defies ‘malicious’ attacks as US Army zeroes in on Iran’s 350,000 troops
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump says Iran's military capabilities have been significantly degraded following U.S. strikes, claiming the country has fewer drones and missiles and asserting that Iran's navy and air force have been destroyed.
Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei claimed Oct. 8 that U.S. and Israeli strikes had failed to undermine Iran's domestic security forces, praising police personnel for resisting attacks launched in February under Operations Epic Fury and Roaring Lion.
Khamenei's remarks on X also came as the U.S. Army released a new battlefield identification guide to help American troops recognize members of Iran's conventional military, known as the Artesh, whose ground forces were estimated by the Jerusalem Institute for Strategy and Security in June at 350,000 personnel.
"The criminal US-Zionist enemy's desperate efforts and malicious attacks on the pillars of social order and security, which are unparalleled throughout history, have not caused the courageous personnel of the Police Force to waver even a fraction in their mission," Khamenei wrote in a statement.
Khamenei specifically praised Iran's Law Enforcement Command, known as FARAJA, accusing the United States and Israel of targeting the institution responsible for maintaining domestic order.
"The focus and persistence of the criminal US-Zionist enemy in striking at the Police Force at its various levels, from its highest command levels down to those who are on the frontline, has only served to underscore the paramount importance of this institution more than ever," he wrote.
IRAN PROVES THAT IT MIGHT CHANGE ITS MILITARY LEADERS, BUT IT’S NOT CHANGING STRATEGY
Khamenei specifically praised Iran's Law Enforcement Command, known as FARAJA, accusing the United States and Israel of targeting the institution responsible for maintaining domestic order. (Photo by Fars News Agency / Handout/Anadolu via Getty Images)
Iran's security apparatus comprises three principal branches: the Artesh, responsible primarily for conventional territorial defense; the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), tasked with protecting the Islamic Republic and projecting military power; and FARAJA, responsible for domestic law enforcement and internal security.
IRAN’S GUTTED RANKS LEAVE LOYALISTS FILLING CRITICAL POSTS — WITH ONE GLARING PROBLEM
Iran's FARAJA  is responsible for domestic law enforcement and internal security. (REUTERS/Mohammed Salem Foreign media)
FARAJA, commanded by Brig. Gen. Ahmadreza Radan, is responsible for maintaining public order, enforcing the country's laws and responding to civil unrest.
According to Iran Human Rights Monitor , the force has evolved into a powerful internal security institution involved in suppressing anti-government demonstrations, monitoring political activity and enforcing the regime's ideological restrictions.
IRAN INSTALLS NEW WAR CHIEFS AS TEHRAN SIGNALS ‘PROLONGED CONFRONTATION,’ EXPERT WARNS
FARAJA is commanded by Brig. Gen. Ahmadreza Radan and is Iran's principal domestic police organization, responsible for maintaining public order, enforcing the country's laws and responding to civil unrest. ((Photo by Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
Radan has also been sanctioned by the United States for his role in human rights abuses.
The Treasury Department designated him in September 2010, citing his responsibility for beatings, killings and arbitrary arrests of protesters following Iran's disputed 2009 presidential election.
Khamenei also called for strengthening FARAJA on Oct. 8 through additional personnel, equipment and technology, including the use of artificial intelligence for data analysis.
AFTER 47 YEARS OF CONFRONTING IRAN, DOES AMERICA HAVE A STRATEGY FOR ENDING THIS WAR?
His remarks come as the U.S. Army's Training and Transformation Command published a "Know the Threat" recognition guide Sept. 24, highlighted by Defense News on Oct. 9.
The guide shows an Iranian special forces soldier and identifies weapons American troops could encounter, including AKM rifles, Iranian-made Masaf-2 rifles, German-designed G3 rifles, MG3 machine guns and RPG-7 rocket-propelled grenade launchers.
The Artesh, Iran's regular military, is separate from the IRGC and its affiliated Basij militia. Its forces operate across four branches: the Ground Forces, Navy, Air Force and Air Defense Force.
A June assessment by the Jerusalem Institute for Strategy and Security estimated the Artesh's Ground Forces at approximately 350,000 personnel, including 220,000 conscripts.
The report found that the Artesh had suffered severe losses across its air, naval and air defense components during the opening phase of the U.S.-Israeli military campaign, while its ground forces remained structurally intact because there had been no ground invasion.
TRUMP OPENS HORMUZ UNDER FIRE WITH ‘PROJECT FREEDOM’ AS IRAN WARNS OF ATTACKS
The Artesh, Iran's regular military, is separate from the IRGC and its affiliated Basij militia. Its forces operate across four branches: the Ground Forces, Navy, Air Force and Air Defense Force. (Photo by Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
The Artesh is commanded by Maj. Gen. Amir Hatami, a former Iranian defense minister who assumed command in June 2025.
Aside from Khamenei, Hatami issued his own warning Oct. 6, claiming Iran's adversaries faced "historic confusion" after failing to halt military production during the conflict.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Hatami also claimed that Iranian defense production continued despite American and Israeli attacks, saying the country's military production lines had continued operating during the conflict.
The extent of Iran's military recovery remains unclear. The Jerusalem Institute for Strategy and Security assessed in June that the country's conventional air, naval and air defense forces had suffered severe damage during the conflict.
President Donald Trump, meanwhile, said Oct. 8 that Washington would not resume military strikes against Iran before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, citing "productive discussions" between the two countries.
Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.
