articles.title_orig: What to know about Pope Leo’s lung surgery for an early-stage nodule
articles.title_zh: What to know about Pope Leo’s lung surgery for an early-stage nodule
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV said Sunday he will have surgery this week to remove an early-stage nodule on his lung.
The Vatican didn’t say what type of lung surgery the pontiff will undergo, but that the “small, localized nodule” was found in his lung during recent medical tests.
A lung nodule is a small mass of tissue detected through X-ray or CT scan screening. According to the American Lung Cancer, nodules can be caused by a number of factors, including irritants such as air pollution, diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis and cancer. They can also be caused by scar tissue from a previous infection.
Leo said the nodule was detected “at a very early stage.”
There are several approaches to surgery, depending on the size and location of the nodule and whether doctors suspect cancer, said Dr. Ankit Bharat, the chief of thoracic surgery at Northwestern Medicine.
Most nodules are benign, and it’s unclear whether the pope had a biopsy after the tests.
“When doctors decide to proceed directly to surgery rather than first obtaining a biopsy, it can suggest a higher level of concern on the lung scan,” Bharat said.
What to know about Pope Leo’s surgery to remove a lung nodule
Lung cancer is more treatable if caught early. The deadly cancer is most often caused by cigarette smoking, but about 20% of lung cancer cases are diagnosed in people who have never smoked or used tobacco, according to the American Cancer Society.
However, finding a nodule on a scan doesn’t confirm a cancer diagnosis, Bharat said, and the surgery will reveal more information as doctors are able to put the nodule under a microscope.
Advances in the procedures mean they are generally less invasive, and some patients begin walking within a day or two.
Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni said in a statement Sunday that “the operation is scheduled for the first days of this week and the estimated post-operative recovery time will be about one week.”
If the nodule is larger and more lung tissue is removed, meaning the surgery is more extensive, it may be three to four weeks before a patient is fully recovered.
“Given the pope’s age, his recovery could be slower than that of a younger, otherwise healthy patient,” Bharat said. Leo is 71.
The pontiff has a major trip scheduled to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru in November. It’s possible he could make the trip, doctors suggest, if the surgery is minimally invasive and there are no surprise findings. If the nodule is cancerous, doctors will determine whether he can be treated while traveling or the trip may need to be postponed.
Dr. Akshay Syal is an NBC News medical contributor and a board-certified internist at Atria Health & Research Institute in New York City.

articles.title_orig: SUN: Isaias sets record as latest Atlantic hurricane, drenches Maryland
articles.title_zh: SUN: Isaias sets record as latest Atlantic hurricane, drenches Maryland
articles.content_orig:
by MATT HUBBARD & KARL HILLE | THE BALTIMORE SUN
This GOES-19 GeoColor satellite image provided by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and taken at 1:06 p.m. EDT, Friday, Oct. 9 2026, shows Hurricane Isaias approaching the Gulf Coast of Alabama and Florida . (NOAA via AP)
MARYLAND (WBFF) — Hurricane Isaias made landfall on the Gulf Coast as a Category 2 Hurricane but has since been downgraded to a Post-Tropical Cyclone. Despite the reduction in strength, the storm now holds the record for the latest start to the Atlantic season, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
At least four deaths were linked to the storm, the Associated Press reported, including two people killed when trees fell onto homes in Florida and Alabama. Forecasters warned that flooding could stretch into the Appalachians.
The Maryland Transit Authority warned that “Wet roads will be a concern throughout the day, with periods of heavy rain likely,” in a post on X. “If you’re heading out, slow down, leave extra space between vehicles, keep your headlights on, and watch out for standing water. Never drive through a flooded roadway. Stay safe!”
The administration said Isaias formed Wednesday, Oct. 7 and is the latest first hurricane of the Atlantic season since at least 1905, when the first Atlantic hurricane also formed on Oct. 7. The administration noted that Isaias is also the first Atlantic hurricane in nearly a year; the last being Hurricane Melissa, which formed Oct. 25, 2025 — just over two months after the 2025 season’s first hurricane, Hurricane Erin, formed.

articles.title_orig: Democrat Chris Pappas says "we're taking nothing for granted" amid "tough race" in New Hampshire
articles.title_zh: Democrat Chris Pappas says "we're taking nothing for granted" amid "tough race" in New Hampshire
articles.content_orig:
Washington — Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas, who's running to represent New Hampshire in the Senate , said on Sunday that "we're taking nothing for granted" as Election Day approaches, amid a "tough race" in the Granite State.
"I'm hopeful about where we're going to end up at the end of this thing, but we've got to put in the work over the next 23 days," Pappas said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."
Pappas, who's represented New Hampshire in the House since 2019, is facing off against former GOP Sen. John Sununu in a race that could be key to determining which party controls the Senate. And although Republicans have been eyeing a possible opportunity to flip the seat, after Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen announced she wouldn't seek reelection, CBS News rates New Hampshire as leaning Democrat.
But Pappas said given New Hampshire's status as a purple state generally and the state's lack of early voting options, his campaign is taking nothing for granted. The focus now is on "how we get to those independent, swing voters, how we energize the base, how we reach out to Republicans over the next 23 days to win a tough race," he said.
Pappas noted that the 2016 Senate race in New Hampshire came down to just over 1,000 votes, and acknowledged how his opponent's family has been dominant in Granite State politics.
"I'm up against a candidate with a very famous political pedigree in New Hampshire. He's been a U.S. senator before," Pappas said. "But this isn't about going back to the failed politicians with failed ideas from the past, it's about looking ahead to the future."
Sununu, the son of former Gov. John H. Sununu and brother of former Gov. Chris Sununu, represented New Hampshire in the House and Senate until he lost his reelection bid to Shaheen in 2008. And with a record of breaking with President Trump, he's distanced himself from the president as he campaigns to return to the upper chamber amid an unpopular war with Iran and high gas prices.
But Pappas tied Sununu's campaign to the president's agenda more broadly, and positioned the contest as a larger fight for the Senate majority.
"The fact is, Donald Trump has said this, that 'pretend I'm on the ballot,'" Pappas said. "He's on the ballot through candidates like John Sununu, who will maintain his majority in the U.S. Senate, will make it harder for us to hold this administration to account to address the culture of corruption in Washington and fight to lower costs for New Hampshire families."
Asked about Democrats' priorities should they win control of the House and Senate, Pappas said "we have to focus like a laser on the economic challenges that people are living right now."
"We have to put some wins on the board for workers and the middle class," he said. "We can do that by building on the success of the housing bill that we passed to invest in the affordable housing stock that we need, to work to end this war and lower energy prices, to restore the cuts to healthcare that are kicking thousands of Granite Staters off of their health insurance and making it harder for people to access the care that they need."
On immigration enforcement, Pappas has emphasized the need for reforms, while other Democrats have called for Immigration and Customs Enforcement to be disbanded entirely.
"We have to be realistic — Donald Trump's going to be president for the next two years. We got to find every point of leverage we possibly can to rein in the disgusting abuses we have seen from ICE," Pappas said. "We have to make sure that we are going after the worst of the worst criminals that are violating the law, while also respecting due process rights and making sure that immigrants are part of our extended American family. And people in New Hampshire support that."

articles.title_orig: Scientists make stunning discovery that could help explain why life exists
articles.title_zh: Scientists make stunning discovery that could help explain why life exists
articles.content_orig:
Imagine a universe where stars still shine, planets still form, and water exists, but liquids are so thick that living cells can barely function. Even with the chemical ingredients for life, the conditions might make living organisms impossible.
Scientists have uncovered a remarkable connection between the fundamental laws of physics and the ability of life to exist. Their findings suggest that even relatively small changes to some of the universe's most basic physical constants could dramatically alter how liquids flow, potentially preventing essential biological processes from taking place.
The discovery, detailed in a study published in Science Advances , came from physicist Kostya Trachenko at Queen Mary University of London. His theoretical analysis identified an additional constraint on the values of fundamental physical constants: They must permit liquids to move in ways that support life within and between cells.
The work raises a profound question about the universe. Why do the fundamental laws of nature have values that appear so well suited to the existence of life?
The Fundamental Constants That Shape Our Universe
Fundamental physical constants are numbers that govern how the universe operates. Examples include the mass and electric charge of an electron and the Planck constant, which plays a central role in quantum mechanics, the branch of physics that describes matter and energy at extremely small scales.
These quantities are generally considered universal and unchanging over time. Their values influence everything from the behavior of atoms and chemical bonds to the nuclear reactions that power stars and produce elements essential for life.
Despite their importance, scientists still do not know why these constants have the particular values we observe.
An important clue emerged in 2020 , when Trachenko and his colleagues demonstrated that fundamental physical constants place a lower limit on the viscosity of liquids.
Viscosity describes how strongly a fluid resists flowing. Water has relatively low viscosity and pours easily, while honey and tar are much more viscous and move slowly. The researchers showed that there is a fundamental limit to how freely a fluid can flow, with that limit ultimately connected to the basic constants of nature.
The 2023 study took this connection much further by examining its implications for biology.
Why Tiny Changes to Physics Could Make Life Impossible
Every living cell depends on the movement of molecules. Nutrients must reach the places where they are needed, waste products must be transported away, and countless chemical reactions must occur in a liquid environment.
Another important process is diffusion, the natural spreading of particles through a fluid. Diffusion helps molecules move around cells and enables many of the chemical interactions required for life.
If the viscosity of those fluids changed too much, these processes could become severely disrupted. Liquids that were too thick might prevent vital materials from moving efficiently, while excessively low viscosity could also interfere with the controlled flow necessary for biological functions.
Trachenko explained the surprising connection:
"Understanding how water flows in a cup turns out to be closely related to the grand challenge to figure out fundamental constants. Life processes in and between living cells require motion and it is viscosity that sets the properties of this motion. If fundamental constants change, viscosity would change too impacting life as we know it. For example, if water was as viscous as tar life would not exist in its current form or not exist at all. This applies beyond water, so all life forms using the liquid state to function would be affected."
The implications extend beyond water. Although all known life depends on water, hypothetical organisms elsewhere in the universe might rely on different liquids. The same fundamental physical constraints would still influence how those liquids behave.
Trachenko suggested that the range of constants compatible with cellular life could be surprisingly narrow.
"Any change in fundamental constants including an increase or decrease would be equally bad news for flow and for liquid-based life. We expect the window to be quite narrow: for example, viscosity of our blood would become too thick or too thin for body functioning with only a few per cent change of some fundamental constants such as the Planck constant or electron charge."
These predictions come from theoretical models rather than experiments in which scientists actually changed fundamental constants. The precise limits that different forms of life could tolerate remain uncertain.
A Cosmic Mystery Billions of Years in the Making
What makes the findings especially intriguing is that the same fundamental constants that influence liquid flow also govern the nuclear reactions responsible for creating heavy elements inside stars.
Long before the first living cells appeared, stars were producing elements such as carbon and oxygen that would eventually become essential components of living organisms.
Physicists have long investigated whether the constants governing these nuclear processes must fall within certain ranges for complex matter to exist. But the ability to create life's chemical ingredients does not necessarily guarantee that life can function.
Trachenko's analysis showed that some physical properties governing liquid flow could change without disrupting the combinations of constants needed to produce heavy nuclei in stars.
In other words, a hypothetical universe might still produce the elements necessary for life while having liquids so viscous that cellular processes could not operate.
That means the conditions needed to support life may involve more than the ability to form stars, planets, and complex chemistry. The physical properties of liquids could impose additional requirements on the universe's fundamental constants.
Follow-Up Research Reveals a Surprising Connection to Blood
The investigation continued beyond the original discovery.
In a follow-up study published in January 2025 in The European Physical Journal E , Trachenko and colleagues examined how fundamental physical constants influence more complicated biological fluids, particularly blood.
Unlike water, blood is a complex mixture containing plasma, red blood cells, platelets, and other components. Its viscosity depends not only on molecular properties but also on how these components interact.
For example, red blood cells can form clusters that increase resistance to flow. As the blood moves faster, those clusters can break apart, allowing it to flow more easily. This behavior makes blood considerably more complicated than a simple liquid.
The researchers found something unexpected. Despite the enormous complexity of blood and the relatively large size of red blood cells, its viscosity remains surprisingly close, on a fundamental physical scale, to a theoretical value derived from basic physical constants.
They proposed that interactions between closely spaced blood cells may help explain this connection. Even though red blood cells are vastly larger than atoms, the forces acting where their surfaces approach one another involve distances small enough for molecular and quantum effects to matter.
The 2025 analysis also emphasized an important complication. Estimating which fundamental constants are compatible with life requires accounting for both the intrinsic properties of liquids, determined by fundamental physics, and the additional effects created by interactions among cells and molecules.
These findings offer a more detailed framework for investigating the connection between the universe's basic physical properties and the biological processes that depend on them.

articles.title_orig: Trump to visit the Philippines next month for ASEAN summit before his second trip to China this year
articles.title_zh: Trump to visit the Philippines next month for ASEAN summit before his second trip to China this year
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — President Trump will travel to the Philippines next month for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit before heading on to China, according to the White House.
Trump will participate in the summit in Manila on Nov. 16 before going to China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, which will take place from Nov. 17-19, the White House said.
Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has been inviting Trump to visit his country for some time, a US official said.
Trump’s last official trip to the Philippines took place in 2017 when he attended the ASEAN summit. Last year, the president attended the ASEAN summit in Kuala Lumpur in Malaysia and APEC in Gyeongju, South Korea, as he works to maintain US influence in Asia.
The president’s goal this year is to demostrate America’s commitment to its allies in Southeast Asia and advance US economic and national security objectives, according to the White House official.
Rumors had been swirling that Trump intended to attend the ASEAN summit this year, but now the White House has officially confirmed it.
Trump will then meet with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in person for the third time this year. Xi last visited with Trump during a summit at the White House last month.
Trump also met Xi in May in Beijing. The two global superpower leaders are slated to meet in person at the Group of 20 Summit in Miami in December, too.
Both leaders have been working to mend US-Sino relations.
During the summit last month, which marked Xi’s first White House visit since 2015, Washington and Beijing announced various diplomatic initiatives, including an artificial intelligence alert system between the two countries, and Xi invited 100,000 young Americans to China for an education exchange.
In addition, the two sides announced an extension of the nation’s trade truce, which was set to expire next month. It will remain in effect until Jan. 10, 2027, buying two more months for negotiations.
Despite all the pomp and niceties, tensions still remain between both sides.
Talks to date have not appeared to yield any sort of significant breakthrough on Taiwan, though Trump has continued to withhold $14 billion in arms sales to Taiwan.
The US is also maintaining key exports controls on China, including for critical technology chips. China has been leveraging its domination of rare earths amid its negotiations with the US on trade.

articles.title_orig: Zelensky says critics blaming him for Russia-Ukraine war ‘can’t find a key how to stop Putin’
articles.title_zh: Zelensky says critics blaming him for Russia-Ukraine war ‘can’t find a key how to stop Putin’
articles.content_orig:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday that only Russia was responsible for the war in his country. He said Ukraine would halt strikes on Russian oil refineries if Moscow stopped hitting Ukraine's energy grid, after U.S. President Donald Trump blamed him for high diesel prices and said it was time for Ukraine to get a new leader.
The exchange came as Kyiv pressed its campaign against infrastructure deep inside Russia, with a drone attack on Sunday shutting down a data center run by Russian technology giant Yandex, the third strike on the company's facilities in four days. Russia and Ukraine are locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line, more than 4 1/2 years since Moscow's full-scale invasion.
"Ukraine will be ready to stop striking Russian oil refineries if Russia stops striking our energy infrastructure," Zelenskyy wrote on X.
"It is possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but Putin does not want to do so," he said, adding that any de-escalation must be reciprocal and backed by real guarantees.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha pushed back on Trump's comments, writing on X late Saturday that Zelenskyy was leading the country through a war for its independence. "He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide. Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well," Sybiha wrote.
Trump said Saturday it was time for Ukraine to get a new president , suggesting Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war and blaming him for high diesel prices in the U.S.
"I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does," Trump said.
The U.S. president, who on Friday struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to buy diesel from Russia to address high fuel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections, has urged Zelenskyy for weeks to stop strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
He has sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran, which has driven up world energy prices. Ukrainian and European officials reacted to the diesel deal with dismay, saying it will help pay for Russia's war effort.
A Ukrainian drone attack shut down a data center run by Russian technology giant Yandex, the company said Sunday, the third strike on its facilities in four days as Kyiv widens its campaign against infrastructure deep inside Russia.
The attack on the data center in the city of Vladimir, east of Moscow, caused outages across Yandex's services, leaving users in dozens of Russian cities and in Kazakhstan, Belarus and Armenia unable to order taxis or access banking services, according to Russian independent news outlet Astra.
Russia and Ukraine are locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line, more than 4 1/2 years since Moscow's full-scale invasion. Ukraine's strikes on data centers follow Russian attacks on data hubs in Ukraine.
"As a result of the drone attack, the infrastructure of Yandex's data center in Vladimir was damaged. Operations at the data center have been completely halted. There were no injuries," said the Yandex Cloud Telegram channel, which provides operational updates on service availability.
On Thursday, a drone attack took a Yandex data center offline in the Ryazan region, southeast of Moscow. A day later, Ukrainian drones hit the company's major data center in the Kaluga region, southwest of Moscow, and Yandex said the attack partially took it offline.
Yandex, often described as Russia's Google, runs the country's most popular search engine and a wide range of digital services, and is heavily involved in Russia's artificial intelligence development.
Elsewhere, Zelenskyy said search and rescue operations ended in the southern city of Zaporizhzhia after a Russian bombing on Saturday, Ivan Fedorov, the former regional head and co-chair of the regional defense council, said Sunday.
Zelenskyy said 23 people were killed in the attack, including four children. More than 30 people were wounded, Fedorov said, eight of whom remain hospitalized.
A man was killed and two women wounded in a Ukrainian drone strike on Russia's Bryansk border region, local officials said Sunday.

articles.title_orig: China calls out western human rights hypocrisy at UN
articles.title_zh: China calls out western human rights hypocrisy at UN
articles.content_orig:
Sun Lei, China’s Deputy Permanent Representative to the United Nations, speaking during the general debate of the UN General Assembly’s Third Committee on October 6, responded firmly to a number of Western countries, urging them to stop fabricating and spreading lies about China and stop using human rights issues for political manipulation.
Sun said that China strongly condemns and is firmly opposed to the groundless accusations and malicious smears of China’s human rights situation made by countries including the UK, Australia, Japan, Ireland, the Czech Republic and Lithuania, in their replies during the general debate of the Third Committee of the United Nations General Assembly.
He went on to note that these countries consider themselves superior to others and often assume the posture of self-appointed “human rights teachers,” yet they have serious human rights problems of their own, adding that these countries are in no position to lecture others on human rights, let alone make irresponsible remarks about China.
In contrast to China, which has eliminated extreme poverty, poverty has continued to worsen in the UK in recent years, he said, with over 14 million people living below the poverty line, half of whom are in “extreme poverty”.
A 2018 report by Philip Alston, then UN special rapporteur on extreme poverty and human rights, said 14 million people, a fifth of the UK population, lived in poverty, and four million of these were more than 50 percent below the poverty line, and 1.5 million destitute, unable to afford basic essentials.
A study by the British Social Metrics Commission in 2024 found the cost of living crisis had plunged two million more people into severe hardship since 2019, meaning more than 16 million people in total are defined as living in poverty, or 24 percent of the UK population, the highest since comparable records began in 2000.
China’s new Ethnic Unity and Progress Promotion Law aims to promote common prosperity and development among all ethnic groups. However, by contrast, Japan has failed to fulfil its commitments to eliminate racial discrimination and has not treated the Ainu (an indigenous people living in the north of Japan) and Ryukyu (Okinawan) peoples as equal ethnic groups, leaving their survival and development under threat. In the UK, Australia and Ireland, colonialism has caused enduring harm to this day, and these countries are facing serious social problems, including racism and ethnic divisions.
And in contrast to China’s concrete efforts to promote dialogue, cooperation and more equitable global human rights governance, countries such as the UK, Australia, Japan, the Czech Republic and Lithuania frequently invoke morality yet remain indifferent to the unjust treatment suffered by the people of Palestine, Iran and Cuba. They repeatedly use human rights as a pretext to interfere in the internal affairs of other countries and impose unilateral coercive measures, infringing on the interests of developing countries and playing a highly disgraceful role, Sun pointed out.
The following articles were originally published by Global Times and China Daily .
October 6 ( Global Times ) – Sun Lei, China’s Deputy Permanent Representative to the United Nations, on Tuesday delivered a rebuttal during the general debate of the UN General Assembly’s Third Committee in response to Western countries, urging a handful of countries to stop fabricating and spreading lies about China and stop using human rights issues for political manipulation.
China strongly condemns and is firmly opposed to the groundless accusations and malicious smears of China’s human rights situation made by countries including the UK, Australia, Japan, Ireland, the Czech Republic and Lithuania, in their replies during the general debate of the Third Committee of the United Nations General Assembly, Sun said, according to a statement released by the Permanent Mission of China to the UN on Tuesday.
These countries consider themselves superior to others and often assume the posture of self-appointed “human rights teachers,” yet they have serious human rights problems of their own, Sun said, adding that these countries are in no position to lecture others on human rights, let alone make irresponsible remarks about China.
According to Sun, China has continued to safeguard and improve people’s well-being through development, eliminating absolute poverty nationwide. Nearly 100 million people have been lifted out of impoverishment, and a middle-income group of more than 400 million people has been established.
By contrast, poverty has continued to worsen in the UK in recent years, with over 14 million people living below the poverty line, half of whom are in “extreme poverty.” In Japan, the relative poverty rate among households stands at 15 percent, while child poverty has become increasingly pronounced. China expresses deep concern over the human rights situations in Japan, Sun said.
Meanwhile, China has continued to advance whole-process people’s democracy and ensure that the people run the country, with public support for and satisfaction with the government exceeding 90 percent for years. The national security law in Hong Kong marked a historic turning point for Hong Kong, bringing it from chaos to governance and from stability to prosperity, while improving and developing its democratic system, winning broad support across the city, Sun said.
By contrast, polls show that about 75 percent of people in the UK are concerned about the future of democracy. In Australia and the Czech Republic, public trust in government has fallen to new lows, with young people’s confidence in democracy also declining significantly, Sun added.
Sun said that all ethnic groups in China are equal members of the family of the Chinese nation and are closely united like the seeds of a pomegranate. The political, economic, cultural, religious and other rights of people of all ethnic groups in Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region and Xizang Autonomous Region are effectively protected. The enactment and implementation of the Ethnic Unity and Progress Promotion Law aims to promote common prosperity and development among all ethnic groups.
By contrast, Japan has failed to fulfill its commitments to eliminate racial discrimination and has not treated the Ainu and Ryukyu peoples as equal ethnic groups, leaving their survival and development under threat. In the UK, Australia and Ireland, colonialism has caused enduring harm to this day, and these countries are facing serious social problems, including racism and ethnic divisions, Sun said.
Sun said that amid global turbulence and headwinds facing multilateralism, China has contributed to the international human rights cause through its development and concrete efforts to promote dialogue, cooperation and more equitable global human rights governance.
By contrast, countries such as the UK, Australia, Japan, the Czech Republic and Lithuania frequently invoke morality, yet remain indifferent to the unjust treatment suffered by the people of Palestine, Iran and Cuba. They repeatedly use human rights as a pretext to interfere in the internal affairs of other countries and impose unilateral coercive measures, infringing on the interests of developing countries and playing a highly disgraceful role, Sun added.
Sun said the global trend toward multipolarity and more democratic international relations is irreversible and called for greater solidarity and cooperation on human rights. He said that China would pursue a human rights development path suited to its national conditions, engage in constructive dialogue and oppose the politicization of human rights, while urging a small number of countries to stop fabricating and spreading lies about China and stop using human rights issues for political manipulation. Otherwise, they will only end up hurting themselves.

articles.title_orig: NASA dumped over 800GB of Artemis II data online
articles.title_zh: NASA dumped over 800GB of Artemis II data online
articles.content_orig:
NASA’s treasure trove of images, audio, and video offers an unprecedented view inside a historic space mission.
NASA’s treasure trove of images, audio, and video offers an unprecedented view inside a historic space mission.
If you thought you’d seen all there is to see from the Artemis II mission , you’re wrong. This week NASA posted over 800GB worth of science data, images, and videos on the Artemis II: Sights & Sounds of Science site. The archive includes over 11,000 photos and videos, over 8.5 hours of audio, and crew-annotated images, such as the one marking where they saw impact flashes on the dark side of the Moon. Together, they offer an unprecedented view inside a historic space mission.
One of the more exciting reveals was footage of the Artemis II team telling the ground team back in Houston about its observation of impact flashes. Impact flashes have been seen before, but these ones on the dark side of the Moon could have been the faintest observed with the human eye, and everyone’s excitement is palpable in the clip.
Alongside the dump, NASA also released a trio of documents that help supplement the trove of unfiltered data. That includes the Artemis II Preliminary Lunar Science Report , the Artemis II Lunar Science Operations Report , and the Artemis II Lunar Science Data User Guide .

articles.title_orig: Europeans back Zelenskyy after Trump calls for new Ukrainian leader
articles.title_zh: Europeans back Zelenskyy after Trump calls for new Ukrainian leader
articles.content_orig:
The United Kingdom, Germany and Poland have reaffirmed their support for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy after U.S. President Donald Trump said the country needed a new leader .
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrote on X that he was “absolutely convinced” nobody could break Ukraine and its president in their “fight against Russian aggression.”
“I have assured [Zelenskyy] that he can count on Poland’s and Europe’s full solidarity with the Ukrainian nation,” he added.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul also reaffirmed his country’s support for Zelenskyy Sunday, while calling for greater pressure on Moscow to return to peace talks.
“We need continued consistency and clarity on the side of Ukraine,” he told Reuters at a meeting of the governing Christian Democrats.
The show of support comes after Zelenskyy and Trump traded barbs Saturday following Washington’s decision to ease diesel sanctions on Russia . “I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president,” Trump told reporters at the White House as he criticized Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil facilities.
On Sunday, the Ukrainian president stated on social media that his country would be prepared to stop attacking Russian oil refineries “if Russia stops striking our energy infrastructure.”
The U.K. also reiterated its support for Kyiv following Trump’s remarks. “We stand with Ukraine. We stand with President Zelenskyy,” British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting told the BBC Sunday morning, adding that Ukrainians alone should decide who leads their country.
Streeting said Russian President Vladimir Putin started the war and could end it, and added that Britain’s priority would be to seek reconciliation between Kyiv and Washington.
On Saturday, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham spoke with Zelenskyy and reiterated Britain’s “complete solidarity,” Downing Street said. Burnham acknowledged that “the last 24 hours had been difficult for Ukraine” and pledged to strengthen sanctions, according to the statement.

articles.title_orig: One hundred years of World Mission Sunday
articles.title_zh: One hundred years of World Mission Sunday
articles.content_orig:
World Mission Sunday, a worldwide day of prayer, solidarity and support for the Catholic Church’s missionary work, celebrates 100 years on Sunday (Oct. 11). Established by Pope Pius XI in October 1927 and organized by the Society for the Propagation of Faith, it is an invitation to all Catholics to participate in the global mission of the Church, particularly in upholding 1,130 mission dioceses most in need through prayer and financial support.
“The day reminds Catholics that the Church is missionary by nature,” states the Pontifical Mission Societies USA website. “Mission is not limited to priests, religious sisters or missionaries serving abroad. Every baptized person shares responsibility for proclaiming the Gospel and supporting the growth of the Church throughout the world.”
The movement started with a young Frenchwoman, Bl. Pauline Jaricot, who in the 1800s saw a great need to support missionaries in the Catholic Church. What started as a fundraising circle intended to prayerfully and financially support the work of missionaries, was eventually established as the global World Mission Sunday.
Every year, the Holy Father chooses a theme for World Mission Sunday. To mark the centenary celebration, Pope Leo XIV chose, “One in Christ, United in Mission.”
This special collection is uniquely relevant to Pope Leo, as it supports priests in missionary dioceses carrying out the work of spreading the Gospel — a role he held as Bishop Robert Prevost, OSA, in Peru before he was elected pope in 2025.
In his message commemorating the occasion, the pontiff prayed that “all members of the Church be united in mission, docile to the Holy Spirit, courageous in bearing witness to the Gospel, proclaiming and daily embodying [God’s] faithful love for all creatures.”
On the weekend of Oct. 18, Catholics are invited to take part in celebrating World Mission Sunday by praying for the missionary work of the Church around the world and making a donation online .
“Together, we can continue bringing Christ’s hope to communities around the world,” states the Pontifical Mission Societies USA website. “The next 100 years of mission begin with us.”

articles.title_orig: Feysa and Kipruto triumph in swift Chicago races
articles.title_zh: Feysa and Kipruto triumph in swift Chicago races
articles.content_orig:
Hawi Feysa wins the Chicago Marathon ( © Bank of America Chicago Marathon Kevin Morris )
Hawi Feysa retained her Bank of America Chicago Marathon title in 2:13:33 and Amos Kipruto won the men’s race in 2:01:09 as both athletes moved up the world all-time lists at the World Athletics Platinum Label road race on Sunday (11).
Feysa produced a decisive late surge to defeat two-time Boston Marathon champion Sharon Lokedi, improving her PB by 84 seconds to move to fourth on the world all-time list. Lokedi followed in 2:14:07, moving to eighth all time, while former world record-holder Brigid Kosgei was third in 2:14:55. It was the first marathon in history in which three women finished inside 2:15.
Kipruto, meanwhile, completed his progression through the Chicago podium positions. Third in 2024 and second last year, the Kenyan broke away from pre-race favourite Jacob Kiplimo in the second half and held on for a 2:01:09 victory – a 30-second PB that moves him to equal fifth on the world all-time list alongside Eliud Kipchoge.
The women set off aggressively from the start. A lead group of seven – Feysa, Kosgei, Lokedi, Joan Kilimo, Brillian Kipkoech, Sutume Asefa Kebede and Loice Chemnung – reached 5km in 15:36, equivalent to 2:11:39 marathon pace.
By about 7km, Feysa and Kosgei had started to pull away. They reached 10km in 31:04, nine seconds ahead of a chase group containing Lokedi, Kilimo, Kipkoech and Chemnung.
Feysa was a stride ahead of Kosgei as they passed 15km in 46:41, still operating at 2:11 pace. Behind them, the chase group had been reduced to Lokedi, Kilimo and Chemnung, who trailed by 12 seconds.
But the leaders were not able to make the break stick. Lokedi and Chemnung gradually closed the gap and by halfway four women were together at the front. They had passed 20km in 1:02:31 before reaching the half-way point in 1:06:06.
The quartet remained intact through 25km, but the complexion of the race began to change over the next five kilometres. Lokedi led Feysa through 30km in 1:34:16, while Kosgei had slipped 11 seconds behind and Chemnung was a further 30 seconds back. By 21 miles, Feysa and Lokedi were together with a 35-second advantage over Kosgei.
Neither could shake the other. They reached 35km in 1:50:23 and were still side by side through 22 miles in 1:51:43. Kosgei remained within striking distance, 39 seconds behind, but the contest for victory had developed into a duel between Feysa and Lokedi.
They passed 24 miles in 2:02:16 and mile 25 in 2:07:27. Even with little more than a kilometre remaining, there was nothing between them. Then, with about 2:10 on the clock, Feysa made her move.
The Ethiopian suddenly opened daylight and, after more than an hour of close racing with Lokedi, the gap grew remarkably quickly. Feysa covered the final mile strongly enough to put 34 seconds into her rival, breaking the tape in 2:13:33.
The performance took 84 seconds off the PB of 2:14:57 she set when winning in Chicago last year and lifted her to fourth on the world all-time list. It was the third major marathon victory of Feysa’s career, following her wins in Frankfurt in 2024 and Chicago in 2025.
Lokedi was rewarded with a huge PB of 2:14:07 in second, moving her to eighth on the world all-time list. Kosgei completed an exceptional podium in 2:14:55, making it the first marathon in history to produce three sub-2:15 finishers.
Mary Ngugi-Cooper was fourth in 2:17:23 and Kilimo fifth in 2:18:39.
The men’s race was similarly ambitious from the outset. A six-man group comprising Kipruto, Kiplimo, Tadese Bikila, Milkesa Mengesha, Boki Diriba and Daniel Mateiko passed 5km in 14:18. A chase pack led by Vincent Mauri reached 5km in 14:53, and by 10km – which the leaders passed in 28:37 – they were about a minute adrift.
The leading six remained together through 15km in 42:55 and 20km in 57:13 before reaching halfway in 1:00:21, eight seconds quicker than Sabastian Sawe’s halfway split during his 1:59:30 world record run in London earlier this year.
Behind them, Mauri was producing an eye-catching run of his own. The self-coached US athlete, who does much of his training on a treadmill and ran 2:05:54 on his marathon debut in Ohio earlier this year, began to break away from the second group. He reached halfway in 1:02:15, 17 seconds clear of his nearest pursuers and on course for a time well inside 2:05.
Up front, the six-man group finally started to fracture after halfway. Kiplimo led through 25km in 1:11:19, alongside Mateiko, Kipruto and Bikila. Mengesha and Diriba had started to lose ground and the leaders were now operating at course record pace.
Soon afterwards Kiplimo increased the tempo again. His move, with about 1:17:30 on the clock, broke apart the group, with Kipruto the only athlete initially able to respond. The pair then covered the five kilometres to 30km in 13:58, reaching that checkpoint in 1:25:28 – a projected finishing time of 2:00:12.
Kiplimo and Kipruto remained together through mile 20 in 1:31:51, but the balance then began to shift. Kipruto edged a second ahead by mile 21 and had stretched that advantage to 12 seconds by 35km, which he passed in 1:39:58.
Kiplimo’s challenge faded rapidly from that point. Kipruto was 17 seconds clear at 22 miles and 47 seconds ahead by 23 miles, while Bikila and Mengesha began to close on the Ugandan. By mile 24, Kipruto’s advantage over Kiplimo had grown to 1:32. He reached 40km in 1:54:31 with Bikila now up into second.
Kipruto continued on to win in 2:01:09. The performance took 30 seconds off the PB he set when finishing fourth in London in April and moves him alongside Kipchoge at equal fifth on the world all-time list. When Kipchoge ran 2:01:09 in Berlin four years ago, it was a world record.
For Kipruto, the 2019 world bronze medallist, it was a second World Marathon Majors victory following his triumph in London in 2022.
Bikila finished strongly to take second in a PB of 2:02:56. Mengesha also came through in the closing stages to claim third in 2:03:46, passing Kiplimo, who finished fourth in 2:04:18. Diriba and Mateiko were fifth and sixth, both timed at 2:05:01.
Clayton Young was the leading US finisher in seventh, improving his PB to 2:05:23 and moving to second on the North American all-time list. Charles Hicks followed in 2:05:35, with Akira Akasaki ninth in 2:05:47.
Mauri, whose early pace had put him on course for a significant breakthrough, was forced to stop briefly with what appeared to be cramp shortly after 21 miles. He nevertheless recovered to finish 10th in 2:06:45.

articles.title_orig: Hangzhou’s two transformations: frontier technology and ecological civilisation
articles.title_zh: Hangzhou’s two transformations: frontier technology and ecological civilisation
articles.content_orig:
In the following article, Friends of Socialist China co-editor Carlos Martinez draws on a recent visit to Hangzhou, the capital of Zhejiang Province, to examine how the city has become at once a centre of frontier technology – home to DeepSeek, Unitree Robotics and Alibaba – and a testing ground for ecological civilisation.
Carlos traces both transformations back to Zhejiang’s “Eight-Eight Strategy”, launched in 2003 when Xi Jinping was provincial Party secretary, and shows how public institutions have created the conditions for innovation while directing it towards wider developmental goals. He sets out the material record of the green transition – distributed solar overtaking coal, clean rivers and a restored West Lake, a metro network that has grown fivefold in seven years – while also confronting the contradiction at its heart: the AI and cloud-computing industries that make Hangzhou a technology leader are among its fastest-growing sources of electricity demand.
The direction of technological change, he concludes, is a political choice, requiring “long-term planning, public investment and institutions capable of subordinating private profit to the common good”. The article complements Gary Wilson’s recent analysis of the US chip blockade and the discussion on AI and the new quality productive forces at our recent Socialist China Conference .
A version of this article first appeared in Beijing Review .
Visiting Hangzhou in April, the signs of change were everywhere: electric vehicles crowding the roads, an extensive metro system, e-bikes as a default mode of transport for millions, and well-maintained residential communities built around shared green space and public amenities.
Hangzhou has emerged simultaneously as a centre of frontier technology and a testing ground for ecological civilisation. It is home to DeepSeek, Unitree Robotics and Alibaba; it is also a city of restored waterways, expanding wetlands, distributed solar power and extensive low-carbon transport.
Both of these development threads have common roots in a strategy laid down more than two decades ago.
Hangzhou is now a megacity of 12.7 million people. Its economy reached 2.3 trillion yuan ($330 billion) in 2025 , while the core industries of its digital economy account for 29.5 percent of GDP. This is not a small technology enclave surrounded by an otherwise traditional economy. Digital development has become one of the city’s principal productive forces.
The Western media discovered Hangzhou’s technology sector in early 2025, after the success of DeepSeek and the emergence of the so-called “six little dragons” : DeepSeek, Unitree, Game Science, Deep Robotics, BrainCo and Manycore Tech. The label is journalistic rather than official; what matters is the ecosystem beneath it.
Three of the six have founders who studied at Zhejiang University , which has established itself as one of the world’s leading research institutions. Those companies have also benefited from dense manufacturing supply chains, a large pool of engineers, competitive domestic markets and a local government willing to build institutions around emerging industries.
Hangzhou’s “Scene” platform , for example, matches hundreds of practical industrial demands with available technological capabilities. The ModelScope Developer Centre provides qualified firms with workspace and access to an open AI ecosystem. In December 2025, the city adopted China’s first local regulations specifically for embodied artificial intelligence , addressing safety, data access, public procurement and the difficult transition from laboratory prototype to commercial application.
This is a story of public institutions creating the conditions in which innovation can occur, then attempting to direct that innovation towards wider developmental goals.
The origins lie in Zhejiang’s “Eight-Eight Strategy” , launched in 2003 when Xi Jinping was provincial Party secretary. The strategy combined advanced manufacturing, regional integration and scientific development with the construction of an “ecological province”.
Over two decades later, Zhejiang is still harvesting the results of that groundwork. DeepSeek was founded in 2023, and within two years had produced a frontier AI model with performance comparable to leading closed systems . A relatively small Chinese team, working under US restrictions on advanced semiconductors , achieved frontier-level performance with unusually low computational requirements. DeepSeek released its model weights and inference code under a permissive MIT licence , which open-weights approach helped drive down prices across the industry and made powerful AI systems accessible to a much wider range of users and countries.
Unitree tells a related story. The launch price of its humanoid robots fell from around $90,000 in 2023 to $5,900 in 2025 , reflecting the depth of China’s component suppliers and manufacturing infrastructure.
Hangzhou’s green transformation has followed the same pattern: targets, infrastructure, experimentation and adjustment.
By the end of 2025, Zhejiang had around 71 gigawatts of wind and solar capacity – more than four times the 2020 level. Solar had overtaken coal as the province’s largest single source of installed power capacity, and more than four fifths of it was distributed , principally across rooftops and commercial and industrial sites. Zhejiang also had 10.3 gigawatts of pumped-hydropower storage , the largest provincial total in China.
The city of Hangzhou itself reached 7.55 gigawatts of solar capacity by June 2026 , already exceeding its 2030 target of 6.5 gigawatts . The provincial energy big-data centre monitors energy systems in real time, while virtual power plants coordinate batteries, electric vehicles and commercial buildings to help balance supply and demand. The energy transition is therefore not simply a matter of installing panels; it involves constructing a more flexible and intelligent electricity system around them.
The progress on water management is equally impressive. Zhejiang’s Five Water Co-treatment campaign , launched in 2013, has vastly expanded sewage-treatment capacity, cleared thousands of kilometres of polluted rivers and tackled agricultural sources of contamination.
By 2025, 99.7 percent of the province’s nationally and provincially monitored water sections were at Grade III or better. All eight major river systems, together with the Grand Canal, reached that level for the first time. In Hangzhou, monitored surface-water sections and drinking-water sources have achieved full compliance for five consecutive years.
The famous West Lake offers a visible measure of the change. Average water transparency increased from 43.7 cm in 2002 to 1.3 metres in 2024 , supported by restored submerged vegetation and a long-running water-replenishment project. Xixi, China’s first national wetland park, has recorded dramatic increases in its numbers of bird and plant species . Hangzhou was accredited as an International Wetland City in July 2025 .
As is the case elsewhere in China, transport has been changing rapidly. The metro grew from 104 km in early 2018 to 516 km by the end of 2025, carrying 1.5 billion journeys that year . Hangzhou had more than 1.25 million new-energy vehicles on its roads by June 2025 , along with an extensive public bicycle network .
None of this means the work is complete. Zhejiang is still adding coal-generating capacity, even as renewables grow, because electricity demand is rising extraordinarily quickly – provincial consumption increased by more than 7 percent in 2025 .
Hangzhou’s two transformations themselves constitute something of a contradiction, in that the AI and cloud-computing industries that make the city a technology leader are among its fastest-growing sources of electricity demand. Electricity use by internet data services rose 159 percent in 2025 , while Alibaba Cloud anticipates a tenfold increase in its energy consumption .

articles.title_orig: China’s Nobel paradox reveals a deeper science challenge
articles.title_zh: China’s Nobel paradox reveals a deeper science challenge
articles.content_orig:
China’s pursuit of scientific superpower status raises a larger question: Can it build a research environment that attracts talent and rewards long-term curiosity?
The author is a professor at Hanyang University.
Once again, this year's Nobel Prizes in science went to researchers from the United States, Europe and Japan. American and German scientists won the medicine prize, an American researcher received the physics prize and Japanese and French scientists shared the chemistry prize.
What particularly interests me this year is China's reaction.
China has enjoyed remarkable scientific achievements over the past year. DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng was named among Nature's 10 people who shaped science in 2025, while Chinese institutions occupied nine of the top 10 positions in the Nature Index.
Two Chinese-born mathematicians, Hong Wang and Yu Deng, who entered Peking University together in 2007, also won Fields Medals.
China already has Nobel laureates, including physicists Yang Chen-Ning and Tsung-Dao Lee, who won in 1957, and Tu Youyou, who received the medicine prize in 2015.
Yet Yang and Lee built their careers in American academia, while Tu lacked a doctorate and was not a Chinese Academy of Sciences member when she won. Their achievements cannot easily be regarded as products of China's established research system.
How, then, does China approach the Nobel Prize as it seeks to become a scientific superpower?
China's response resembles Korea's. Despite expectations surrounding candidates such as Southern University of Science and Technology President Xue Qikun, no Chinese scientist won this year, reviving the country's longstanding Nobel complex.
The China Association for Science and Technology urged respect for the Nobel Prize without blind devotion. That sounds reasonable, but it contrasts sharply with China's celebration of its Fields Medal winners as a historic breakthrough.
An interesting distinction has emerged in Chinese commentary: Nobel Prizes recognize the past, while Fields Medals point toward the future.
Nobel Prizes often honor discoveries made decades earlier, reflecting accumulated scientific capabilities. Fields Medals recognize both accomplishments and future potential, emphasizing promising young mathematicians.
But another question follows. Both Chinese-born Fields Medal winners developed their award-winning research after studying abroad and joining foreign universities. Can their success demonstrate the strength of China's domestic scientific ecosystem?
Chinese scientific leaders recognized this problem long ago.
Qian Xuesen, considered the father of China's rocket and space programs, questioned in 2005 why Chinese universities struggled to produce outstanding scientists. Yang warned in 2010 against excessive impatience over Nobel Prizes.
Around 2012, Turing Award laureate Andrew Yao observed that China's longstanding emphasis on practical applications had weakened the scientific foundations of computer science.
China continues searching for answers.
Another problem is particularly revealing. Despite research funding freezes, tighter student and employment visa screening and a $100,000 fee for new H-1B petitions under President Donald Trump's second administration, scientists considering leaving America have favored Europe and Canada.
China should therefore worry less about how many Nobel laureates it recruits, which prizes Chinese-born researchers win or whether fewer students study in America.
The more important question is whether foreign scientists genuinely regard China as an attractive place to conduct research and voluntarily choose to work there.
That is a meaningful measure of China's progress toward becoming a global scientific powerhouse.
China's attitude toward Nobel Prizes can appear contradictory. It recruits laureates while advocating technological self-reliance, celebrates Fields Medals while questioning the Nobel Prize's authority.
Yet these contradictions reflect serious institutional concerns rather than mere attempts to rationalize disappointment.
Chinese academics themselves have questioned whether young, unproven researchers can receive sufficient freedom, patience and tolerance for failure.
Another concern is whether successful approaches associated with Nobel laureates might be standardized and imposed indiscriminately across regions and academic disciplines.
Korea should examine these questions against its own experience. Our scientific community has pursued programs to attract foreign Nobel laureates and cultivate basic research talent, but results have often fallen short of expectations.
Meanwhile, intensifying technological rivalry between Washington and Beijing has concentrated attention on strategic technologies and industries, potentially pushing basic science further down the priority list.
As Korean scientists recognize, winning Nobel Prizes should never become an objective in itself. Instead, Korea must develop its own system for patiently supporting research that advances human knowledge and addresses difficult problems. Curious researchers should have the freedom to explore uncertain questions and the security to continue even after failure.
Many valuable academic disciplines also fall outside the Nobel Prize categories. We should acknowledge existing gaps without allowing them to dictate our ambitions. Korea must pursue its own research at its own pace.
In an era of profound uncertainty, even waiting several more decades for a Nobel Prize would be acceptable. What matters is making Korea a country where talented young researchers from around the world, driven by scientific curiosity and dreams of discovery, genuinely want to work.
A Nobel Prize may eventually follow. If it does not, that should be acceptable too. The award is merely a possible byproduct of a scientific environment worth building.

articles.title_orig: Social Security announcing benefits change on Oct. 14
articles.title_zh: Social Security announcing benefits change on Oct. 14
articles.content_orig:
Each year, many current and future Social Security beneficiaries wait eagerly for news of the Social Security cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) . In most years, a COLA results in an increase to monthly Social Security payments.
While this number can impact seniors' finances, it's actually not the increase that most people should focus on. Instead, there's a much more meaningful one that could affect retirees' finances in profound ways. This is the increase retirees should focus on earning if they can.
Image source: Getty Images.
The increase that retirees should focus on is the benefits bump that can come with waiting to claim their retirement checks. See, the COLA simply increases retirement benefits each year based on inflation . It does not give retirees more buying power through their benefits . It helps them to avoid losing ground when prices rise over time.
But if you delay your Social Security claim, you permanently increase your benefit for each month you wait beyond the earliest eligibility age of 62. This increase comes from either avoiding early-filing penalties that apply when you claim Social Security before your full retirement age (FRA) or from earning delayed retirement credits that are available any month you wait for benefits beyond FRA.
Waiting to claim to grow your benefits not only helps you to earn a higher monthly check. Multiple studies have demonstrated that it maximizes your odds of earning the most lifetime benefits. In some cases, delaying until 70 can result in hundreds of thousands of dollars in extra lifetime discretionary spending.
So, how much can waiting to claim Social Security increase your monthly payment? It depends on how long you delay.
Let's say, for example, that you have a standard benefit of $2,000 that you would receive if you claimed at FRA. That's your primary insurance amount. If you claim it at 62 with an FRA of 67, however, you would reduce that amount to just $1,400 after early-filing penalties reduce your payment by 30%. If you wait until 70, though, you would increase it by 24% and end up with $2,480 per month.
That's a $1,080 per month increase, and your benefit at 70 is just over 77% higher if you claim it at 70 compared with 62.
This benefit increase actually has a material impact on your ability to enjoy your retirement. If it is possible for you to wait to claim Social Security benefits and you have no reason to believe that you'll pass away before you break even for delaying your claim, then you should think seriously about putting off starting your benefits for as long as you can, ideally until you've maxed them out at 70.
If you've already retired, it may not be too late to increase benefits either. If you're less than 12 months out from claiming, you could potentially rescind your benefits claim if you could pay back any benefits you received to date. And if you've already passed your FRA and can afford to, you could suspend your benefit to start earning delayed retirement credits that give you more money later.
It's worth considering these options if getting a larger Social Security benefit would help your financial situation in the long run.

articles.title_orig: Pennsylvania mass shooting: What we know about 9 people killed
articles.title_zh: Pennsylvania mass shooting: What we know about 9 people killed
articles.content_orig:
ERIE, Pa. — Ten people, including two children, a woman who was eight months pregnant and her unborn child are dead following a shooting near East 7th and Perry streets in the City of Erie Friday evening.
The death toll includes nine victims and the suspected shooter, according to Erie police. Erie County Coroner Lyell Cook confirmed Saturday afternoon to Erie News Now that the death toll now includes an unborn child.
Police said officers responded around 4:53 p.m. to a ShotSpotter alert indicating two gunshots in the 700 block of Perry Street. Officers arrived within minutes and found two women dead outside a residence.
Investigators said video evidence and witness accounts show the two women had arrived at the residence appearing distressed and sought help from neighbors. Police believe gunfire had already occurred inside the home before the suspected shooter came outside and fatally shot both women.
When officers arrived, they did not know whether the suspect remained inside, whether there was an ongoing threat or whether additional people, including children, were in danger.
Police worked to gather information while seeking a search warrant. After attempts to contact anyone inside failed, officers deployed drones. SWAT officers later breached multiple doors and used a robot to assess the home before entering.
Investigators have determined that all eight victims had been killed and the suspected shooter had died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound before police arrived. No gunshots were fired after officers reached the scene.
Police Chief Rick Lorah said sounds heard during the tactical response that were initially believed to be gunfire were actually flash-bang devices and chemical munitions used by SWAT.
The victims include two women, ages 51 and 37, who were found outside the home.
Inside, police found a 5-year-old boy and a 1-year, 10-month-old girl on the first floor. A 24-year-old woman, a 44-year-old woman, a 19-year-old man and a 21-year-old man were found on the second floor and stairwell.
The suspected shooter, a 45-year-old man, was found dead on the second floor with an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound. Police said a firearm was recovered from his person.
Police have not released the identities of those killed or discussed a possible motive.
“Our investigation is ongoing, and the details are difficult,” Lorah said. “But it’s important that our community understands what happened, what our officers encountered when they arrived, and what we have learned through our investigation so far.”
Mayor Daria Devlin expressed condolences to the victims’ families and the broader community.
“I want to start by speaking directly to the families who lost loved ones last night. I am so deeply sorry,” Devlin said. “What happened was horrific, and I know there is nothing I can say today that will make this any easier.”
Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro said he spoke with Devlin and offered the support of his administration.
“I’ve spoken with Mayor Devlin and offered my Administration’s full support following the tragic mass shooting in Erie last night — killing nine of our fellow Pennsylvanians,” Shapiro said. “My heart breaks for this family. Lori and I are praying for their loved ones and the entire Erie community.”
The City of Erie is coordinating with UPMC Crisis Services, AHN Behavioral Health, local schools and other community organizations to provide trauma support and other assistance to families, neighbors, students and first responders.
“The trauma of an event like this doesn’t end when the scene is cleared or the headlines fade,” Devlin said. “Grief affects people differently, and the need for support may emerge in the days, weeks, and months ahead.”
The investigation remains ongoing.
Stay with Erie News Now for the latest information as it becomes available.

articles.title_orig: Report: HomePod mini 2 to release on October 30 with these upgrades
articles.title_zh: Report: HomePod mini 2 to release on October 30 with these upgrades
articles.content_orig:
In just a couple days, Apple should be unveiling its long-awaited new lineup of new Home products. That includes an updated HomePod mini, Apple TV 4K , the brand-new smart home hub called ‘HomeView’ , as well as a new lineup of smart home accessories, in collaboration with LG. Here’s what to expect with the HomePod mini 2.
According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman , the new HomePod mini should equip the S10 chip, up from the current S5 chip. This isn’t quite the latest silicon, but it’s still a massive step-change from the outgoing model.
With the S10 chip, the HomePod mini will be able to offer Siri AI features – a first for any of Apple’s Home products. It’ll also “extend” your HomeView throughout your house, with voice control and music playback all being able to sync up to your HomeView. Of course, the updated Apple TV and HomeView will also support Siri AI.
The new HomePod mini will come in a fresh array of colors, including pink, green, and blue – on top of the traditional midnight and white.
Outside of the S10 chip, the HomePod mini 2 is expected to offer Apple’s N1 networking chip to serve as a Thread and Matter radio, as well as offering Wi-Fi 7 support. Currently, the HomePod mini only offers Wi-Fi 4.
While pricing isn’t necessarily clear, it’s worth noting that HomePod mini increased in price from $99 to $129 back in June with Apple’s wave of memory-related price hikes. I personally expect pricing to stay the same, as Apple likely anticipated the upcoming hardware when it set them. Only time will tell, though.
As for release date, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reports that the second-generation HomePod mini should arrive in stores on October 30th, alongside the new Apple TV 4K . The HomeView, on the other hand, is expected to slip into mid-November. You can read more about the HomeView here .

articles.title_orig: Justice Department investigating major TV networks over suspending pool coverage of Trump
articles.title_zh: Justice Department investigating major TV networks over suspending pool coverage of Trump
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — The Justice Department said it is investigating five major TV broadcast networks for potentially violating federal antitrust laws after the networks temporarily declined to provide pool coverage of President Donald Trump, a department spokesperson said.
The investigation into the networks that make up the White House TV press pool — NBC, ABC, CBS, CNN and Fox News — is underway, and the department sent out “civil investigative demands” on Friday, according to a Justice Department official.
“Members of the television press pool have boycotted covering White House events. Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act. The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws,” department spokeswoman Emily Covington said Saturday.
The pool is a rotating group of networks that share the duties of recording the president’s activities during public appearances and travel. The network performing pool duty then distributes information and media, such as video footage and audio, to other outlets.
The New York Times first reported the investigation .
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
ABC News said it has not received any notification from the Justice Department but expects to. Representatives for NBC, CBS and CNN declined to comment. Fox did not respond to requests for comment.
The investigation appears to be the latest move from the White House in its escalating feud against the press corps.
Last month, Trump barred CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House grounds, citing what he said was “their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” The other networks in the TV pool briefly declined to participate in pool duties after CNN was removed from its spot in the rotation.
CNN, MS NOW and Politico sued to block the ban, claiming it was a violation of the First Amendment. They were reinstated about a week later after a judge ruled that the administration had to temporarily restore their access for 14 days. A federal judge this week extended the order to Tuesday.
The five major networks released a joint statement at the time, saying: “The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting.”
The pool system has been recognized by administrations from both parties for decades, and the coverage is used by pool members and subscribers, which include outlets like Newsmax, One America News Network, C-SPAN and international outlets.
During the time the outlets declined to provide pool coverage, individual TV networks, including NBC News, continued to provide coverage of White House events that were open to the press, outside of the pool.
Bruce D. Brown, president of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, said in a statement that the First Amendment protects the decisions news organizations make about coverage and called the investigation “another and even more brazen attempt to try to intimidate journalists.”
Kelly O’Donnell reported from Washington and Marlene Lenthang from Los Angeles.
Chief Justice and National Affairs Correspondent
Marlene Lenthang is a breaking news reporter for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Apple planning huge iPhone Duo demo experiences at select retail stores: report
articles.title_zh: Apple planning huge iPhone Duo demo experiences at select retail stores: report
articles.content_orig:
iPhone Duo is just about two weeks away from releasing, and according to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman , Apple has big retail plans ahead for its first foldable iPhone, to make sure every customer gets to see it to the fullest.
Apple is gearing up for a major launch with the iPhone Duo, which should be no surprise. What is a surprise though, is the amount of attention Apple is putting into making sure this launch goes as smoothly as possible.
In the newsletter , Gurman reports that the company is planning to have over a hundred demo units at some of its biggest stores:
The company is preparing a major retail push, with a huge number of demo units at its flagship stores. The Fifth Avenue location in New York City is expected to have more than 150 units across hands-on demo stations and in-store fixtures. The Apple Park Visitor Center at the company’s home base, meanwhile, will have nearly 100. Other locations, including Michigan Avenue in Chicago, the Grove in Los Angeles and the Upper West Side in Manhattan, will each have roughly 30 to 40 units.
Some of its smaller stores will only have around 20 units, which still seems bigger than usual, given the fact that there are only two colors. Given how hard it’ll be to buy a Duo at launch, allowing a lot of hands-on demos at once seems sensible.
Beyond the number of demo units, the company has also designed a new MagSafe stand that can hold an unfolded iPhone Duo, alongside two “standard” iPhones (likely iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max.) There’ll also be iPhone Duo demo units without a security tether “along the sides of stores,” so users can demo StandBy mode and other features.
Lastly, the company is planning a new fixture for some Apple Stores that showcase the iPhone Duo opening and closing, so it’s “impossible to miss” when you walk into an Apple Store.
All in all, iPhone Duo will become the forefront of Apple Stores after its launch on October 23rd. It’ll be hard to get, so if you’re interested in owning one – make sure you’re geared up to preorder it on October 16th.
