articles.title_orig: China Expands Its Presence In Peru’s Critical Electricity Infrastructure – Analysis
articles.title_zh: China Expands Its Presence In Peru’s Critical Electricity Infrastructure – Analysis
articles.content_orig:
The Chaglla hydroelectric plant in Huánuco, Peru, is part of China Three Gorges Corporation’s growing presence in the Peruvian electricity sector. The 456 MW plant is operated by Empresa de Generación Huallaga, which is affiliated with the Chinese group. (Photo: Peru’s Ministry of Energy and Mines)
State-owned China Three Gorges Corporation (CTG) expanded its presence in Peru’s electricity sector in 2026 by acquiring the remaining stake in Hydro Global Perú, a company linked to the San Gabán III hydroelectric plant in Puno. The transaction adds to the group’s other major assets in the country, including the Chaglla hydroelectric plant in the department of Huánuco and Luz del Sur, one of Peru’s leading electricity distributors.
CTG’s expansion has unfolded over several years. In 2019, the company completed its acquisition of Chaglla, a 456-megawatt (MW) facility and Peru’s third-largest hydroelectric plant. Chinese state-owned companies subsequently expanded their presence into other segments of Peru’s electricity market, including power distribution in Lima and Callao.
“In recent years, South American governments have shown great interest in developing international partnerships to better develop their energy resources and improve the reliability of their power grids,” Peruvian analyst Pedro Yaranga told Diálogo . “China took advantage of that opening to become the leading investor and lender in Latin America and the Caribbean’s energy sector.”
More than 80 power generation companies, 21 transmission companies, and 23 distribution companies operate in Peru. The two largest distributors are Pluz Energía, controlled by China Southern Power Grid International , and Luz del Sur, owned by China Three Gorges Corporation. Together, they serve nearly 3 million customers and account for one-third of the national electricity distribution market, according to Dialogue Earth .
Yaranga distinguishes between two areas of that presence. “Chinese investments in South American energy infrastructure span two distinct sectors: generation and distribution,” he said. Generation produces electricity at hydroelectric, thermal, wind, or solar facilities; transmission carries electricity at high voltage across the power system, while distribution ultimately delivers it to homes, businesses, and public facilities.
China’s footprint extends beyond the electricity sector. Writing in the Argentine newspaper La Nación , international relations specialist Patricio Carmody said China has invested in Peru’s mining — including copper and iron — infrastructure, and energy sectors. According to Carmody, Chinese investments total $30 billion, equivalent to 25 percent of foreign direct investment. The deep-water Port of Chancay , operated by Chinese company COSCO, provides a direct maritime route to Shanghai and also aims to establish itself as an export gateway for Brazil. Combined with the presence of Chinese state-owned companies in electricity distribution in Lima and Callao, these investments have raised concerns about growing dependence, Carmody said.
That expansion could continue. Peru’s Ministry of Energy and Mines estimates the country’s hydroelectric potential at approximately 70,000 MW, its largest renewable energy resource alongside wind, geothermal, and solar resources. About 8 percent of that potential is currently being harnessed, while projects under development represent another 4 percent.
Peru is not alone. In Chile, state-owned State Grid Corporation of China controls Compañía General de Electricidad (CGE) and Chilquinta Energía, two of the country’s leading electricity distributors. Through those acquisitions, the company accounts for approximately 57 percent of customers in Chile’s electricity distribution market . In Brazil, State Grid Corporation of China has also expanded its presence in transmission infrastructure, including an extensive direct-current transmission line designed to carry renewable energy from the northeast to the country’s main consumption centers.
In Ecuador, the Coca Codo Sinclair hydroelectric plant, built by Chinese company Sinohydro, a subsidiary of state-owned PowerChina , has faced years of technical problems and controversies related to its construction. In August 2026, an Ecuadorian court convicted 20 people of bribery in a scheme involving illicit payments tied to the awarding and execution of the project.
China’s economic expansion also comes with a central diplomatic condition from Beijing: Countries that establish official relations with the People’s Republic of China must end diplomatic recognition of Taiwan. Honduras established diplomatic relations with Beijing in March 2023, while Nicaragua did so in December 2021. Chinese companies have subsequently participated in infrastructure and energy projects in both countries, including hydroelectric and solar projects.
The scale of these investments is redefining Beijing’s role in the hemisphere. “China is no longer merely a buyer of raw materials; it is becoming deeply embedded in key sectors across the region, including lithium, copper, ports, telecommunications, artificial intelligence, mining, energy, digital surveillance, and electric mobility,” Yaranga said.
In early September, Chinese Ambassador to Peru Song Yang met with business leaders in the Pacific coastal department of La Libertad and representatives of Chinese companies to explore new opportunities in energy, technology, trade, infrastructure, and logistics. During the meeting, Pluz Energía representatives highlighted the need to expand electricity infrastructure to support industrialization and proposed electrifying freight transportation to the Port of Chancay. COSCO Shipping representatives also explored logistics and commercial opportunities with companies in the region.
The growing presence of Chinese companies in strategic sectors raises challenges that go beyond commercial competition. Those concerns are not limited to state-owned companies: China’s legal framework also requires private companies and other organizations to cooperate with authorities on national security and intelligence matters. That relationship takes on particular significance in sectors such as energy, where operations depend on digital systems, communications, and data .
In Peru, the Supervisory Agency for Investment in Energy and Mining (Osinergmin) and the National Institute for the Defense of Competition and Protection of Intellectual Property (Indecopi) retain regulatory oversight of the sector. “It is essential to remain vigilant about the control Chinese companies exercise over critical infrastructure, such as electricity distribution, which could compromise energy sovereignty,” Yaranga said. He called for robust laws to protect strategic assets and prevent monopolies imposed by Beijing.
With only 8 percent of Peru’s hydroelectric potential currently being harnessed, considerable room remains for new investment. Strengthening oversight, diversifying sources of investment, and preventing greater dependence on Chinese companies will be key to preserving Peruvian control over infrastructure essential to the country’s security and development.

articles.title_orig: ‘Not Pleasant’ but ‘Necessary’: Support at Trump Rally for Public Execution
articles.title_zh: ‘Not Pleasant’ but ‘Necessary’: Support at Trump Rally for Public Execution
articles.content_orig:
US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth’s plan to livestream the December 3 firing-squad execution of Nidal Hasan has drawn objections from the UN, Republican and Democratic lawmakers, and the US Conference of Catholic Bishops, while the Trump administration has not made a final decision on the broadcast.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers and wounded 32 others at the Fort Hood military base in 2009. A Defense Department official announced that his execution would be livestreamed.
“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth told podcaster Jack Posobiec aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln on Wednesday.
Hegseth separately told Real America's Voice that Hasan was "gonna get a firing squad of soldiers - as it should be.” Asked about any final requests from Hasan or contact with US President Donald Trump, Hegseth said: "Don't care. We'll see him on December 3rd."
The UN human rights office told AFP that livestreaming the execution would be "tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture.”
A Pentagon spokesperson said Monday that Trump had approved Hegseth’s recommendation. Trump said Friday that Hasan deserved execution by firing squad but did not address livestreaming at the time. Speaking to reporters Friday evening, he said the administration would decide on the broadcast.
Vice President JD Vance also questioned whether it would happen, saying, “I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen.” He said he would not watch .
The last public US execution was Rainey Bethea’s 1936 hanging. Hasan’s execution would be the US Army’s first execution of a soldier since World War II and the first death penalty imposed on an armed service member in 65 years.
Of the more than 2,700 executions recorded in 17 countries last year, public executions occurred in just two. Amnesty International documented 11 such executions in Iran in 2025 and six in Afghanistan.
Republican lawmakers joined the criticism. Outgoing Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina said public executions belong to “oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan,” while Georgia GOP Rep. Austin Scott said “live-streaming executions is what jihadists do. America is better than that.”
Republican Sen. John Curtis warned against turning executions into “bloody spectacles,” while Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut called the proposal “disgusting” and “medieval.”
The president of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops called the plan a “barbaric promotion of a culture of death.”

articles.title_orig: What to Know About Isaias, the First Atlantic Hurricane of the Season

articles.content_orig:
Pensacola, Florida, was among the areas hardest hit by Hurricane Isaias, as the FOX Flight Team surveyed widespread damage from above.
PENSACOLA, Florida – The most dangerous Gulf Coast impacts from Hurricane Isaias have passed, but the deadly storm continues to spread heavy rain, damaging winds and flooding inland after making landfall along Florida’s Gulf Coast Friday night.
From the U.S. Gulf Coast to the East Coast, Isaias has already carved a destructive path with damaging winds, torrential rain, life-threatening storm surge and a tropical tornado threat, in total resulting in the deaths of least four people and injuring others.
WHAT'S THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN A HURRICANE MAKING A DIRECT HIT AND LANDFALL?
In an aerial view, an apartment complex is seen after the roof was blown off when Hurricane Isaias passed through the area on October 10, 2026, in Milton, Florida. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

In an aerial view, trees litter the street and tops of homes after Hurricane Isaias passed through the area on October 10, 2026, in Milton, Florida. Hurricane Isaias made landfall as the season's first Atlantic hurricane with category two winds. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)
Items are tossed off the shelves of the Milton Quick Stop after Hurricane Isaias tore off the roof when it passed through the area on October 10, 2026, in Milton, Florida. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)
A boat is seen on the road in Navarre, Florida, on October 10, 2026. (RONALDO SCHEMIDT / AFP via Getty Images)
Storm damage is seen at a gas station in Gulf Breeze, Florida, on October 10, 2026. (RONALDO SCHEMIDT / AFP via Getty Images)
An overturned boat is seen in Tiger Point, Florida, on October 10, 2026. (RONALDO SCHEMIDT / AFP via Getty Images)
An overturned truck is seen in a flooded parking lot in Tiger Point, Florida, on October 10, 2026. (RONALDO SCHEMIDT / AFP via Getty Images)
Isaias is now a post-tropical cyclone after losing its tropical characteristics and is no longer fueled primarily by warm ocean waters as it moves inland toward Tennessee .
TROPICAL STORM RACHEL FUELS MAJOR WEST COAST FLOOD THREAT WITH MONTHS OF RAIN POSSIBLE IN HOURS
The storm continued to produce heavy rain across Alabama and Georgia , while a dangerous tornado threat lingered across parts of the Florida Panhandle, Georgia and South Carolina , spawning numerous confirmed tornadoes on Saturday.
A confirmed tornado touched down near Allendale, South Carolina, as outer bands from Hurricane Isaias fuel a heightened tropical tornado threat. FOX Weather Exclusive Storm Tracker Brandon Copic is on scene tracking the twister as the severe thunderstorms erupt across parts of the Southeast.
Hurricane Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida , Friday night as a Category 2 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 105 mph and a minimum pressure of 971 millibars, according to the FOX Forecast Cente r.
Isaias made landfall at approximately 9:30 p.m. ET — just one hour shy of two years since Hurricane Milton’s Gulf Coast landfall near the same time on Oct. 9, 2024.
Isaias marked the first Gulf Coast hurricane landfall since Milton, and the first hurricane of the Atlantic Basin season.
The storm’s rapid evolution began Saturday night, when the National Hurricane Center identified an area to watch with a 20% chance of development. By Monday, the system had become Invest 92L, with development odds rising to 80%.
Pensacola, Florida, was among the areas hardest hit by Hurricane Isaias, as the FOX Flight Team surveyed widespread damage from above.
Tropical Depression Nine formed Tuesday evening, followed by Tropical Storm Isaias early Wednesday.
After Hurricane Hunter reconnaissance found 75 mph winds and a pressure of 982 millibars, Isaias strengthened into a hurricane late Wednesday night. By Thursday evening, it had become a Category 2 hurricane with winds of 105 mph.
HURRICANE SEASON 2026: THESE ARE THE STORM NAMES YOU'LL SEE THIS SEASON
Isaias briefly intensified into a Category 3 major hurricane Friday morning with winds of 120 mph, building upon the thousands of evacuations for Gulf Coast communities in Florida to Alabama ahead of the storm's arrival.
Hurricane Isaias on Thursday afternoon.
The storm weakened back to Category 2 strength Friday evening while approaching the Florida coast before making landfall near Destin with winds of 105 mph.
In the hours before landfall, Isaias unleashed a devastating barrage of hurricane-force winds, torrential rain, storm surge and tornadoes across the Gulf Coast, hammering communities across Florida and Alabama before moving inland, where dangerous threats still unfolding.
The powerful storm turned deadly across Florida and Alabama, where falling trees and a generator-related carbon monoxide incident claimed four lives as Isaias battered the Southeast Friday night into Saturday.
A woman in Florida and another person in Birmingham, Alabama , were killed in separate incidents when trees fell onto their homes during the storm.
At least one person has died as result of Post-Tropical Storm Isaias. FOX News Multimedia Reporter Asher Redd confirmed a tree fell on a home in East Birmingham, Alabama, killing one. He brings us the latest as conditions worsen from the storm's impacts.
In Florida, one man was found dead inside a garage following an incident involving a power generator, while four others inside the home were treated for carbon monoxide poisoning.
The group had been running a generator indoors without proper ventilation, Escambia County Sheriff's Office said.
7 FACTS TO KNOW ABOUT HURRICANES

Alabama officials also confirmed a second storm-related death in the state, though additional details were not immediately available.
EL NIÑO SURGES TOWARD 'MONSTER' TERRITORY, SIGNALING AN ACTIVE WINTER FOR EAST AND WEST COASTS
In an aerial view, a worker with Southern Land Services removes a tree that landed on a home when Hurricane Isaias passed through the area on October 10, 2026, in Milton, Florida.
(oe Raedle/Getty Images / Getty Images)
Panama City Beach recorded its second-highest storm surge on record, with water rising 5.60 feet above the average high tide, according to the FOX Forecast Center.
The record was set during Hurricane Opal on Oct. 4, 1995. Hurricane Michael produced a 3.86-foot surge on Oct. 10, 2018, which ranked fifth.
Hurricane force winds are hammering Destin, Florida, where FOX Weather Senior Field Correspondent Robert Ray is braving the blast fueled by the dangerous Category 3 Hurricane Isaias forecast to make landfall in just a few hours.
Power outages continued across the Southeast as Isaias moved inland, with over one million Americans in the dark at the storm's peak.
As of 10 p.m. ET Saturday, more than 450,000 customers were without power in the Southeast.

articles.title_orig: Pope criticizes death penalty after Hegseth announces public execution
articles.title_zh: Pope criticizes death penalty after Hegseth announces public execution
articles.content_orig:
ROME — Pope Leo XIV on Saturday declared capital punishment “inadmissible” as he marked the World Day Against the Death Penalty and his native United States announced plans to livestream an execution by firing squad.
In a post on X, the American pope quoted the revised Catholic teaching on capital punishment ushered in by Pope Francis that the death penalty attacks the inherent dignity of a human being.
“The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment,” read the post under Leo’s official handle, @Pontifex. “Effective systems of detention have been developed that protect citizens while at the same time do not completely deprive those who are guilty of the possibility of redemption.”
The post ended with the hashtag #NoDeathPenalty.
The U.S. Defense Department announced Thursday that the firing squad execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, convicted of a 2009 shooting at the Fort Hood military base, will be livestreamed. Hasan, scheduled to be executed at Fort Hood on Dec. 3, was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding 32 others.
Why Hegseth's decision to livestream execution is raising questions
Leo didn’t refer specifically to the planned execution, or the botched lethal injection in Tennessee last week that has revived debate over the death penalty in the United States. Saturday is World Day Against the Death Penalty, and it is common for the pope’s official social media accounts to post messages marking such commemorations.
But Leo’s post came just hours after his top deputy, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, said explicitly that the planned U.S. public execution was “unacceptable.”
Pope Francis in 2018 amended official Catholic teaching to declare capital punishment “inadmissible” in all circumstances.
Previously, the Catechism of the Catholic Church, the official compendium of church teaching, said the church didn’t exclude recourse to capital punishment “if this is the only possible way of effectively defending human lives against the unjust aggressor.”
Past popes had upheld that position, though St. John Paul II began urging an end to the practice and stressed that guilty people were just as deserving of dignity as innocent ones.
Like Francis before him, Leo has made visiting prisons a key part of his papal travel in a bid to give a message of hope to inmates and underscore their inherent dignity, that God loves them and that there is always a chance for redemption.
“If any of you fear being abandoned by everyone, know that God will never abandon you, and that the church will stand by your side,” Leo told inmates at the notorious Bata prison in Equatorial Guinea during his visit in April. Leo is to visit a prison in Buenos Aires during his upcoming tour through Latin America.
Pope Leo asked if he helped with historic White Sox turnaround
Speaking specifically about the United States, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, said the planned livestreamed execution was “truly incomprehensible” and “unacceptable to turn death into a spectacle.”
“The Church’s position is one of total opposition to the death penalty; it is incompatible with human dignity and serves as no deterrent—,” Parolin said in comments carried by Vatican News. “It is truly incomprehensible that anyone would want to use this system today — I don’t know for what purpose. It is certainly unacceptable to turn death into a spectacle; even if the person is guilty, of course, there are other methods.”
The head of the U.S. bishops conference, Archbishop Paul Coakley, expressed “shock” and “great sorrow” at the Pentagon’s plans.
“In no way can Hasan’s actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered,” he said in a statement Friday. “The public execution even of one who has done grave harm will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people.”

articles.title_orig: Storm Isaias leaves 4 dead, thousands without power as it moves across southern US
articles.title_zh: Storm Isaias leaves 4 dead, thousands without power as it moves across southern US
articles.content_orig:
Storm Isaias has left four people dead as it moves across the southern United States , officials said Saturday.
Two of the deaths were in Florida, while the other two were in Alabama.
The storm originally made landfall on Friday evening as a Category 2 hurricane near Destin, Florida. It is the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season.
Florida, Alabama and Georgia have all declared states of emergency due to the storm. According to PowerOutage.com, over 500,000 customers are without power in Florida and Alabama.
The Florida Division of Emergency Management said approximately 5,000 Florida National Guard soldiers and airmen have been "activated to support impacted communities."
The storm brings heavy rainfall and powerfall winds, bringing the risks of flooding and tornadoes. It has ripped the roofs off buildings and downed trees in its wake.
The storm has weakened into a post-tropical cyclone and is moving over the southern US states of Tennessee and Kentucky into West Virginia, according to the National Hurricane Center (NHC).
In its latest update, the NHC warned of possible flash and urban flooding and said "landslides are possible across the Southern Appalachians." It also warned of wind gusts along with additional power outages and downed trees.
In addition, swells from Isaias will continue to impact much of the Gulf coasts of the US, Mexico and western Cuba, and are "likely to cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions." NHC said a couple of tornadoes are also possible across eastern Georgia and the Carolinas.
Meanwhile, Hurricane Simon has hit Category 4 strength as it barrels towards Mexico's Pacific coast, where it is expected to make landfall on Sunday. The storm is expected to impact Puerto Vallarta, a popular destination for American tourists.

articles.title_orig: It's 'probably not plausible' that a strong economy can steady U.S. debt as 5%-6% growth is needed
articles.title_zh: It's 'probably not plausible' that a strong economy can steady U.S. debt as 5%-6% growth is needed
articles.content_orig:
Congressional Budget Office Director Phillip Swagel said faster economic growth is unlikely to keep U.S. debt in check, even if GDP expands at more than double its current pace.
Gross debt is now $40 trillion, and publicly held debt is 100% of GDP. Just keeping that ratio flat, let alone bringing it down, would require a massive, sustained boom. For now, CBO see the debt-to-GDP ratio soaring to 120% by 2036.
During a Minneapolis Fed conference on Thursday, Swagel said stronger economic growth will help by bringing in more revenue for the federal government, but it’s not that simple.
Federal spending also boosts growth, which lifts wages that in turn affect outlays on Social Security benefits, he pointed out. A robust economy also tends to send interest rates higher, which adds to debt interest costs.
“So growth will help, but it’s probably not plausible that growth alone will stabilize our fiscal trajectory,” Swagel added. “So then we’re left with changes in revenues and changes in spending, and those are inherently political choices.”
Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari asked if AI can help supercharge economic growth, and he replied that CBO has detected an increase in total factor productivity, which measures the efficiency of labor, capital, and other inputs.
The CBO’s next batch of economic forecasts due early next year will incorporate its views on AI, Swagel said, adding that future growth will be stronger. Still, the budget deficit is so deep that even the extra AI-powered growth won’t be enough, he warned.
Kashkari then asked how much faster growth would have to be in order to stabilize the debt. Swagel cautioned against doing arithmetic on the fly but offered some back-of-the-envelope numbers.
Assuming interest rates of 4%-5%, he estimated that nominal GDP growth would have to reach 7%-8% and real GDP growth would have to hit 5%-6%.
That’s more than double the latest real GDP pace of 2.2% in the second quarter. Meanwhile, even bullish Wall Street forecasts put full-year GDP growth at 2.5%.
The rough numbers from the CBO chief also far exceed what Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said would be needed to overcome the debt.
“With 3% growth, we grow our way out of this,” he said at Southern Methodist University last month. “We’ll get to the other side of this Iran conflict, and the underlying economy is very, very strong, and I think reaccelerating.”
Meanwhile, other estimates fall somewhere in between. According to the Penn Wharton Budget Model, growth would have to average 3.5%-4% over a decade to maintain the debt-to-GDP ratio.
Swagel also noted that an economic shock that sends interest rates up suddenly would set off a vicious fiscal cycle.
“So there’s almost like a turbocharger,” he explained. “An interest rate shock feeds into the deficit, feeds into the debt, feeds back into interest rates.”
So far, the bond market is absorbing all the debt the U.S. Treasury is issuing to fund the budget deficit, but long-term yields have surged to the highest levels in 24 years.
Some of that is due to the strong economy, expectations for Fed rate hikes, high oil prices keeping inflation high, and the flood of AI hyperscaler debt competing for bond market demand.
But the enormous scale of U.S. debt is also a factor. Swagel said it’s small now, with a 1-percentage-point increase in the debt ratio leading to a 0.015-percentage-point hike on long-term interest rates.
“So it’s modest, but the fiscal trajectory is really quite challenging,” he added. “It adds up, and of course there’s that turbocharger type effect that I mentioned where it feeds back into deficits.”
Jason Ma is the weekend editor at Fortune , where he covers markets, the economy, finance, and housing.

articles.title_orig: Tropical Storm Rachel's surf drives out Long Beach residents, briefly shuts Newport Beach beaches
articles.title_zh: Tropical Storm Rachel's surf drives out Long Beach residents, briefly shuts Newport Beach beaches
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
A coastal flood warning covered beaches from Malibu to San Diego on Saturday as Tropical Storm Rachel moved toward Southern California, while Long Beach kept some oceanfront residents under an evacuation order, and Newport Beach closed piers and temporarily shuttered beaches before a reopening.
“There is growing confidence that the expected coastal flooding impacts on Sunday morning for vulnerable south-facing beaches of LA County could be the most significant we have seen so far this season, including those seen with Marie,” the National Weather Service’s Oxnard office said Saturday.
Its San Diego office said Sunday morning would carry the highest flooding risks along the Orange and San Diego coasts as swells, onshore winds and high tides combine.
The center of Rachel was expected to move onshore in northern Baja California on Saturday night, the National Hurricane Center said.
Those warnings remained in effect even as Rachel’s forecast track shifted farther south, leaving most of San Diego County outside its projected path, said Adam Roser, lead meteorologist at the National Weather Service in San Diego. “Even though the track has shifted a little farther to the south, we’re still expecting wind impacts,” Roser said during a briefing.
A tropical storm watch remained in effect for all of San Diego County, the weather service said.
Long Beach’s mandatory order covers homes on Seaside Walk between 64th and 66th places. It took effect at 7 p.m. Friday and runs through noon Tuesday, city officials said. A commercial crane is scheduled to drop sandbags on 65th Place and westward in front of addresses between 65th and 64th, city officials said.
“The return date is subject to change based on evolving conditions,” a city announcement said.
Waves topped the bulkhead and sent water into homes and streets, according to city officials. Inspectors red-tagged eight buildings across 13 addresses, including apartments, and yellow-tagged at least one, Mayor Rex Richardson said Saturday. A red tag marks a building as unsafe to enter, and a yellow tag restricts its use.
The city closed the Peninsula to nonresident traffic, with more street closures starting at 62nd Place.
Richardson urged residents to “take this seriously and be prepared.” Todd Leland, a manager in the Long Beach Parks, Recreation and Marine Department, said the city’s bulkhead and pedestrian boardwalk had already sustained significant structural damage.
Workers are bracing damaged sections with timber and thousands of sandbags to stabilize the compromised areas and prevent collapse.
“Prepare right now for the impacts,” Richardson said. “Our infrastructure was not built for this.”
Long Beach City Manager Tom Modica said that he expected a lengthy recovery. “We will be asking for assistance from the governor, and potentially also from the federal government,” Modica said. “We don’t think this is just going to be this weekend. This is going to be the entire next couple of months.”
Water at the Los Angeles Harbor tide gauge peaked at 7.7 feet Saturday morning, about 1.6 feet above the predicted tide, the National Weather Service said. “The projected high tides of around 8 feet for Sunday morning would approach or exceed recent record tide levels for L.A. County,” it said.
In Newport Beach, police posted an alert online Saturday morning saying flooding closed all city beaches and piers until further notice.
“Stay away from these areas,” police said. The announcement followed Newport Beach declaring a local emergency Friday after overnight flooding on the Balboa Peninsula.
By early afternoon, police said the beaches were open, but Newport Pier, Balboa Pier and the Wedge, from the rock jetty to M Street, remained closed.
In a video uploaded to the city’s Instagram account, an official asked people to stay off the berms. The man said the flooding would continue over the next couple of days. “We want the public to be safe during this time. We will get through this,” his post said.
The weather service expects more coastal flooding Sunday, when high tide at Newport Beach is forecast to reach 7.6 feet at 9:48 a.m. “Low-lying property including homes, businesses, and some critical infrastructure may flood,” the agency’s San Diego office said. Surf could reach 6 to 9 feet, highest at south-facing beaches, especially in Orange County, Roser said.
Joe Angelo has lived in the Newport Beach area for 60 years and bought his beachfront home 27 years ago. He said the flooding left him in “shock and disbelief.”
“I haven’t seen one drop of water on that sand in 27 years. All the sand, not one drop of water,” Angelo said. “We all love living on this oceanfront. But, boy, it makes you think twice.”
Sandbags lined dozens of homes and businesses near Balboa Boulevard on Saturday morning. Beachgoers strolled with coffee in hand, went for morning runs and walked their dogs. Despite the warnings, many climbed sand berms to watch the waves. Some did backflips off the sand.
Chris Perkins of Orange County brought his son Connor to see the surf. “I grew up around the ocean, and [I’m] just trying to expose my kid to the gnarly waves, and show him how to be safe and how to do it the right way,” Perkins said.
In Long Beach, cars lined up Saturday at a Peninsula parking lot as fire department workers loaded sandbags into trunks. Light rain began falling shortly before noon.
Monica Shephard, who lives in a beachfront apartment complex, said she was worried, noting that ocean water reached her doorstep three years ago. She planned to pick up sandbags for her complex Saturday night and praised the city’s precautions. “They’re doing a great job,” she said.
Huntington Beach also activated its emergency operations center Friday, the city said. Many spectators watched pounding waves there at high tide Saturday morning. Cyclists, walkers and runners packed the white concrete trail along Bolsa Chica State Beach. A section that flooded Friday appeared to escape more trouble Saturday, despite signs that said “flooded.”
The heaviest rain is expected late Saturday night into Sunday morning, Roser said. Most coastal areas could get about an inch or a little less. Some mountain areas could get more than four inches.
Many areas west of the mountains will stay in the 60s on Monday, and Big Bear may only reach the 40s, Roser said. Temperatures should warm by the end of the week, he said.
Inland, southern San Bernardino County faces at least a 40% chance of excessive rain that could result in flash flooding through Saturday night, said Julie Phillipson, lead meteorologist at the National Weather Service in Las Vegas. “Our primary concern is still the heavy rains and the flooding that can occur.”
Deputy Managing Editor Shelby Grad contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: WHO says no plague case registered after Russian lab worker’s death
articles.title_zh: WHO says no plague case registered after Russian lab worker’s death
articles.content_orig:
The World Health Organization (WHO) has said it still does not know what caused the pneumonia that killed a laboratory worker at a Russian plague research institute and that no case of plague has been registered.
Russia’s state health regulator told the WHO that tests on the worker and people who had been in contact with her were negative for the dangerous pathogens they tested for, the United Nations health agency said in a statement on Saturday.
Her contacts still showed no symptoms, and no further linked cases of severe pneumonia had been found, the WHO added.
“Based on the information provided… WHO has not identified evidence of ongoing transmission associated with this event. A key uncertainty remains the absence of a confirmed diagnosis in the deceased laboratory worker,” it said.
The worker fell ill and died in undisclosed circumstances on October 2, prompting authorities to quarantine about 200 people and stoking public health fears on social media.
Russian media named her as Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old laboratory technician at the Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, in the Siberian region of Irkutsk.
Pneumonic plague, a lung infection caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, which is usually found in small mammals and their fleas, was suspected early on.
The governor of neighbouring Buryatia said the woman had “died, maybe of the plague”.
Russia’s health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor said she had been diagnosed with “pneumonia of unknown aetiology”.
Russian authorities said the worker was appropriately vaccinated and that no microorganisms linked to her work were found in her body. They say post-mortem tests did not detect plague.
On Thursday, Russia said it had completed health checks on all her contacts and had given the WHO all the information.
A local official said on October 6 that 60 percent of those placed in quarantine had already been released.
WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus asked Russia on Wednesday to respond to media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause. Russia dismissed the reports as “false information”.
The United States has also called on Russia for transparency.
Global health officials have been extra alert to deadly pneumonia cases of unknown cause since the COVID-19 pandemic, which began with a cluster of fast-spreading, fatal respiratory illness in China.
The cause of individual pneumonia cases often cannot be determined.

articles.title_orig: Police officer dies after West Philadelphia shooting; another injured with 12 gunshot wounds
articles.title_zh: Police officer dies after West Philadelphia shooting; another injured with 12 gunshot wounds
articles.content_orig:
Video taken in cities including Paris, Lyon and Strasbourg showed demonstrators facing off with police, lighting fires and dodging tear gas. France’s interior ministry said over 6,000 people had been taken into custody.
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu defended the police response to student protests after one teenager lost a hand in an incident involving a police grenade and another lost sight in one eye after being struck by a projectile.
In parliament on Tuesday, Lecornu pushed back on accusations of police brutality or state repression, adding that the term "police brutality" implies that officers had been instructed to use force, according to Politico.
"What triggers police action is the occurrence of urban violence," Lecornu said.
"Can accidents happen? The answer is yes," he added.
FRANCE EXPLODES AGAIN AS STUDENTS RIOT OVER EDUCATION
French riot police stand near burning objects during clashes with protesters in Paris on Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026. (Reuters)
Lecornu and Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez have both argued that the police response was sparked by urban violence, arson and vandalism, while maintaining that officers have acted within their authority. Nuñez also called the police response proportionate in "almost all cases."
The prime minister also accused opposition party France Unbowed of exploiting the student protests to sow chaos and score political points ahead of next year’s presidential election.
President Emmanuel Macron convened an emergency meeting with senior ministers to address the nationwide student protests and their potential political fallout.
The French government is facing mounting pressure after more than 6,500 people were arrested and hundreds were injured as students demand better funding and learning conditions in schools. Most of those arrested were minors, according to The Associated Press.
Riot police use a water cannon as they face students during a protest against under-resourced schools in Rennes, western France, on Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026. (Jeremias Gonzalez/AP)
Lecornu said 215 students and 85 school staff members had been injured since the protests began, while his office said 715 police officers had also been injured.
"I hope we can provide a political response to a very real anxiety among high school students," Lecornu acknowledged.
As Lecornu delivered his remarks on Tuesday, demonstrators from several French unions and teachers’ groups gathered with high school and university students. Members of France’s left-wing parties were also at the protest, according to Politico.
The Interior Ministry estimated that 266,000 people took part in demonstrations nationwide Tuesday, including 56,000 in Paris.
The Paris demonstration was largely peaceful, although smaller groups later clashed with riot police, according to The Associated Press.
The protesters' movement began at high schools in the Paris region in mid-September before spreading nationwide.
TEEN'S HAND BLOWN OFF BY POLICE GRENADE DURING FRENCH STUDENT PROTESTS: REPORT
French riot police officers remove elements of a burning street barricade during a demonstration by French high school and university students in Lyon on Oct. 6, 2026. (Reuters)

On Monday, a 15-year-old boy in northern France lost a hand after a police grenade exploded during the protests, Politico reported. A prosecutor said he could not "say for certain whether the student picked up the grenade or whether it was thrown at him."
In the city of Tours, a 16-year-old lost sight in one eye after being hit by a projectile, according to the outlet. The prosecutor said the projectile may have been fired from a sub-lethal riot-control weapon used by police.
Boris Vallaud, leader of the center-left Socialist group in parliament, said the group's lawmakers would introduce legislation restricting the use of sub-lethal riot-control weapons at student demonstrations, warning that they can cause irreversible injuries, the outlet reported.

articles.title_orig: 9 dead, including children, in mass shooting in Erie, Pennsylvania
articles.title_zh: 9 dead, including children, in mass shooting in Erie, Pennsylvania
articles.content_orig:
Nine people, including children and a gunman, were killed in a mass shooting in Erie, Pennsylvania, officials said.
A man killed eight people including a pregnant woman, children and other relatives at his home in Erie, Pennsylvania, before taking his own life as well, authorities said Saturday.
Police first responded to a home on Perry Street in Erie on Friday, Oct. 9, around 5 p.m., after witnesses reported seeing a gunman firing shots outside the house before entering the residence.
Stream Philadelphia News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC10.
When police arrived, they found two women who had been shot to death in the street.
The shooting escalated into a standoff as Erie Police and SWAT teams surrounded the home. More shots were then heard inside the home. When police entered, they found the bodies of seven other people, including children, as well as the gunman who died from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound, according to investigators.
Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah described the incident as one of the most difficult and heartbreaking scenes he had ever encountered.
“The loss of life is devastating and the circumstances we are working through are deeply disturbing,” Chief Lorah said. “At this time, we can confirm that the suspect is deceased. Based on the information currently available to us, there is no ongoing threat to the public. Our hearts are with the victims, their families, and everyone affected by this tragedy. There are no words that can be adequately express the magnitude of the loss of life here.”
Investigators are currently working to determine what led to the shooting.

“We will not speculate about a motive, or at least information that could compromise this investigation,” Chief Lorah said. “It's just a devastating loss of life. It's a terrible, terrible scene at this point, and we just need time to piece together what happened here.”
